d08b439a3394.text: President Trump had a candid phone call with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu Saturday about the state of U.S. negotiations with Iran and how quickly to return to combat, according to one Israeli and one U.S. source. Why it matters: The sources said Netanyahu is pressing Trump to strike Iran immediately after the midterm elections on Tuesday. But Trump, for now, wants to let negotiations play out — a strategy Netanyahu is concerned about. The Israeli source said the call was "tough," while the U.S. source described it as "direct." The White House and the Israeli prime minister's office declined to comment. Driving the news: As he did before Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025 and Operation Epic Fury in February, Trump is pursuing dual tracks — trying to reach a deal to restart peace talks while also preparing for a possible resumption of major combat operations after the midterms. Last week Vice President Vance sent a letter to Iran's national security chief Mohsen Rezaei about the possibility of restarting negotiations . It was the most senior-level outreach by the U.S. to Iran in several months. Trump told reporters on Saturday that negotiations with Iran are "going fine" and noted he is not "in much of a hurry." While the Iranians want to make a deal, the president said they "are not very reliable. ... They make a deal and then they back out." At the same time, Trump said the U.S. still has to "take care" of one or two nuclear sites in Iran. "We can do that in 10 minutes. We have that planned. You can look at Pickaxe Mountain. We need to take care of that. We can do that very quickly," Trump said, referring to a suspected nuclear site built into a mountain. The Wall Street Journal first reported the Trump-Netanyahu call, but did not describe its contents. State of play: Qatari mediators met with Iranian officials on Sunday for the third consecutive day in an effort to reach a deal to restart direct negotiations between the U.S. and Iran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Sunday that there is no agreement yet and stressed that a deal depends on the U.S. answering Iran's questions. "We are making every effort in this regard and hope that the other side will demonstrate enough rationality to choose diplomacy over other paths," he said.

5fbb6b8edab9.text:
- Published
Heavily-armed police officers have started patrolling Sydney's streets, as part of heightened security measures following last year's deadly shooting at Bondi Beach.
The Armed Response Command (ARC) will see specially trained officers in busy tourist areas carrying long-arm rifles â an unfamiliar sight for most residents.
New South Wales police say the officers will also patrol major events like sports matches and places of worship "to prevent, deter and rapidly respond to serious threats, including active armed offender incidents".
Fifteen people - including a 10-year-old girl â were killed in December when two gunmen opened fire on an event marking the Jewish festival of Hanukkah at the popular beach.
The attack was Australia's worst mass shooting in almost three decades and prompted sweeping gun law reforms and a crackdown on hate speech.
One resident told ABC news that the sight of armed police was "unnerving".
"They are just everywhere. Those guns are huge."
But another woman told the broadcaster that seeing police with weapons made her feel safe.
ARC is specifically designed to be "highly visible across Sydney, driving specialist vehicles and carrying rifles," New South Wales police said in a statement.
Its role "is built on a simple principle - preserving life," Detective Superintendent Andrew Evans said.
The shooting on 14 December put huge pressure on Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's government, with calls for immediate action on antisemitism.
Jewish communities have welcomed the new police operation, which will eventually consist of 250 officers, but others have called for safeguards to protect human rights.
"No Australian wants to see officers with military weapons on our streets, but the sight of body bags is far worse," Alex Ryvchin, co-CEO of Executive Council of Australian Jewry, said.
But Amnesty International Australia said it was concerned about the "militarisation of policing", and asked for assurances from the state government that ARC will not be used to suppress peaceful protests.
"Any expansion of police powers and capabilities must be accompanied by clear, publicly accessible rules, robust independent oversight and accountability," said the organisation's Andrew Witheford.
The New South Wales administration defended the new measures.
"Our world changed forever. That's just the truth of it, right across this country. And I said it at the time, we will never be the same again," the state's Police Minister Yasmin Catley told the ABC.
One of the alleged gunmen, Naveed Akram, has been charged with 78 offences including 15 counts of murder, 40 counts of attempted murder, and one count of committing a terrorist act.
His father, Sajid Akram, 50 - who was also armed and shot at the crowd on Bondi Beach - was killed by police at the scene.

165c3c7f264f.text: By — John Raby, Associated Press John Raby, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/dozens-injured-at-least-6-dead-in-halloween-weekend-gun-violence-at-nightlife-districts-across-u-s Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Dozens injured, at least 6 dead in Halloween weekend gun violence at nightlife districts across U.S. Nation Updated on Nov 1, 2026 2:36 PM EST — Published on Nov 1, 2026 12:49 PM EST Dozens of people were injured and at least six people died in mass shootings as gun violence broke out at nightlife districts in half a dozen cities across the country over the Halloween weekend. Police in Dallas, the site of the deadliest violence, said four people are dead and 15 others were injured following a handful of shootings in the city's Deep Ellum neighborhood, a center of music, restaurants and nightlife in the city. Police in college towns like Fayetteville, Arkansas; Birmingham, Alabama; Newark, Delaware, and Bloomington, Illinois, also reported shootings in their nightlife districts this weekend. WATCH: Two doctors offer new ideas to prevent gun violence in America Dallas Police Chief Daniel Comeaux said investigators are still trying to determine if the shootings Saturday night over the span of about an hour and 15 minutes were related. Comeaux said three separate shootings occurred, and it wasn't immediately known why they started. Comeaux said some arrests were made but he didn't specify how many or what charges were involved. "This is a really big scene. It's spread out," Comeaux said. "We are interviewing some individuals right now that we have arrested, still trying to figure out exactly how it ties into all the shootings out here." The department had increased police presence in the district before the shootings. No police officers were injured. One shooting happened after an HBCU football game In Birmingham, Alabama, one person was killed and eight others were wounded in a mass shooting just outside Legion Field after the annual 'Magic City Classic' football game on Saturday night, police said. Michael Pickett, chief of the Birmingham Police Department, said most spectators and families had left the stadium property after the game, but the shooting happened nearby, where vendors were set up along Graymont Avenue. He said he was "very grateful that more people weren't injured." The circumstances of the shooting were unclear. Police spokesperson De'Rell Freeman said one person had been detained and transported to police headquarters for questioning, and "multiple weapons" had been found and secured. WATCH: 'There's babies in there': Oregon father describes stopping school shooter Alabama State and Alabama A&M are historically Black universities and archrivals whose annual contest has been played for more than 100 years. Nearly 70,000 fans attended Saturday's game, won by Alabama A&M 31-28. The event draws some of the largest crowds in the country for games played in their college football division. The Magic City Classic has such a deep history that Alabama State coach Eddie Robinson Jr., a former NFL linebacker and alumnus of the school, proposed creating a Hall of Fame for the game. In Newark, Delaware, six people were shot late Saturday near the University of Delaware campus, Newark police Lt. Greg D'Elia said. All six were transported to hospitals for treatment, police said early Sunday. No updates on their condition were available as of Sunday afternoon. A university spokesperson said they would provide updates on the investigation online as they become available. Video shared on social media showed people running for safety from the scene. One stretch of the city's Main Street was closed for several hours after the shooting, police said. A shooting early Sunday in Bloomington, Illinois, left a 19-year-old woman dead and another woman in critical condition. Six others had injuries that were not life-threatening, but it was unclear from a statement by the city's police department and McLean County Coroner's Office if those people had gunshot wounds. The shooting happened near the campus of Illinois Wesleyan University. Bloomington is about 135 miles (217 kilometers) southwest of Chicago. Two mass shootings occurred in Arkansas A shooting early Sunday near a strip mall southwest of Little Rock, Arkansas, left one man dead and "several more" injured, city police said on Facebook. Police didn't specify the exact number of injured. And in Fayetteville, Arkansas, six people were taken to hospitals with gunshot wounds from a shooting that happened early Sunday. No arrests have been made, police said in a news release. A preliminary investigation indicates an altercation preceded the shooting. Halloween stores were the scene of two attacks On Friday, two people were killed in separate shootings at Spirit Halloween stores in California and Michigan. Police said a shooting inside a store at an indoor shopping mall in Fairfield, California was a targeted attack. Family members told police that the 31-year-old woman who died was pregnant. Six other people were wounded, police said. In Madison Heights, Michigan, just north of Detroit, a 21-year-old man was fatally shot Friday afternoon at a Spirit Halloween. Another man who was assaulted by bystanders as officers took him into custody was hospitalized with injuries that were not life-threatening, police said. Raby reported from Charleston, West Virginia. AP reporters Claudia Lauer in Philadelphia and Laura Turbay in Little Rock, Arkansas, contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Stevens endorsed Rogers after attending a Detroit church service with him. The remarkable show of support for the President Donald Trump-backed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated the congresswoman by a slim margin in the August primary. "Our Democratic nominee for Senate said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away," Stevens said in a video announcing the endorsement, which led her top aide to quit. "And he's right. And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today." Tensions between the two Democrats have festered since the primary. Stevens is a staunch supporter of Israel, while El-Sayed is a fierce critic of the U.S. ally. He has also been criticized by some in the community for past remarks regarding a Michigan synagogue attack and for appearances with controversial streamer Hasan Piker. READ MORE: Trump escalates rhetoric against El-Sayed as he tries to undermine Democrat in Michigan Senate race Democrats had hoped that Sunday would be a show of unity. Instead, Stevens swayed to gospel music alongside Rogers in the pews at Perfecting Church, while El-Sayed was a few miles away at a different house of worship campaigning alongside prominent Democrats, including South Carolina Rep. Jim Clyburn. The Associated Press attended both services as the dramatic split-screen unfolded. The latest and late-stage infighting comes as Democrats look to drive turnout among Black and Jewish voters in key strongholds. El-Sayed, a former Michigan public health official, is in a tight race with Rogers, an ex-congressman, for the seat held by Democrat Gary Peters, who is retiring. Keeping Michigan in Democratic hands is vital to the party's effort to win a majority for the final two years of Trump's second term. Stevens' team resigns as Democrats are stunned by reversal Plans for Stevens to join El-Sayed and Clyburn unraveled after a dispute over Israel and an outside group's campaign advertisement escalated into a public exchange of criticism between the rivals. After the church service north of Detroit, where Stevens and fiance Jason Turkish worshipped with Rogers and his wife, Kristi, the congresswoman told reporters, "I'm not turning my back on Democrats. It is this one vote." Rogers, standing beside her, said he was "honored" by her support. Their appearance stunned Democrats, coming days after Stevens publicly reaffirmed she would vote for the nominee, and led her longtime chief of staff to resign with a number of staff members expected to follow soon, according to a person familiar with the developments who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss internal matters. "We are shocked and heartbroken," the aide said in a statement. Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed attends a church service at Greater Emmanuel Institutional Church of God in Christ in Detroit on Nov. 1, 2026. Photo by Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP The state party chair, Curtis Hertel, said Stevens' endorsement "shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about." "We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these eleventh-hour distractions deter us," Hertel wrote. Among the Democrats who joined El-Sayed at church were U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell of Michigan, U.S. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland and state Sen. Mallory McMorrow, who dropped out of the Senate primary before voting began. El-Sayed spoke for nearly 10 minutes at the service. He did not address the latest controversy. "It's in churches like this, in pews like the ones in which you sit, that the foundation of my life was built," El-Sayed said. Dingell says she disinvited Stevens after it became 'distracting' Dingell, a senior Democratic figure in the state who helped organize the planned joint appearance in hopes of bringing together Democrats in the final days before Tuesday's vote, said she asked Stevens not to attend and that Stevens told her she would abide by that. "I'm the one who pulled it because it had become way too distracting," Dingell said in a telephone interview before Stevens appeared with Rogers. "This is not how I was going to spend my weekend before the election, to be perfectly frank." Early voting has been underway since Oct. 24, before the latest tensions resurfaced, complicating efforts to deliver a unified closing message in crucial areas such as Detroit, where turnout could prove decisive. Lindsay Clancy, the US woman accused of murdering her three children, will return to a Massachusetts court on Monday as lawyers debate retrying the case.
Her defence team and Massachusetts prosecutors are expected to discuss how to move forward, with both parties seeking different outcomes.
Last week, in response to a defence request to dismiss the trial, prosecutors offered their clearest hint yet that they are seeking a new trial before a different jury. "The Commonwealth [Massachusetts] should be permitted to continue to pursue justice for Cora, Dawson and Callan Clancy," her three children, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors could also reduce the charges in a potential second trial or dismiss them altogether.
Clancy's first trial ended in a mistrial after a 12-person jury failed to reach a consensus.
The 36-year-old has not denied killing her children in 2023, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors say the killings were intentional.
What happened when Clancy was last in court?
A jury first heard Clancy's case in August 2026, but failed to reach a unanimous agreement on whether the prosecution had proved Clancy was guilty "beyond a reasonable doubt" as required by US law.
A judge declared a mistrial in early September.
At a court appearance later that month, Clancy's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, argued the judge should dismiss her case. Meanwhile, prosecutors said the state had "met its burden" in proving her guilt.
But the hours-long back-and-forth ultimately didn't lead to a clearer answer about what might come next for Clancy - a dismissal of charges, retrial of the same charges, or retrial of lesser charges. These discussions will resume on Monday.
Judge William Sullivan seemed confident the case would be retried, saying in September he wanted to "get this thing moving".
He asked both sides to prepare to discuss possible trial dates at the November hearing.
Reddington said he would be unable to go to trial until at least June 2027 if the case was retried.
District Attorney Timothy Cruz said at the time that prosecutors had not yet decided whether to retry Clancy.
"We're doing our due diligence; we're going to continue doing that," he said. "We're going to do what we can for the children. That's what this case is about."
What do Clancy's legal team want?
Fundamentally, Clancy's legal team - with Reddington at the helm - is pushing for the charges to be dismissed or dropped. They've explored a variety of legal avenues.
In September, he asked for her to be found not guilty under Rule 25 - a Massachusetts provision that states a defendant should be found not guilty if prosecutors do not present enough evidence at trial.
That request was denied.
Judge Sullivan will hear arguments on several motions on Monday, but Heather Cucolo, a New York Law School professor and mental health law expert, told the BBC that the hearing will likely focus on a narrow point: was this an instance of a routine deadlocked-jury mistrial - in which the jury genuinely could not agree - or was this an improperly terminated trial?
She said Reddington may argue that a retrial could violate Clancy's Constitutional protection against double jeopardy - a legal standard that says a person cannot be tried for the same crime twice.
But legal experts agree that outcome is unlikely.
"The public attention that's been put on this trial and the need to have some conclusion in the near future, I think that the judge is going to say that this mistrial was appropriate, was legally accurate, and that they need to now look to set a date for a retrial," Cucolo said.
What do prosecutors want?
While the state's legal team has not explicitly said they will pursue a retrial, Cruz and the prosecutors who argued the case have consistently said they want justice for Clancy's children.
Last week, prosecutors asked Judge Sullivan to reject the motion to dismiss charges against Clancy on the grounds of double jeopardy.
They argue mistrial procedures were properly followed by the court, and thus they have a right to seek justice again on behalf of the children.
"Because a mistrial was properly declared due to the manifest necessity of a deadlocked jury, the defendant's motion to dismiss should be denied," prosecutors wrote in the motion.
What could happen on 2 November?
Judge Sullivan could make a determination over whether the case can proceed on Monday or he could rule later in writing, criminal defence lawyer Elyse Hershon told the BBC.
And how the District Attorney's office wants to proceed could be determined ahead of Monday's hearing, during it or even days after, she said.
"The three charges of first-degree murder are still pending; they are still hanging over Lindsay Clancy's head unless and until the DA announces otherwise," Hershon said.
Historically, Cruz, the district attorney, has made comments and announcements about the case at press conferences after court finishes. That could happen again this week, she predicted.
It is also likely, Hershon said, that Judge Sullivan pushes the lawyers on both sides to get a trial date on the calendar during Monday's hearing.
"It does not mean it's definitely going to be a jury trial, but [they will want to] put something in the books, hold those dates. It's a big chunk of time. It's four, five, six weeks of the court calendar; that's hard to fit in at the last minute," she said.
"I would anticipate they block off the time while they go through all these motions and the DA's office figures out what it wants to do."

Israeli strikes in Gaza have killed at least eight people, including a child, according to hospitals, despite a year-old ceasefire.
In Gaza City to the north, hospital officials said a missile attack hit a group of civilians next to Cairo School in the Al-Rimal neighbourhood, killing three people, including a four-year-old boy.
In the southern city of Khan Younis, the Hamas-run ministry of interior said a drone attack targeted a group of police officers in the Al-Mawasi area, killing five, as they were carrying out their routine duties.
The Israeli military said it had carried out two attacks on what it described as military operatives but has not yet provided evidence or further information.
Outside Gaza City's Shifa Hospital, video showed a crowd of men gathered to pray next to two body bags and the tiny body of the child, which was wrapped in a white towel.
"My son and his child were martyred. They were sitting in their tent, bothering no one, and nothing else was happening in the area when suddenly, a missile struck them, and they were martyred," Ali Oweis told AFP news agency. "There is no ceasefire; the war is ongoing, don't you see?"
At Nasser hospital in Khan Younis, women despaired as body bags lay on the floor, video showed. The interior ministry named the five police officers killed, who were between the ages of 23 and 53, and called the attack a "horrific massacre".
A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.
Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.
Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.
The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war.
The conflict was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.
Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.
Additional reporting by Jacob Phillips

An award-winning University of Cambridge researcher died in the Spanish train disaster while on her way to collect a prize for scientific excellence.
Dr Marta Shahbazi was travelling to an awards ceremony on Wednesday when the train she was on crashed into another near Urda, south of Madrid, killing 69 people.
The mother of two was an affiliate associate professor leading a group of researchers at MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) in Cambridge and had earned several awards for work on human embryos and cell biology.
In a statement, the LMB paid tribute to the "inspiring, talented and passionate scientist" and described her death as a "profound shock and a huge loss".
The expert in cell biology ran the Shahbazi Laboratory at the LMB, based on the Cambridge Biomedical Campus.
She had been announced as the winner of a Spanish Society for Developmental Biology award for her contributions to the study of early human development and was due to collect the award at a conference in El Rompido in Andalusia.
The LMB said: "As a wife and mother of two young children, Marta wrote eloquently about balancing her family and career, serving as a much-admired role model for a 'mother scientist', a term she used to describe herself.
"Marta was an inspiring, talented and passionate scientist whose research shed light on the earliest steps in the development of human embryos and how errors occur that lead to failed pregnancies," the LMB said.
The institute said her death was "a profound shock and a huge loss for LMB".
Her work had been recognised with "many awards and prizes", the laboratory added.
Shahbazi is listed on the University of Cambridge website as a principal investigator at its Stem Cell Institute (CSCI).
Institute director Prof Bertie Gottgens said its community was "shocked and deeply saddened" by her death.
"Marta led her primary research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology (LMB) alongside her roles as an affiliate principal investigator and affiliate assistant professor at the CSCI," he said.
"Across both institutes, she was highly respected for her pioneering research on early human development and valued for her collaborative spirit.
"Her creativity, passion, and generosity will be greatly missed."
The news of her death was first confirmed in a social media post, external by the CiMUS, based in Santiago de Compostela where Shahbazi's aunt works.
Shahbazi undertook her PhD at the Spanish National Cancer Research Centre, before joining the University of Cambridge as a post-doctoral fellow and then the LMB in 2020.
The crash in Spain happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of a stationary train operated by the Iryo company.
It is one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.
Three days of national mourning were declared in the country.
More than 540 people were on board both trains.

READ MORE: Attorneys for Alaska say 'meritless' Trump demand to set aside Senate ballots 'not even possible' Sullivan, an ally of President Donald Trump, faces Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola in one of the country's most closely watched races, with Senate control at stake. Tuesday's ranked-choice election also includes two candidates who have done little campaigning, one of whom shares the incumbent's name. It was that candidate's presence on the ballot that prompted Trump to push for the lawsuit out of fear he would siphon votes from the incumbent. The lawsuit, filed less than two weeks before the election and as early voting was underway, called for an investigation into whether votes for retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan were intended for the senator. The state said the case lacked merit and argued there would be no way to determine that without violating voter privacy. U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason wrote in the order that the relief the United States seeks is "infeasible" because many voters have already cast their ballots. "More fundamentally, the United States provides no workable plan as to how it proposes to segregate ballots cast for Daniel J. Sullivan on Election Day and then conduct a court-ordered unspecified 'investigation' of those ballots in a manner that would preserve voter secrecy," she wrote. The Department of Justice, attorneys for the state and Peltola's campaign did not immediately return messages seeking comment. Senator says he expects 'to lose a lot of votes' to the other Dan Sullivan Peltola's campaign and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee argued that the case lacked any legal basis and amounted to interference. The senator and his allies, including Trump, for months have portrayed Dan J. Sullivan as a sham candidate intent on confusing voters and helping Peltola. Earlier Sunday, Sen. Sullivan told CNN that he thought the presence of the second Sullivan on the ballot would affect the election. "I'm sure I'm going to lose a lot of votes to that trickery," he said. He also said he doubted claims by Peltola that she had no idea her top political aides were involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan to run as a way to confuse voters. READ MORE: FBI visits Dan J. Sullivan donor in candidate's hometown as Alaska Senate inquiry widens "There is no way this went on for a year that they weren't informing her," Sullivan told CNN's "State of the Union." "She got caught lying, and she's still lying to the Alaskan people, the media, to all of us." The senator's campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Sunday court ruling. In the week before Election Day, The New York Times reported that Peltola's campaign was involved in efforts to recruit the second Sullivan. Dan J. Sullivan in June, shortly after entering the race, said he'd had no contact with the campaign about running. He has not responded to multiple messages over the past few days. Peltola's campaign responded to the Times story by saying it had no involvement in the campaigns for either Sullivan: "I am not interested in tricking voters," Peltola said during a recent campaign event. Multiple investigations look into whether Dan J. Sullivan was recruited as a decoy candidate State courts, including the Alaska Supreme Court, rejected Republican-backed efforts to block the retired teacher from the August open primary ballot on which he appeared as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., with no party affiliation. The senator was listed as Dan S. Sullivan, Republican and incumbent. Both Sullivans appear the same way on the general election ballot. Peltola placed first in the primary, followed by the senator. Dan J. Sullivan received about 2.5% of the primary vote, but that was enough to finish within the top four and qualify for the Nov. 3 ranked-choice election. Attorneys for the Alaska Department of Law represented state elections officials in the case and asked Gleason, who was appointed by former Democratic President Barack Obama, to toss the lawsuit. They filed a scathing response to the federal government's complaint, calling it "meritless." Alaska also said the state had taken "significant steps" to distinguish the two Sullivans on the ballot. Voters who still might be confused could ask for help or look up candidate biographies and other information in state-distributed election pamphlets. The governor, a Republican, has ordered an investigation and suggested he may not certify a possible Peltola victory. In her ruling, Gleason wrote that the Trump administration's attempt to block certification ran counter to the Constitution, which gives states the authority to run elections. 348774900701.text: By — Bernard Condon, Associated Press Bernard Condon, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/fbi-says-north-korea-was-behind-6-3-billion-binance-heist-the-biggest-crypto-hack-in-history Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter FBI says North Korea was behind $6.3 billion Binance heist, the biggest crypto hack in history World Nov 1, 2026 11:20 AM EST NEW YORK (AP) — The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday. READ MORE: What to know about the $6.3B hack on Binance, likely the biggest-ever crypto theft The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to "malicious cyber activity" by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year. The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins. It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum. The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and "instant swap services." Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, President Donald Trump suggested investigators weren't yet certain that North Korea was involved. "I'm not concerned. We're learning about it," Trump said of the case. "We don't know if it's North Korea." Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was. WATCH: $6 billion cryptocurrency heist puts investors on edge Crypto expert Ari Redbord said he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months. "It's bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the Internet," said Redbord, chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. "However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds." He added: "It's just this cat and mouse game." On Thursday, $6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack. The company said Saturday that it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen to cover 90% of the missing assets and promised that customers would be fully reimbursed. 613db46e78a2.text: By — Cybele Mayes-Osterman Cybele Mayes-Osterman By — Jack Brook, Associated Press Jack Brook, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/ice-agent-charged-with-assault-for-hitting-fleeing-man-with-car-in-houston-will-turn-himself-in-attorney-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter ICE agent charged with assault for hitting fleeing man with car in Houston will turn himself in, attorney says Nation Nov 1, 2026 11:01 AM EST A federal immigration officer charged with aggravated assault after he ran over a Mexican man with his car in Houston will turn himself in on Monday, according to his attorney. Mario Alberto Morales, a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer, struck Miguel Parra Hernandez, a 48-year-old construction worker, with his unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as he chased Parra Hernandez through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales on Friday on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon. READ MORE: An ICE officer is charged with assault for striking a man with a car in Houston Morales is planning to turn himself in at a courthouse sometime on Monday, David Lindenmuth, his attorney, told The Associated Press. Lindenmuth previously told the AP that the incident was "clearly just an accident" and that local officials had "invented a crime out of thin air." Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told reporters on Friday. ICE has said Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales' car. Previously released surveillance camera video shows Morales' vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away. Teare played footage from Morales' body camera on Friday that showed the agent making sharp turns with his steering wheel. He then stops and exits the vehicle and turns toward Parra Hernandez, who is lying on the ground, screaming. "I was coming in, and I hit him with the car," Morales can be heard saying after another ICE agent arrives. Parra Hernandez told deputies that he fled the traffic stop when Morales started pulling on a mask, and Morales "threw the car" at him, according to a Harris County Sheriff's Office incident report reviewed by the AP. Morales told deputies that he did not brake before he hit Parra Hernandez, but that he did not intentionally strike him, according to the report. ICE said after the incident that the target of the operation was a man named Jose Mendoza-Cervantes, who the agency said was seen getting into a car with Parra Hernandez. Mendoza-Cervantes' daughter told the immigrants' rights group FIEL that her father has been dead for nearly a decade. READ MORE: ICE officer appeared to intentionally hit a man with a vehicle in Houston, Texas, prosecutor says Morales is among a small handful of federal agents who have been criminally charged for wounding people during the Trump administration's aggressive immigration crackdown. ICE agent Christian Castro pleaded not guilty last month to charges that he lied to the FBI after he shot and wounded a Venezuelan man as immigration agents swept Minneapolis earlier this year. Many other ICE shootings, including some that were fatal, have not ended in charges for the agents involved. Morales, 33, has served as an ICE agent for a little over a year, according to Lindenmuth. Teare said on Friday that authorities have a "significant amount of information" on Morales, and that, in his experience, law enforcement agencies would not hire someone with his background. He did not elaborate. Morales was charged with a misdemeanor in 2013 for stealing four DVDs, according to Harris County Court records. Those charges were dismissed after he paid a $270 fine and struck a plea deal. Morales unsuccessfully ran to represent Texas' 34th congressional district in this year's election cycle under the name "Bam Morales," which Lindenmuth confirmed. Morales served in the U.S. Army's 82nd Airborne Division and later as a corrections officer and law enforcement officer, he wrote in a Ballotpedia candidate survey. He wrote that his top priorities were veterans' rights, economic issues and service guided by the Christian principles of "compassion, integrity, service, and accountability." He listed illegal immigration as one of the country's greatest challenges. Morales also wrote in the survey that he was endorsed by an organization called "Make America Godlier Again." Morales appeared at a 2024 Christian conference held by televangelist Johnson Suleman. In video of the conference, Morales appears to act as a Spanish translator as Suleman serves free food and "extends his touch of love to migrants." The News
Democratic party leaders have found themselves unable to stave off an embarrassing schism in Michiganâs must-win Senate race, a crisis that may offer a glimpse of internal battles to come.
Days of frantic shuttle diplomacy and attempts to organize a joint appearance by erstwhile Senate primary rivals Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens culminated in Stevensâ surprise Sunday endorsement of Republican nominee Mike Rogers.
Stevens appeared with Rogers at a Black church in Detroit less than 24 hours after vowing to colleagues that she would back El-Sayed, winning praise from President Donald Trump and calls for her eviction from the House Democratic Caucus. But perhaps the most stunning aspect of the crackup was how hard senior Democrats had worked to avoid it.
Party leaders like Reps. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., and Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., were pushing hard to get El-Sayed and Stevens on the same page for a show of unity going into Tuesdayâs critical elections. Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., said on national TV hours before Stevensâ defection that she had personally assured him on Saturday night sheâd be backing El-Sayed.
Raskin told Semafor in an interview Sunday: âI was blindsided, and I feel dumbfounded by the whole thing.â
While the Senate race remains very close, itâs not clear how much Stevensâ turnabout will affect the final balloting. She has, however, laid bare deep divides within the party â principally over Israel and the establishmentâs relationships with the left wing.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffriesâ statement backing El-Sayed after the flap did not mention Stevens, a member of his caucus, by name. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, who had initially favored her as a better general election candidate than El-Sayed, called her endorsement of Rogers a âdespicable betrayal.â
Many in the party believe leaders were powerless over Stevens: âI certainly donât think itâs somebody elseâs fault, other than Haley Stevens,â said a Michigan Democratic operative.
Yet Michigan, where El-Sayed was struggling to win over some Jewish and Black voters even before this week, is now set among the first-in-the-nation Democratic nominating states. And the partyâs inability to come together during the final week of the election is likely to haunt it well into the 2028 primary.
what happened
Stevens kept her allies and staff in the dark through the whole process as she privately insisted she would keep backing Democrats, including El-Sayed.
As she and El-Sayed squabbled publicly over the last week, a few of her staff reached out to her discouraging her from endorsing Rogers, according to a source whoâd worked on her race. Stevensâ response, according to the source: âOmg why would you think I would do that?!!â
By Sunday, many of her staff had resigned, slamming her Rogers endorsement.
âShe lied to the people that she says she respects,â said the Michigan Democratic operative.
El-Sayed, who had implored Stevens not to campaign with him last week, brushed aside the news. âNone of this matters,â he told reporters in Detroit.
State Party Chair Curtis Hertel Jr. said Sunday on X Stevens was expelled from the state party, and although national party leaders across the board were united in saying they supported El-Sayed.
what happens next
Stevens faces rough waters ahead. She appears to have violated House Democratic caucus rules banning campaign activity for non-Democrats, and some in the caucus want to punish her. Itâs not immediately clear whether Jeffries and Stevens have talked.
The Stevens-El-Sayed crackup had been building in the months since she lost to him in the primary. Stevens and other Michigan Democrats kept their distance from El-Sayed over his association with controversial streamer Hasan Piker and his positions on Israel.
The feud accelerated over the closing weeks of the campaign when Cenk Uygurâs Rebellion PAC began running the anti-Israel ad that would eventually convince Stevens to endorse Rogers. Now, Uygur says he never imagined that outcome when he aired it.âIt wound up creating the perfect storm because it caused two weather fronts to collide,â Uygur told Semafor. âThe establishment hated it with a passion and the internet loved it with equal passion. Thatâs what caused this explosion.â
Nicholas and Davidâs view
Democrats are closing their campaigns this cycle with fairly unified, populist messaging about âaffordabilityâ and âcorruptionâ that helps the super-rich stay wealthy. Underneath that messaging is a feud between the partyâs left flank and centrist arm thatâs bound to erupt after Tuesdayâs results.
If El-Sayed loses, there will be a fight over blame between Democrats who spent tens of millions of dollars to support him and progressives whoâll argue that the party establishment canât be trusted when leftist candidates win a nomination. This is in the air already, given Andrew Cuomoâs decision to run a third party campaign after losing the Democratic primary to democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani.
But if El-Sayed wins, his faction of the party will be able to say he did it with a knife plunged in his back by pro-Israel Democrats. That will weaken pro-Israel Democratsâ ability to say, as AIPAC does, that their agenda is âgood policy and good politics.â Thatâs in the air too, with Democrats already gearing up to challenge Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., whoâs stopped campaigning for other Democrats after feuding with pro-Palestine activists.

00e013dec3a2.text: By — Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Nicholas Riccardi, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/justice-department-urges-sanctions-for-database-analysis-critical-of-its-noncitizen-voting-claims Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Justice Department urges sanctions for database analysis critical of its noncitizen voting claims Politics Nov 1, 2026 6:18 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department on Sunday defended the accuracy of a list of what it says are more than 20,000 suspected noncitizens registered to vote in California and suggested that a federal judge consider whether an immigrant rights group and its lawyers should face contempt charges after they published an analysis of the names. READ MORE: Analysis: More than 40% of names on DOJ list of alleged noncitizens not on California's voter rolls On Friday, U.S. District Court Chief Judge James Boasberg allowed the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA, access to federal government data on 20,000 people the Trump administration alleges are noncitizen voters in California. Boasberg, based in Washington, D.C., ordered the plaintiffs not to disclose any names on the list and use the data only for their arguments about why they have legal standing to challenge the Trump administration's use of it. On Saturday, attorneys for the immigrant rights group filed court papers revealing that their analysis found more than 40% of the people on the list do not appear in the state's voter file. It also identified 22 people on the list who were likely naturalized U.S. citizens while saying that thousands more U.S. citizens appeared to be on it, as well. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The Justice Department said in a filing Sunday that the analysis by the immigrant rights group had nothing to do with the group's legal standing and therefore violated Boasberg's order. "The report's political grandstanding about alleged inaccuracies that purportedly impact California voters generally, or comparisons between the government's list and the full 'California voter file,' has no relevance to whether the particular plaintiffs in this case have standing," it said. The filing also suggested Boasberg refer the matter to the Justice Department for investigation for possible criminal contempt of court. Alberto Lammers, a spokesman for the University of California, Los Angeles' Voting Rights Project, which filed the case and did the data analysis for the immigrant rights group, said in an emailed statement: "Plaintiffs' counsel and their experts fully complied with the Court's orders." READ MORE: Appeals court rejects Justice Department request for California to set aside disputed ballots In a separate case, the Justice Department on Sunday also appealed a decision from Friday night by U.S. District Court Judge Trina L. Thompson. The ruling by the San Francisco-based judge barred the department from demanding that election offices remove possible noncitizens from voter rolls, separate their ballots or threaten legal action. The Justice Department has noted that Thompson ruled before the federal government was able to file its initial arguments. Thompson scheduled a Monday hearing on the appeal. That case is one of many the Trump administration has lost in its battle over its lists of alleged noncitizen voters. A federal judge in California rejected its demand that election officials there be forced to separate ballots cast by those voters, writing that such last-minute orders could "wreak havoc" on the state's election. Two appellate judges agreed. California election officials also contend the list is riddled with errors and say they have no way to do the painstaking work required by law to remove voters from the rolls in the days before the election. People attest to being U.S. citizens when they register to vote and risk felony prosecution if they cast a ballot when they are not eligible. The administration has said its list was carefully compiled from the state's own voter registration data and compared to federal citizenship records. The Justice Department issued a series of subpoenas for election offices in California and warned election officials who knowingly let noncitizens vote that they could face criminal charges. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez 's future hinges on whether a fellow progressive can carry a swing state, for once. California Gov. Gavin Newsom has to show that his congressional redistricting gambit worked for Democrats — and he needs to beat back a state wealth tax proposal supported by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.). Driving the news: Democrats eyeing White House runs have spent the past year preparing to emerge from Tuesday's midterms with momentum, and an argument for a 2028 candidacy. They want Democrats to do well — but to each, some races are especially important. Some have focused their time and money on particular contests for ideological reasons, or a desire to show strength in their home states. Others have hedged their bets across the nation, so that Tuesday is unlikely to be a huge victory or a significant defeat. Here's how the top potential Democratic contenders for president have placed their bets in this week's elections — and what success or failure will look like for them. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez A great night: AOC has wagered just about everything on the Senate race in Michigan, where she's said that a win by progressive Abdul El-Sayed would "break open the entire political calculus in America" and show that "anybody can win anywhere." She's weighing whether to run for president or the Senate, and much of her electability argument for a national campaign hinges on an El-Sayed victory. Progressives are desperate to establish that one of their own can carry a presidential battleground state. Ocasio-Cortez has contributed $1 million to help El-Sayed and stumped for him at several events. An El-Sayed victory "would prove to the country, and the world, that competent, courageous progressive populists can win in the most competitive swing states in America," said Bhavik Lathia, a left-wing strategist from Michigan. "The implications for 2028 would be enormous." AOC would get bonus points Tuesday if other progressives she's supporting — such as House candidate Randy Villegas in California and Senate candidate Angie Nixon in Florida — win their swing-seat races. Worst-case scenario: If El-Sayed loses, many progressives think AOC would be less likely to run for president. That's why she's widely viewed as having more on the line Tuesday than any other potential Democratic contender for president, followed by Shapiro. Josh Shapiro A great night: Shapiro needs to win so big Tuesday that it makes Democratic presidential primary voters see his technocratic "get shit done" brand of governing as the party's best bet to take down the GOP in 2028. Shapiro is less known nationally than many 2028 hopefuls, and that has been by choice. He's largely focused on Pennsylvania this year, even as would-be rivals for president crisscrossed the country. A blowout in America's biggest swing state could help him stand out. A good night for Shapiro would be defeating Republican Stacy Garrity by double digits and carrying three Democratic House candidates — Janelle Stelson, Bob Brooks and Paige Cognetti — across the finish line to defeat Republican incumbents. He'd have a great night if his coattails were so long that he pulled a fourth Democratic House hopeful, Bob Harvie, to victory — taking down GOP Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, who's known for surviving difficult electoral cycles. Shapiro would get extra credit if he helped Democrats win a trifecta in Harrisburg for the first time in decades by flipping control of the state Senate. Worst-case scenario: If only one or two Democrats in his state flip House seats or he wins by less than 10 points, Shapiro's setup for 2028 would fall short. Andy Beshear A great night: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who moonlights as chair of the Democratic Governors Association, put his chips this year on helping his party take control of a majority of the nation's governorships. Beshear would earn bragging rights if Democrats flip the two governors' seats needed to do that. He's eyeing the races in Iowa, Ohio, Georgia and Nevada. "I am laser-focused on these governors' races," he told us, arguing that the results will help determine what's possible in the 2028 presidential contest. "Rob Sand wins Iowa, Iowa's in play. When Amy Acton wins Ohio, Ohio's in play," Beshear said. Worst-case scenario: Beshear made enemies among some Latino Democrats this year when the DGA rebuffed calls to invest heavily in Gina Hinojosa's campaign for Texas governor. If Hinojosa loses to Texas Gov. Greg Abbott by a razor-thin margin or pulls an upset, Beshear's decision-making will come under heavy scrutiny — and he could have a problem with some Latino leaders in a 2028 campaign. Gavin Newsom A great night: Newsom won over many MS NOW moms and "resistance" liberals across the country when he responded to President Trump's push to create more GOP House seats in other states by fighting back with a successful voter proposition to do the same in California. His goal has been to gain five Democratic seats from the change to help Democrats take back the House. That's his bar to clear Tuesday. Some political insiders now think Democrats could gain 20 or more House seats across the country, so Newsom's contribution might not be as decisive as once thought. Newsom would score a political win if a proposed billionaire wealth tax on the ballot in his home state, which he opposes, fails. Worst-case scenario: If California voters approve the tax or Democrats flip fewer than five House seats there, it would diminish Newsom's California clout. Jon Ossoff A great night: A long-running knock against Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff has been that he won his seat in 2021 by riding his fellow Peach State Sen. Raphael Warnock's coattails. (AP) — A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway. All passengers on board were killed, the nation's transportation secretary said. Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the aircraft plunged from the sky, before striking near the roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as people milled about, expressing shock that it landed only feet from homes and only inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site. READ MORE: California helicopter crash kills 2 people, leaves 2 hospitalized and 1 missing Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X on Sunday that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County at 12:50 p.m. and called it a "horrific tragedy." The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board's investigation into the cause, he said. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said the crash left a crater in the ground and spewed debris. There were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed, he said. "It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis told reporters at the scene on Sunday. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road." Rain pounded the region on Sunday. A flood watch due to excessive rainfall was in effect through Monday afternoon, the National Weather Service said. The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it. The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb 2,000 feet (about 610 meters). Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data. A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it crashed steeply into the ground. READ MORE: Firefighting helicopter crashes near Yosemite, killing both pilots Minutes before the crash, the pilot reported ice accumulating on the jet and turbulence that was jolting it by as much as 700 feet, according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net. "We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence," the pilot told controllers. But the situation rapidly deteriorated. After encountering precipitation and requesting to climb, the pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate. "We're descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday - we're descending 10,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed. "We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. "We're going to crash into the ground." Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said it was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight. Local authorities are evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash. A rare humanitarian ceasefire in Ukraine's front-line Kherson region that allowed civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky has ended.
The localised ceasefire was due to end at 22:59 Ukrainian time (21:00 GMT) on Sunday. While the truce had held since it was implemented last week, fighting had continued elsewhere.
On Sunday evening, Ukraine's air alert system was apparently hacked, the country's air force said, warning of radiation over Kyiv - a reference to a possible nuclear attack.
The Air Force message read: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our channel."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had struck energy infrastructure in four regions overnight on Saturday, leaving hundreds of thousands of homes without power. Some connections were restored on Sunday.
Another overnight strike killed two people, including a 13-year-old girl, in the Vinnytsia region, the State Emergency Service of Ukraine said.
Meanwhile, Ukraine hit a major missile fuel producer in Russia's Rostov region, which caused a fire and damaged four production facilities, Zelensky said.
In Ukraine, repair works to restore power continued throughout the day. Most customers in the Dnipropetrovsk region had their connections restored by early evening, but more than 60,000 were still without power, the governor said.
Because of regular attacks on energy infrastructure, emergency power cuts have been introduced across the country. Even in the capital Kyiv, electricity is cut off for most of the day, and water supplies are also disrupted.
Zelensky said in a social media post that the intensity of Russian strikes has been "extremely high" over the past week, adding that Russia was "trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic missile interceptors".
He added that "every day" Ukraine communicated its need for Patriot missiles - the only effective weapon for downing Russia's deadly ballistic missiles - to the US, Europe and other partners. He thanked countries for their support so far and longer-term commitments, but called again for more immediate aid.
The limited pause in hostilities, which started on Tuesday, was brokered with the help of US First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo.
It was originally confined to the city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, and was expanded across the wider region of Kherson.
Oleshky had been trapped on one side by the Dnipro river and the other by Russian forces, with routes out mined and subject to drone attack.
Residents trapped there were suffering severe shortages of food, water and electricity, with many resorting to cooking garden weeds to survive.
The truce allowed for Oleskhy residents to evacuate if they wanted, and there were emotional scenes on Saturday of reunions between loved ones who hadn't seen eachother for years.
There are Ukrainian military positions just 5km (3.1 miles) from Oleshky, but evacuees had to travel through Russian-occupied territory to southern Russia, where they flew to Belarus, before finally being driven across Ukraine's northern border.
The oldest evacuee was 94 years old, while the youngest was one, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman.

Chris Murphy is in the hospital after having a stroke, his office says Politics Nov 1, 2026 4:20 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Sen. Chris Murphy is in the hospital after having a stroke and is "awake and alert" as he receives treatment, the Connecticut Democrat's office said Sunday. Murphy's chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said in a statement the 53-year-old senator "started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game" on Saturday. Please check your inbox to confirm. "He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke," she said. "He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment. The doctors are encouraged by his progress, he is awake and alert, and we are optimistic he will make a full recovery." Murphy was elected to the House in 2006 and to the Senate in 2012. He is not on the ballot Tuesday. In the Senate, he serves on the Appropriations Committee and is a leading voice on immigration and gun policy. He is considered a contender for more senior leadership positions in the Senate and among the many Democrats seen as potential 2028 candidates for the White House. Three other Senate Democrats have had strokes in recent years. Sens. Ben Ray Lujan of New Mexico and Chris Van Hollen of Maryland had strokes in 2022 and have since recovered. Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman had a stroke while campaigning for his seat that same year and now uses adaptive technology in the Senate, including live captioning on a phone or tablet that transcribes words as people speak to him and helps him process the conversation. Fetterman said on social media Sunday that his family "is rooting for Chris and his family for a full and speedy recovery." Several Republican senators, including Chuck Grassley of Iowa and Pete Ricketts of Nebraska, also offered prayers for Murphy. President Donald Trump said he was "really surprised" to learn about Murphy's stroke. "Nobody wants to have that," he said. Murphy has been traveling the country in support of House and Senate candidates as his party races for majority control. On Friday, he posted that he had been campaigning in his home state for Gov. Ned Lamont. Last week, Murphy posted from Minnesota campaigning with Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, the Democratic nominee for Senate. The final sprint before Election Day capped Murphy's whirlwind trip to the Middle East at the start of October for meetings with several leaders, including Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. In early September, Murphy completed his annual "walk across Connecticut," covering about 70 miles over four days, talking with residents about their concerns along the way. "Thinking of my great friend & colleague, Chris Murphy," wrote Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., in a statement Sunday. "I know how fiercely he fights & I'm certain I'll be welcoming him back to the Senate soon." Associated Press writers Mary Clare Jalonick and Lisa Mascaro contributed to this report. e1aa62e17343.text: By — Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/israeli-officials-say-elections-wont-be-undermined-and-suspects-in-bribery-case-are-freed Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Israeli officials say elections will stand after Netanyahu claimed Arabs stole vote World Updated on Nov 1, 2026 4:54 PM EST — Published on Nov 1, 2026 2:57 PM EST TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's efforts to question last week's elections weakened Sunday as officials said the vote would not be undermined by the allegations and a court ordered suspects in one case released. In an image that indicated officials were on the same page, the head of Israel's elections committee was shown sitting between Israel's attorney general and the head of the Shin Bet intelligence service for a statement making clear that even if claims of foreign interference raised last week are substantiated, the vote would stand. Netanyahu's Likud party has said, without giving evidence, that Arab-led parties "stole" the elections in which Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority of seats in parliament. By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appears to be trying to block any potential alliance in the opposition with the Arab parties that could force him from office. WATCH: What Israel's election deadlock means for Netanyahu and the region Likud has cited a handful of cases, including the arrests of three political activists before polls opened on Oct. 27 with envelopes of cash, allegedly to bribe voters. Two days later, police arrested four more suspects. Police said the suspects were connected to the Islamist party Ra'am, which denied that it was involved. A judge on Sunday questioned or rejected police requests for further restrictions on the three suspects. Police later said one was released subject to unspecified "conditions" and another was ordered to remain on house arrest for eight days. The detention of the third suspect was extended for two days. Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra'am party, which won eight seats in the Knesset, denounced the arrests as undemocratic and "an attempt to influence the election results." Netanyahu suggests joining with Arab parties is treason Netanyahu saw his parliamentary bloc of allies drop to 53 seats in the 120-member Knesset, down from a peak of 68 in the outgoing parliament. A bloc of parties led by his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, won 48 seats, while Arab-led parties, including Ra'am, won the remaining 19 seats. Together, those two blocs opposing Netanyahu have enough seats to form a new government, though it remains unclear whether they will agree to do so. The results are due to be officially certified this week, and President Isaac Herzog on Wednesday will begin meeting with each of the parties elected to parliament after that to see who they prefer to be the next prime minister. READ MORE: Israel's election results are in. Here's what could happen next Following those consultations, he will choose the candidate — most likely Netanyahu or Eisenkot — who he believes has the best chance of forming a coalition government. That would set the stage for weeks of negotiations. If they are unsuccessful, Herzog could ask another candidate to try. Otherwise, the country would be plunged into a new election early next year. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for Eisenkot to join with Arab parties. Some Israelis agree. A few dozen people protested outside Eisenkot's home on Sunday night. "We have a tiny country, a very tiny Jewish country. We want to keep it as a Jewish country," said one protester, Shoshana Idasis. Other, larger rallies in recent days have called for a Jewish-Arab coalition. Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of trying to delegitimize the vote Likud also has alleged foreign interference in the vote. The Shin Bet security service, at the request of Israel's election commission, has opened an investigation. But the head of the elections committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, said that "our position is that even if the suspicions are substantiated, this would not undermine the integrity of the electoral process or the election results as a whole." Likud quickly issued a statement asking how the committee chief can acknowledge there are serious allegations while saying there will be no effect on the final outcome. Eisenkot on Sunday accused Netanyahu of launching an "orchestrated and organized campaign to delegitimize the election results" by insinuating that Qatar had supported opposition parties to unseat Netanyahu. Eisenkot said that Shin Bet briefed him on the investigation into foreign interference. WATCH: Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us Qatar has denied funding any activities meant to influence the election's outcome. Many Israelis see the Gulf Arab country as a patron of Hamas, and allegations of its influence have roiled Israeli politics in other cases, including one in which close aides of Netanyahu allegedly accepted money from Qatar while working for the prime minister's office. Netanyahu's opponents have accused him of using scare tactics and trying to create a narrative to further discriminate against Arab-led parties and Israel's Arab citizens, who make up 20% of the population. Yousef Jabareen, leader of the Joint List of Arab parties, which won 11 seats, noted last week that more than half the content published by Likud and Netanyahu on election day was directed against Arab voters as a tactic to encourage right-wing Israelis to vote. "In moments of crisis, he reverts to his familiar tactic: racist incitement and the delegitimization of the Arab public," he said. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Melanie Lidman, Associated Press Melanie Lidman, Associated Press

The Pentagon’s IT agency wants to bridge network gaps in the Pacific
“The old ways of connecting with partners are simply no longer sufficient,” says INDOPACOM deputy commander.
HONOLULU—Lags in communication could undermine even the most advanced technology available, the deputy chief of Indo-Pacific Command warned Thursday.
“If we field cutting-edge compute and advanced software applications, but retain rigid, multi-layered bureaucracies requiring hours to authorize time-sensitive engagements, then we've negated our technological overmatch,” Lt. Gen. George Rowell, deputy commander of INDOPACOM, told attendees at TechNet Indo-Pacific. “No competitor on Earth can match America's network of capable allies and partners. That network is our greatest advantage. It is our strategic center of gravity. But the old ways of connecting with partners are simply no longer sufficient.”
Upgrading military networks in the Pacific so the U.S. can quickly share battle details with allies has been a key priority in recent years. The command recently deployed the Pacific mission partner network, a unified version of a series of bespoke networks for individual allied or partner nations in the region. Throughout the year, the command has tested the network in military exercises, where it has shown progress and allowed better coordination, with fewer devices to toggle between.
Still, there are still gaps that need to be addressed to improve communications with allies and partners.
“We're in the middle of a transition right now,” said Col. Michael Hlad, who leads the Defense Information Systems Agency’s regional field command in the Pacific. “We are migrating to a data-centric environment, helping our partners understand what does it mean to be zero trust? What are the key items that we need to agree on, let's say, from an identity standpoint, a data standardization standpoint?”
While some nations are more technologically aligned, such as the Five Eye partners, the plan is to build a data-sharing environment malleable enough to bring in other nations as well.
“I don't know what the coalition of the future necessarily looks like,” Hlad said. “So how are we, DISA, building a coalition environment that is agile and common enough that we can bring in those partners instead of making it brittle…where it's just bilateral or just multilateral? We've got to bring that agility to [Indo-Pacific Command] as well as our partners, so they're able to integrate for an [humanitarian assistance and disaster relief] scenario as well as a high-conflict scenario of the future.”
Getting to that common digital ground means agreeing on what tools and methods to use.
There must be “clear standardization of what that common architecture looks like,” Hlad said. “This only works if we get the data right. And we are still siloed.”
In addition to improving communication with allies and partners, one of DISA Pacific's top priorities is to improve data transfer, speed, and security in the region.
“How do we have better transport resiliency in the Pacific so that we can make sure that the critical feeds and data are where we need them?…How do we deliver those for the warfighters in the Pacific so the data is closer to the operational need?” Hlad said.
The field command recently unveiled the Regional Network Operations Security Center Pacific—which aims to increase network support for INDOPACOM’s headquarters.
“That's an enhanced [network operations center]. That's an enhanced [security operations center]. That's a regional service support desk, and that's some data fusion capabilities that were not resident in this theater to synchronize,” Hlad said.
The idea is for the center to respond to connectivity challenges, including when undersea cables cut out and during electromagnetic spectrum or application disruptions.
The center has yielded a 20 percent personnel increase to assist in solving those connectivity problems, Hlad said.

- Published
In the last weekend before the pivotal midterm elections, Donald Trump has made a final pitch to voters in hopes of keeping Republicans in control of the US Congress.
Trump held rallies in Florida, Iowa and Kansas - states he won in past elections - in a sign of Republicans' defensive stance in Tuesday's elections.
Facing voter frustration over rising prices, particularly fuel, Trump sought to tamp down such concerns and shift focus on attacking Democrats, saying they would "bankrupt" families if elected.
Polls suggest that Democrats have a good chance at winning at least partial control of Congress, which would act as a check on Trump's power and upend the last two years of his presidency.
Trump has been campaigning non-stop across the country ahead of the election - even in areas that were once thought to be safe Republican strongholds.
Throughout the weekend, Trump made the case for his party at rallies in Kansas, Florida and Iowa as well as at tele-rallies for candidates in states including Michigan, Ohio and Pennsylvania.
In previous years, Trump easily won Florida, Iowa and Kansas - once considered reliably Republican states - but the president's visits there in the final days of his election drive highlighted just how competitive these states have become in determining control of Congress.
Trump told supporters he had transformed the country, saying Democrats had left the US in a "dark age" but under his command, "we quickly turned it into the golden age of America".
Trump is facing a backlash over the cost of living. Prices have gone up, particularly for fuel, groceries and health care, since the war in Iran began over eight months ago. At these rallies, Trump appeared to have two aims: to change the subject from those issues and use fear to turn out the Republican vote.
At rallies in Florida and Iowa, he highlighted his policies on trade and immigration and said if Democrats were given power, they would "open the border", "bankrupt your family", "take away your guns" and "mutilate your children". He played video montages of Democrats criticising ICE and supporting transgender rights.
In the room at the rallies, supporters cheered, but there has also been disquiet among some Republicans over Trump's appeal with more moderate voters.
Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries said this weekend that he was "very confident" his party was on course to win control of the House of Representatives, as senior Democrats including former President Barack Obama made final appeals to voters.
A forecasting tool from Harvard University that analyses and compiles multiple polls and historical data suggests that Democrats have a 96% chance of taking the House and a 76% chance of taking the Senate.
A national poll from NBC News posted this weekend suggests that registered voters prefer a Democrat-controlled Congress by a 7-point margin, leading Republicans 52% to 45%.
But along with the last-push campaign stops, this weekend featured a dramatic turn in the Senate race in Michigan - a tightly contested seat currently held by Democrats.
Haley Stevens, a sitting congresswoman who lost the Democratic Senate nomination to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday.
The move led to widespread condemnation from fellow Democrats and praise from Republicans, including Trump who called her "very brave".
In Alaska, home to another crucial Senate race, a judge on Sunday dismissed an attempt by the Trump administration to delay certifying election results if the Republican incumbent candidate loses due to two candidates appearing on the ballot with the same name.
In the lead up to the election, Trump and his administration have repeatedly cast doubt on both the credibility and security of the vote, despite evidence showing voter fraud is rare. The justice department has launched investigations or demanded votes be set aside in multiple US states.
The stakes are high for Trump, as midterm election results are seen as a measure of how satisfied Americans are with a president's performance.
In most midterm elections, the party that holds the White House typically loses seats in Congress to the opposing party - meaning Trump's Republican party has the most to lose.
Republicans, who currently hold a slim majority in both the House of Representatives and Senate, don't want to relinquish their party's majority in Congress, as losing any seats would hinder their ability to pass laws and shape policies.
Democrats, however, are keen to gain control from Republicans. Holding a majority would enable them to challenge Trump's agenda, give them investigative powers over his administration, and could also help them showcase their vision for America ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
For lawmakers, it's all about gaining or maintaining power and control, but it's Americans who will feel the impacts of their policies.
Who gets elected at the city, state, and federal level affects many aspects of voters' everyday lives, including the cost of gas, rising inflation and grocery prices, healthcare and abortion access, income and property taxes, and immigration.
