The News
For all the talk of AI bubbles and market crashes, Scandinavian private-equity giant EQT says itâs making a bet that regardless of what happens with the frontier labs, AI is still going to need a massive amount of power, energy, chips, and data centers.
âAll of a sudden, we find ourselves with $100 billion of energy assets, which are really the limiting factor for AI right now,â said Jean Salata, global chair of EQT, which has $400 billion in assets under management.
âA lot of people went out and signed tons of contracts with anybody â they call them âbragawatts.â But signing something and delivering it on time, and with power connected, are two very different things,â Salata said. âSophisticated investors understand that, but thereâs a lot of things happening in the public markets where people are investing in things that they really donât understand.â
EQT is a unique animal in an industry where exits have dried up, a generational bet on software companies looks vulnerable to AI, and higher interest rates have broken the math of cheap leverage and multiple expansion. Since 2018, PE firms have asked their investors for $1.5 trillion more capital than theyâve given back, and the industry is sitting on nearly $4 trillion worth of businesses it canât sell.
EQT has largely stayed out of the private credit and insurance boom that has turned its US rivals into asset-gathering giants â a âbeta business,â said Salata, an artisanally crafted Wall Street dig. And it has an unusual backstop: The Wallenbergs, Swedenâs most powerful business dynasty, helped found EQT in 1994 and remain its largest shareholder. The familyâs patient approach to ownership is close to the long-hold model that much of private equity is now trying to reinvent.
Q&A
This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.
Liz Hoffman: For a long time, private equity firms could borrow cheaply, ride a rising market, and look like geniuses. It feels like the jig is up, and I know you have some thoughts on that.
Jean Salata: Our industry needs to remember what we are meant to be doing, which is delivering returns for our clients. If weâre not doing that, weâre going to end up in a very difficult place. Thereâs been a lot of attention on the growth in assets under management, a business model that has really benefited from the tailwinds of the private credit run of the last five years. But weâre in an environment where the tide is going out and that means youâre going where there is real value being created.
There are something like 10,000 private-equity firms out there. What should that number be?
The industry already is consolidating and that will accelerate. This year the top 10 firms in the world have raised 50% of the capital. When you raise smaller funds, people donât see the carry coming in and so they leave and you get zombie funds.
EQT has chosen not to chase those credit tailwinds you mentioned. It doesnât have the big lending business that Apollo, Blackstone, and others have ridden to huge AUM piles. Do you feel good about that decision?
I think thereâs a role for private credit, but the question is whoâs best positioned to deliver that? Weâre good at being an equity investor, being really close to the sectors that we invest in, bringing the best operational talent, bringing the technology and the AI capabilities that we have to the company. None of those are really relevant to the credit business. Itâs an origination business. Itâs a beta business. Best case scenario, you make 8% return on your money. So, the answer is yes, I think we are happy with the decision.
But how do you resist the pressures to be a one-stop shop?
Eventually there is a feedback loop. Second-quartile [performance] is, maybe, good enough. But when you start talking about third- and fourth-quartile returns, clients will either stop or reduce the amount that they invest with you.
Itâs hard to take anything public right now that isnât a giant AI company and private equityâs track record on returning capital has been abysmal. How does the industry get out of this funk?
There are a lot of assets for sale that need to find a home and there arenât that many buyers. At EQT, weâve been able to take advantage of where there are pockets of opportunity and liquidity. We had $33 billion of distributions to our investors in the last 12 months, and as a result, weâre continuing to attract capital.
Thereâs this strange incentive structure in our industry, where you sell businesses that you otherwise wouldnât want to sell because of this finite [fund] life. Thereâs a bit of frustration on the part of sellers that have sold assets because they need to go fundraising, only to see the buyers make like another 3x on it, which is why youâre seeing these longer-hold vehicles like evergreen structures, open-ended structures, continuation vehicles.
But then isnât the market saying that the 10-year closed-end fund is outdated and should probably go away?
One of the reasons we bought [secondaries firm] Coller is we think there is a convergence happening between the primary market and the secondary market. Thereâs a case to be made for the secondary market essentially becoming the private equity market, as it is in the world of listed equities. Remember, the stock market is a secondary market. Yes, you have some IPOs, but the vast majority of the trading is in existing shares. Where weâre heading in private markets is not quite that extreme, but itâs going to be a much bigger part of the industry. There were $250 billion of PE secondaries deals last year. Thatâs doubled in the last three or four years and itâs probably going to double again in the next five.
One other tension in PE right now is that everyone seems to be in the same trade â the AI trade. Are you worried about correlation?
Thereâs no patents in finance. Weâre all moving in a similar direction and itâs going to boil down to execution. A lot of this is about talent. Thereâs a shortage of really good

The Scoop
Wall Street is finding out just how expensive things can get in a matter of months.
For a look at how much investorsâ jitters are reshaping AI-related debt financing, look to QTS, an investment-grade Blackstone-backed data center operator, that just six months ago was weighing a deal to borrow $800 million at a rate of 1.7 percentage points over Treasurys.
That deal never went through. And now, that same debt is being shopped to investors at 2.2 to 2.50 points above comparable Treasury yields for a nearly identical offering, according to people familiar with the matter. Both offerings involve the same company, same blue-chip Wall Street backing, and the same collateral â just for a lot more money. Blackstone declined to comment.Â
As debt jitters spread and borrowing gets more expensive, itâs a lesson in just how much sentiment has shifted in such a short amount of time.
Know More
On Friday, the Financial Times reported that Blackstone told investors it no longer expected Anthropic to get an investment-grade credit rating immediately after its IPO, a reversal of previous guidance about the frontier lab, which is raising billions of dollars to finance its AI buildout. And investment-grade SpaceXâs $40 billion debt launch saw its pricing widen out â reaching an expected 8.75% yield for the riskier portion of its recent debt deal, up from where pricing was discussed just a week earlier, Semafor reported.

acbd6f830fe3.text: President Trump said Monday he'd move to protect Elon Musk if Democrats investigate the SpaceX and Tesla CEO after midterm elections. He also suggested the possibility of pre-emptive pardons for staff and others around him if Democrats win the election. Why it matters: Trump is positioning himself for a combative final two years in the White House, as polls increasingly point to the prospect of a significant blue wave. What they're saying: In an interview for the "Pod Force One" podcast published early Monday, host Miranda Devine asked Trump about rumors of Musk being investigated or having assets seized. "It's talk. But if it is talk, we'll have to protect them," Trump said. He went on to say he wouldn't hesitate to pardon staffers if he thought Democrats were pursuing them. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated with more information.

The News
The African National Congress is on course to lose control of most of South Africaâs major cities in Wednesdayâs local elections, according to polling data, potentially disrupting power dynamics in the national coalition government.
Several polls suggest the partyâs remaining support is increasingly concentrated in smaller towns and rural provinces as opposition parties make deeper inroads in the biggest cities that drive Africaâs largest economy. The local government vote will decide who runs 250-plus municipalities responsible for basic service provision including water, sanitation, and refuse collection. It is the ANCâs first nationwide test since falling support forced it to share power in 2024 after losing its parliamentary majority â unprecedented in the democratic era.
The latest Ipsos poll, conducted between Sept. 12 and Oct. 13, put the ANCâs national support at an âall-time lowâ of 30%, reflecting just how far its backing in urban areas has fallen. Roughly 30% of respondents in Johannesburg, the nationâs commercial hub, and Tshwane, home of the capital Pretoria, said they would vote for the ANC. And that figure fell to just 10% in the port city of Durban, where the populist uMkhonto weSizwe Party (or MK), which is pressing for sweeping state control of the economy and built around former president Jacob Zuma, is comfortably ahead in polls.
Support for the ANC, the party once led by Nelson Mandela, remains near 60% in Limpopo and the Eastern Cape, vast provinces of villages, small towns, and dispersed settlements that remain far less urbanized than Gauteng or the Western Cape, an earlier Ipsos poll showed. âAfter 30 years of democracy, voting patterns are changing and we are moving into a completely new reconfiguration of the political spectrum,â said Andre Duvenhage, a political analyst at South Africaâs North-West University.
The Ipsos survey and several other polls â if replicated on voting day â indicate that most metropolitan municipalities would require coalition governments after the local elections. This broadly matches the assessment of think tank Oxford Economics, which has predicted that voting in six of the eight metros would fail to produce an outright winner, creating the need for coalition negotiations.
A poor ANC showing would âupend the power dynamicsâ inside the national coalition government, said William Gumede, a political analyst and governance professor at the Johannesburg-based University of Witwatersrand. He argued that if the ANCâs share of the vote was close to or fell below the Democratic Alliance, it would force the former liberation movement to treat its junior partner âas an equal powerâ in policy-making and government decisions.
The two parties became governing partners after the 2024 general election for the first time, bringing ideological rivals into the same government where the ANC remains committed to state-led economic transformation policies while the DA has pushed for bigger private investment.
Know More
Political parties have entered the final stretch of campaigning with failures of local government providing much of the ammunition. Unreliable water supplies, deteriorating roads, corruption, and mismanagement of municipal finances, have left many councils struggling to provide basic services.
Companies are increasingly paying for the failures, said Busi Mavuso, CEO of lobby group Business Leadership South Africa, whose members account for nearly a third of the countryâs $490 billion GDP. She said businesses are investing in backup water storage, private security, and road repairs to remain operational. âCapital is not sentimental,â she said, warning that investors can redirect money when infrastructure and municipalities fail.
That makes the quality of municipal governments formed after the election important to investors, according to Awongiwe Booi, a fixed income analyst at South African lender Investec. âThe alignment and performance of the coalition post the election will matter more than the poll results themselves,â she said. South Africaâs eight metros house about 40% of the population and account for an outsized share of economic activity.
Tiisetsoâs view
The theory from an investorâs perspective is that a weaker ANC is better for public finances. That deserves testing. Even so, an electoral decline makes saying no politically harder, creating a longer term political risk. It might just embolden those arguing that a post-President Cyril Ramaphosa ANC should move toward MK Party and Economic Freedom Fighters, a radical left movement advocating for nationalization of mines and banks, and ditch the market friendly DA, which has long struggled to shake off its image seen by many Black voters as a party of white interests.
Thereâs nothing irrational about voters demanding more from a state where a third of the work force is unemployed and ranks highest in the World Bank inequality index. The problem is that political need does not create fiscal space.

Ryanair is considering a temporary wage freeze for staff and confirmed airfares will be "materially higher" next summer because of a sharp rise in fuel costs following the US-Israel war with Iran.
The airline said it expects fuel prices to remain high "well into 2027" unless there is a "swift resolution" to the conflict.
Ryanair said its fuel bill is forecast to be â¬2bn (Â£1.6bn) higher in the short-term and its boss, Michael O'Leary, said airfares would have to rise by "double-digits" to help cover the cost.
But the firm said that was unlikely to be enough and it is looking into pay freezes. Unite, the union representing Ryanair staff, said it had not been told of "any such proposals".
O'Leary also said the company would slow down hiring as airline's costs rise.
The airline said its pre-tax profits fell by 16% to â¬2.4bn during the six months to the end of September, largely due to fuel costs jumping by 15%.
The company said that although 80% of its fuel bill had been "hedged" â in effect, bought in advance at fixed prices â the cost of the remainder was elevated.
O'Leary reiterated forecasts from earlier this year Ryanair would "need a 20% fare increase" to cover the cost of jet fuel.
"I'm not sure we'll get to 20%," he said. "But we're certainly looking at double-digit fare increases across Europe from all airlines in 2027."
Aviation fuel prices have surged this year as a result of the US-Israel war with Iran, which has dramatically reduced the supply of refined products coming from the Gulf and increased competition for those produced elsewhere.
Ryanair also said it was weighing up whether to freeze pay, as multi-year wage deals with unions come to to an end. The policy could be implemented from April next year.
Oliver Richardson, national officer at Unite, said the union "hasn't been advised of any such proposals and we have a multi-year pay deal in place which covers next year. A number of Unions across Europe have the same".
He said: "Our pay agreement was not attached to, nor dependent on company performance. This was something that the Ryanair was at pains to emphasise. As such we would expect it to be honoured."
Ryanair also said it would increase its use of artificial intelligence within its back office and support functions.
Meanwhile, Ryanair has cut back on winter flights and said on Monday there would be more to come. It said this was happening across the airline industry, particularly with short-haul carriers.
O'Leary said: "We believe those cuts will continue into the summer of 2027. Over the medium term, we expect short-haul capacity will remain constrained out to the early 2030s."

Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.
Uganda's acting army spokesperson Chris Magezi on Monday said the first group of troops deployed to Somalia through a bilateral arrangement had already arrived back home and others would follow in a few days' time.
He said all forces, including those under the African Union (AU) mission, would exit by the end of 2027 in the phased withdrawal.
Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.
A first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.
Last week, Kainerugaba said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces.
"As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.
On Monday, Magezi said this would mark the end of Uganda's operations in the Horn of Africa country, with Somalia expected to "assume full responsibility for security".
The withdrawal comes after Somalia President Sheikh Mohamud met his Ugandan counterpart Yoweri Museveni in Kampala last week.
The meeting was planned to discuss Somalia's security situation, as well as trade and economic ties between the two countries.
The Somali president reportedly sought to persuade Uganda to extend its military presence.
In remarks during the visit, Museveni urged Somali leaders and citizens to unite in the fight against the militant insurgency led by al-Shabab, which is part of al-Qaeda.
An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements.
Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency for more than two decades.
After Ugandan forces were first deployed to the country in 2007, they played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns.
They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.
Ugandan troops were involved in successive Africa Union missions, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.
This was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.
Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support.
A 12-month transition plan is due to begin in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.

The move comes amid early signs that investors are approaching the limits of how much debt they can absorb: Morgan Stanley said AI-related borrowing ballooned to almost $500 billion through September, up from $100 billion during the same period last year.
The surge comes despite rising interest rates, including for the worldâs largest firms â SpaceX is paying as much as 8.75% on parts of its latest loan, Semafor reported. âThis may be the most transformative tech boom yet, but itâs not big enough to defy the high price of money,â an expert wrote.

e1f200e6b0a3.text:
Amenaâs view
The drums of war are beating again, and the oil-exporting states are bracing âfor the worst,â as the UAEâs presidential advisor Anwar Gargash recently put it. Eight months into the US-Iran war, one lesson is clear: There is no amount of operational resilience that can shield energy infrastructure from an unresolved political conflict. Renewed strikes will put more of the regionâs oil supply at risk.
Saudi Arabia and the UAE have demonstrated exceptional levels of resilience, activating contingency plans, carrying out repair works in record time, and keeping customers supplied. Their bypass pipelines have proven the value of planning for the shift from the âjust in timeâ model to the âjust in caseâ approach.
The UAEâs 1.8 million-barrel-per-day (bpd) pipeline from Abu Dhabi to Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman was once questioned as an investment. Its cost was recovered after just one month of conflict, according to people familiar with the matter. A second link with similar capacity is expected to be completed by July 2027. Saudi Arabia is considering expanding its larger East-West Pipeline and may bring in countries like Iraq and Kuwait that donât have shipping outlets outside the Gulf.
Within the industry, thereâs a growing consensus that the pre-war oil flows will not return. More investment will be earmarked for contingencies, reflecting in part the view that reaching a diplomatic resolution to the Iran war is unlikely anytime soon.
So far, the global energy system has performed better than expected. Gulf exporters kept their oil flowing despite the risks faced in Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb, inventories were released, and some demand was curtailed, all of which combined to limit the oil price spike. But this resilience should not be mistaken for future security of supply, especially as this potential escalation comes at a time when global inventory levels have been drained by around 1 billion barrels. Brent is trading above $110 a barrel, of which perhaps $40 could be attributed to geopolitical risk.
While much of the focus is on guessing what US President Donald Trump is planning, the reality for the oil industry is that higher prices may have eroded around 3 million bpd of demand, according to energy industry executives. This assumption is even more pessimistic than the IEAâs forecast of demand declining by around 2.6 million bpd this year. Another rise in prices, or oil prices sustained at this level, will only lead to even more demand destruction.
This week, ahead of Abu Dhabiâs flagship energy conference ADIPEC, senior executives and CEOs from the energy industry gathered to discuss the challenges facing the industry under the Chatham House Rule. There was frustration about the lack of policy support, especially from European governments, for investment in the upstream sector and the construction of refineries. Over the past two decades, around 25% of Europeâs refineries were shut down, mainly as a result of policies related to the energy transition. Today, energy executives from European oil majors are pressured to address rising prices of oil products without having the facilities needed to deliver the energy to consumers.
If thereâs one silver lining from this crisis, itâs prioritizing investments in new supply and abandoning the dichotomy between the concepts of âold energyâ and ânew energy.â At the opening of ADIPEC on Monday, Sam Altman, the CEO of OpenAI, was asked what the biggest challenge facing his industry is. He replied with one word: âenergy.â
Another round of war will make that energy costlier, and less abundant.
Amena Bakr is the Head of Middle East Energy & OPEC+ research at Kpler, an independent global commodities trade intelligence company.
Notable
- The UAEâs race toward its âZero Hormuzâ strategy runs through Fujairah, where investments can be seen in all directions intended to move the fossil fuels and products that would otherwise be trapped in the Gulf, Semafor reported.

Western countries are also growing increasingly worried about Chinese industrial expansion into new sectors, challenging other advanced economies. In just the last five years, the Asian giant has doubled its chemical production, now accounting for around half the worldâs products in a sector once dominated by Western firms, âraising the prospect of further tensions with the EU and US,â the Financial Times said.

A shortage of oil and gas workers in Venezuela is holding up investment and frustrating Washingtonâs plans to tame soaring fuel prices. Decades of mismanagement and corruption have hollowed out Venezuelaâs oil industry, while a government crackdown and an economic crisis led to a mass exodus.
Spurred by the Trump administration, Big Oil has again set its sights on the country, which holds the worldâs largest stated oil reserves, but a talent shortfall â around 5,000 Venezuelan oil and gas workers are believed to be in the US alone â is proving a bottleneck, with many wary of returning, fearing a resurgence in authoritarianism. âThere are no guarantees for a family that has been abroad for 15 years,â an expatriate said.

A prominent Michigan Democrat who switched her endorsement to the Republican candidate in the final days of the vital Senate race has defended her decision, saying simply: "I changed my mind".
Haley Stevens, who unsuccessfully ran to become the Democratic nominee, withdrew support for the Democratic candidate who beat her in the primary contest, Abdul El-Sayed.
Ahead of the US midterm elections on Tuesday, Stevens gave her last-minute backing to Republican Mike Rogers, sparking widespread condemnation from her Democratic colleagues.
Stevens and El-Sayed have clashed on a range of issues, including US support for Israel. Michigan is considered critical for Democrats' hopes of winning control of Congress in the midterms.
Hours after the announcement, appearing on CNN, , externalshe said: "I woke up this morning clear-eyed, fresh and focused on what was in my heart, and that's that."
The seat is currently in Democratic hands. Analysts say the party needs to retain it, and win a handful of others from the Republicans, if it is to gain control of the US Senate and try to challenge US President Donald Trump in his final two years.
Stevens had previously offered her endorsement to El-Sayed after conceding defeat to him during a closely-fought primary contest in August.
As recently as Saturday night, she was said by CNN to be sticking with the fellow Democrat, and was denying any suggestion she would switch sides.
In her interview with the network the following day, Stevens did not provide her specific rationale, saying: "I changed my mind. (El-Sayed) said, 'Hey, I don't need your endorsement.' That's fine. Why the anger? Why the frustration?"
Stevens insisted that "nothing with me changed". She added that she was now "rock solid" in her choice to back Rogers, although insisted: "I still love my party a whole lot."
Fellow Democrats who condemned the Stevens endorsement were also critical of her interview performance. It was described as "painful" by Debbie Dingell, who, like Stevens, currently represents Michigan in the House of Representatives.
A public feud between Stevens, a centrist Democrat, and El-Sayed, who represents the party's left wing, has boiled over in recent days.
Stevens gave her endorsement to Rogers just two days before the election - making a surprise appearance alongside the Republican on Sunday.
"I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly afterwards. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate," and then went on to say: "That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.
The move stunned many of her fellow party members, who condemned her decision to switch her support just two days before the election.
Chuck Schumer, the top Democrat in the US Senate, called it "despicable betrayal", and many of the Stevens staff reportedly resigned immediately after her announcement.
Michigan Democratic Party chair Curtis Hertel wrote on X that Stevens is "not a current member of the Michigan Democratic Party, nor will she be in the future".
Republicans, meanwhile, applauded the move. Rogers himself said the move showed "courage", and Trump agreed that Stevens had been "very brave".
Stevens's schedule for Sunday initially involved her appearing at an event alongside El-Sayed, but she was reportedly asked by him not to come earlier in the weekend.
As Stevens instead made her appearance alongside Rogers, she said: "This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me there."
When asked about Stevens' endorsement, El-Sayed told reporters he was focused on the problems that were facing people in the state.
"At the end of the day, I don't think about Haley Stevens," he said on Sunday. "None of this matters."
Throughout the Michigan race, El-Sayed's strong criticism of Israel has been a source of tension within his party.
A recent flashpoint involved an advert that came from an outside liberal group. The advert linked rising prices in the US with American support for Israel. Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn it. El-Sayed said he did not agree with the advert's contents and said he had nothing to do with its contents, which was welcomed by Stevens.
The Michigan contest more broadly is one of the most closely-watched and bitter contests of the midterms.
El-Sayed, who would be the first Muslim person ever elected to the US Senate, has faced a variety of attacks from Rogers and Trump.
The president has invoked 9/11 and called him a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.

South African police have arrested five people in connection with a brutal attack on a cattle farmer, who was assaulted and tortured in what has been described as a "senseless and barbaric" act.
Donovan Marx, 50, was attacked during a house robbery on his farm in Ventersdorp, a small town in South Africa's North West province, last Wednesday.
Marx was ambushed as he returned home, shot and stabbed and had his ears cut off in the horrific ordeal, police said.
All five of his alleged attackers were arrested over the weekend, a move welcomed by Marx's wife and family.
They added that the "legal process must [now] take its course".
The horrific attack has caused widespread outrage in a country which is used to high levels of violence.
Police last week explained how the attack on Mark happened.
A group of masked men armed with guns approached a worker at Mark's house as he was mowing the lawn, they said in a statement.
The attackers then demanded to know where Marx was before tying the worker's hands and feet with cable ties.
When Marx returned home, police said two of the suspects allegedly approached him and shot him in the upper body.
"They [then] dragged him inside the house, tied his hands and feet with cable ties, and allegedly stabbed him."
The suspects then ransacked the house and took three firearms from a safe before escaping with Marx's van.
The ordeal ended after the farm worker managed to free himself and call for assistance.
Marx was rushed to hospital, where he remains, but may need prosthetic ears after surgeons were unable to save his own, local news site IOL reported.
South Africa's Agriculture Minister Willie Aucamp condemned the attack on Marx, adding there was no "place in our country for such senseless and barbaric acts".
The chair of parliament's police committee, Ian Cameron, praised police for the swift arrests and called for a "strong, properly investigated case" to follow.
The five suspects, aged between 26 and 56, will appear in local courts on Tuesday and face house robbery, attempted murder and illegal possession of firearms and ammunition charges.
Some right-wing groups have used such attacks on white farmers, who are often from the Afrikaner community, to say there is a genocide against white people in the country - a claim that has been widely discredited.
Although the claims have been dismissed by every political party in the country, including those representing Afrikaners, US President Donald Trump has repeated them and has offered white Afrikaners asylum in the US.
South Africa's latest crime statistics, covering the period between April and June 2026, do not specify how many attacks took place on farms and only recorded one robbery in a rural area.
However, police data show most victims of crime in South Africa, including on farms, are black.

a43157dfe0bc.text: Pharmaceutical companies facing a steep patent cliff are concluding the key to future profits may be customized treatments tailored to patients' genes and lifestyles — not blockbusters aimed at large patient populations. Why it matters: The pivot could influence which diseases get treated in the decades to come, and how much the health system pays. The stakes are huge. More than $500 billion in brand-name drug sales is potentially at risk from generic competition between 2026 and 2032, according to the consulting firm Evaluate. The latest: The race is on to find new treatments that each generate at least $2.4 billion in global sales, a new Iqvia Institute report finds. They're increasingly specialty treatments, biologics and rare disease drugs — with a small group of flagship products accounting for an outsized share of industry sales. GLP-1 drugs like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Zepbound now define that elite category. The next wave could include "biological missiles" that combine antibodies with chemotherapy to target specific cancer cells. "As precision medicine continues to advance, similar approaches may extend beyond oncology into areas such as immunology, metabolic disease and neurology," the report states. Reality check: It's not clear whether all of the innovation will cure more people, or just make health care more expensive. Novel RNA drugs and cell and gene therapies are expensive, hard to make and target small groups of patients. Challenges identifying eligible patients and getting insurers to pay for treatments have already revealed a disconnect between promising R&D and patient benefit. Widespread concern over high drug prices will force manufacturers to find more unmet needs and build sales more quickly after a drug's launch, according to the report. Context: Top-selling drugs historically were aimed at large patient populations with chronic conditions like high cholesterol. The ulcer drug Tagamet became the first to exceed $1 billion in sales in 1986. Over time, cancer and immunology drugs became major drivers of growth, followed by GLP-1s, which are sparking huge demand for conditions beyond obesity and diabetes but also driving up health costs. Iqvia found that blockbusters on average maintain a dominant market position for 12.1 years before losing market exclusivity, or nearly 80% of their commercial life. Specialty drugs for rare or complex diseases lasted even longer. Yes, but: A substantial number of top-sellers will lose patent protection and face potential competition from generics between 2028 and 2036. Bristol Myers Squibb's blood thinner Eliquis and Merck's cancer blockbuster Keytruda, which are both due to lose market exclusivity in 2028, accounted for a combined $65 billion in global sales in 2024. Follow the money: The search for new blockbusters is playing out in a highly charged environment. Drugmakers and biotechs not only have to figure out how to grow outside of crowded categories but also how much payers value new classes of drugs, Evaluate says . There's also uncertainty over China , where Western drug giants have invested tens of billions of dollars to bolster their product pipelines. Evaluate predicts that only autoimmune disease drugs will come close to rivaling GLP-1s, because of their potential to treat dozens of conditions. One example is AbbVie's injectable Skyrizi for plaque psoriasis, arthritis, Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, which could find more uses and generate more than $33 billion in sales in 2032. Iqvia identifies RNA therapeutics as a potentially important middle ground between traditional "small molecule" drugs for chronic diseases and highly specialized genetic treatments. These drugs can target disease-causing mutations across many genes and conditions, with applications for central nervous system, cardiovascular and kidney disease, as well as rare conditions. The bottom line: The success at innovating while also making sure patients have access to the new treatments "will ultimately determine whether the growth in blockbuster medicines observed over the past 25 years can continue at its extraordinary pace," Iqvia concludes.

3d8acbe44bb1.text: Republicans are burning tens of millions of last-minute ad dollars to try to rescue three red-state senators who they say ignored months of warnings that their campaigns were in danger. Why it matters: Senate races in Kansas, South Carolina and Mississippi are normally GOP layups. This year, Republicans have diverted resources from swing-state battles to defend them. The frustration with Sens. Roger Marshall (Kansas), Darline Graham (South Carolina) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (Mississippi) comes amid broader GOP finger-pointing as polls show a nationwide backlash against President Trump . "Democrats may win these seats in a wave ... but not a blue wave. It's the wave of arrogance [and] laziness ... that washed over these GOP incumbents and made them think they were invincible," said a national GOP operative involved in several key Senate races. By the numbers: National Republicans have spent $33 million in Kansas, $21 million in South Carolina and $2.4 million in Mississippi, according to data compiled by campaign finance expert Rob Pyers. Trump also has spent valuable campaign time in all three states. Behind the scenes: Republicans say the three senators ignored warnings to raise more money and build stronger campaign operations. National Republican Senatorial Committee chair Tim Scott warned all GOP senators in February 2025: "We do not need to spend time and money in places where races should not be competitive." Trump's political operation also warned Senate Republicans that they would need to pull their own weight. The most complaints center on Marshall, who has raised just $7.5 million compared with $19 million for his Democratic opponent, Adam Hamilton. Republicans blame his strained relationship with the banking and credit card industries — major GOP donors — and a lack of outreach to K Street. Republicans describe Marshall's campaign as overconfident. About a month ago, his team told aides to other GOP senators that the race would be effectively over within 10 days once it released opposition research on Hamilton. It wasn't. Strategists blame chief of staff Brent Robertson for Marshall's weak campaign operation. The campaign only recently tapped veteran Trump operative Chris Grant as part of a last-minute rescue effort. Alex DeGrasse, another veteran strategist recently hired to help Marshall, pointed to millions in spending by national Democrats and said the senator has made "hundreds of stops across all 105 counties in Kansas" and continues to "work hard for the people of Kansas." In Mississippi, Republicans have long viewed Hyde-Smith as a political underperformer. In 2020, she ran six points behind Trump. She has raised just $6.5 million despite warnings that Democratic megadonors, including George and Alex Soros, were preparing to spend heavily against her. Democratic groups have poured $13.7 million into the race. Republicans also fault Hyde-Smith for holding too few campaign events and underestimating her Democratic opponent, district attorney Scott Colom. Hyde-Smith's campaign did not respond to a request for comment. In South Carolina, Republicans fault Graham for failing to tap her late brother Lindsey Graham's donor network and showing little interest in soliciting contributions. In the first two weeks of October, Democrat Annie Andrews outraised Graham $4.2 million to $570,000. Graham spokesperson T.W. Arrighi said the senator "has faced unprecedented headwinds since losing her brother three months ago, and has risen to the occasion." Some Republicans are sympathetic to Graham, a political novice thrust into the Senate after her brother's death who faced a grueling primary and little time to campaign. They blame Trump for pushing her to run. Yes, but: Republicans point to Idaho Sen. Jim Risch, whose campaign required no spending from national GOP groups, as an example of an incumbent who took the political environment seriously. What they're saying: Representatives for the NRSC and the pro-GOP Senate Leadership Fund super PAC didn't respond to requests for comment. What's next: Top Republicans say the party needs to rethink how it deals with complacent incumbents in 2028 — and make clear that its campaign organizations can't be treated like a charity.

3c1e3405fb34.text: A powerful El Niño could bring major shifts in electricity supply and demand across the U.S. this winter, posing new challenges for utilities. Why it matters: The U.S. power grid has far more solar, wind and battery storage than during the last major El Niño, and the ongoing event could reveal whether that changing energy mix has made the grid more resilient or left it vulnerable in new ways. Driving the news: A very strong El Niño is strengthening in the tropical Pacific and is expected to continue into spring 2027, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says. NOAA's latest outlook favors wetter-than-normal conditions across California , the Southwest and much of the southern U.S. this winter, while the northern Rockies and parts of the Great Lakes lean drier and much of the northern U.S. leans warmer. The intrigue: El Niño doesn't affect every electricity resource the same way. A March study found that previous super El Niños were associated with reductions in potential solar power output of nearly 5% in parts of California over 12 months — and more than 10% in the state's north during winter. Vincent Tidwell, chief scientist at Pacific Northwest National Laboratory, says a wetter California winter could boost hydropower, while reduced precipitation or snowpack in the Pacific Northwest could cut generation there. Erik Smith, a climate scientist at the Electric Power Research Institute, tells Axios the Southeast is another region to watch for reduced solar generation as El Niño favors cloudier conditions. California now has more than 21 gigawatts of battery capacity , giving the grid another tool to manage fluctuations in electricity supply — one it barely possessed during the last very strong El Niño. The Columbia and Snake river basins accounted for roughly 62% of Western U.S. hydropower generation between 2001 and 2020, according to a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory analysis . Tidwell tells Axios that the Western grid is accustomed to shifting electricity between regions when hydropower conditions differ, helping compensate for shortages. Federal water managers, states and utilities use seasonal forecasts to plan for potential hydropower availability at Hoover and Glen Canyon dams on the Colorado River, Tidwell says. Zoom in: Tidwell expects natural gas to play a larger backup role if El Niño reduces Pacific Northwest hydropower and California solar generation this winter. Other resources, including wind, geothermal and nuclear power, provide additional options, though he says El Niño's effects on wind generation remain poorly understood. The big picture: A very strong El Niño could actually ease some pressure on the electricity system, Smith says. Warmer-than-normal conditions across the northern U.S. could reduce winter heating demand, potentially offsetting some of the pressure from changing electricity supplies elsewhere. Yes, but: Even a very strong El Niño doesn't guarantee specific weather impacts. A severe cold outbreak could still stress the grid despite a warmer-than-average winter, while a few major storms could radically alter regional rainfall and snowpack, Smith says. The bottom line: "We have a lot of confidence in how the averages are going to play out, but we don't have a lot of confidence in the day-to-day, week-to-week, particular weather events that could drive those averages," Smith says. Sign up here for Axios' Future of Energy newsletter.

3877f7c2cdbd.text: I've spent the past week trying to figure out whether Apple's $2,000 iPhone Duo is the future of smartphones or just an expensive way to do things I could already do on my regular iPhone. The answer, unsurprisingly, is a bit of both. Why it matters: Apple wasn't first to the folding smartphone party. Samsung, Google and others began making them years ago. But Apple's arrival in a category has a way of reinventing it. The big picture : The most exciting thing about Apple's first foldable iPhone isn't necessarily what it can do today but what it can become. Already, it's inspiring developers to explore possibilities that could reshape how we use our devices. Old habits die hard One of my first surprises was how little I initially used the Duo's biggest selling point: its folding screen. While other reviewers talked about endlessly opening and closing their devices, I found myself mostly using the smaller outside display. After years of conventional iPhones, it was a mix of instinct and muscle memory. Zoom in: Over time, though, I found reasons to unfold it. Watching sports was one of the clearest advantages. I pulled out the Duo at Starbucks to watch the 49ers with my son and later followed a tied World Series game in a doctor's waiting room. At the WNBA Finals, having forgotten my laptop, I managed some quick edits to a story about Anthropic's IPO . I wouldn't want to write a full article that way, but it was reassuring to have the option. Playing the New York Times' Spelling Bee alongside its Spelling Bee Buddy helper was a small but delightful example of multitasking without constantly switching apps. Between the lines: The Duo's advantages aren't always about more screen space. Sometimes they're about what you can physically do with a phone that bends. I tried watching Netflix with the phone unfolded, propped up like a tent and partially folded into a miniature laptop. I also used the Duo's ability to stand on its own to capture wide shots of the WNBA Finals from a press-box ledge without needing a tripod. Other experiences were less seamless, including getting the orientation right when trying FaceTime's option to use multiple camera views. The developer wild card Perhaps the biggest difference between the Duo and the Android foldables is the enthusiasm Apple's device has sparked among independent developers. Zoom in: Some of the early experiments are more entertaining than useful, including apps that turn the Duo into a virtual cassette player or a grilled cheese toaster . My favorite was Tiny Computers , which let it simulate a semi-functional 1984 Mac, Windows 95 PC or candy-colored iMac. Nearly two decades after the App Store debuted, we aren't all using our iPhones as virtual cigarette lighters. And I doubt we'll all be making imaginary grilled cheese sandwiches on our phones 20 years from now. Zoom out: But these early experiments offer glimpses of what might be possible when developers start thinking beyond a conventional rectangular screen. The question isn't whether today's novelties become hits. It's whether all this experimentation eventually produces genuinely new ways of using our phones — the kind of breakthroughs that make today's smartphones feel indispensable. The $2,000 question For all the fun I've had with the Duo, its price is an insurmountable obstacle. At $2,000, it's simply not a purchase I could justify for myself, much less recommend broadly. The catch: There are other compromises. I missed Face ID, occasionally fumbling for the side-mounted Touch ID sensor until I started wearing an Apple Watch to make unlocking the phone easier. And when I needed to accomplish something quickly, I often instinctively reached for my familiar, traditional iPhone. What I'm watching: On Friday, I tried putting the Duo away to see if I missed it. I didn't find myself longing for it the way I sometimes felt when I only had the Duo only and missed having a better camera. The bottom line: The Duo is a fascinating glimpse of where smartphones could go next. But early buyers are paying a steep premium to participate in an experiment whose biggest rewards may still be years away.

Georgia Helped Inspire the Medicaid Work Rules. Its Own Rules Could Soon End.
After years of searching for affordable health insurance, Trey Wright discovered Georgia Pathways to Coverage.
The state’s limited Medicaid expansion program allowed the 27-year-old living in the rural city of Jesup in southeastern Georgia to finally visit a primary care doctor regularly. It also covered weekly shots to manage an array of allergies, saving him more than $1,700 a year in out-of-pocket costs, he said.
Gov. Brian Kemp pursued Pathways as an alternative to full Medicaid expansion, which 40 other states and Washington, D.C., adopted as part of the Affordable Care Act to make more low-income people eligible for healthcare coverage.
Launched in 2023, Georgia’s program currently provides health coverage through Medicaid, the federal-state insurance program, to more than 20,000 people. It requires those enrolled to prove they’re working or doing other qualifying activities such as workforce training or community service — and it served, in part, as a model for the Medicaid work requirements that will roll out across most of the country starting Jan. 1.
Now Pathways, one of Kemp’s main health policy initiatives, is slated to expire at the end of the year unless it’s renewed. That would coincide with the Republican’s term ending, leaving his successor with big decisions about the program and challenges delivering on promises for Medicaid.
It’s a tight race between Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former Atlanta mayor who wants to fully expand Medicaid eligibility, and Republican Rick Jackson, a healthcare staffing executive and billionaire who has pitched “intelligent Medicaid expansion” but has provided few details.
Whoever wins the governor’s race must decide whether the state can afford to bring Pathways in line with new federal Medicaid work rules established under President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The federal rules include more exemptions than Georgia’s, and state officials said that would make the program fiscally unsustainable, by expanding coverage to an estimated 100,000 more people.
Joining the states that have expanded Medicaid coverage under the ACA could open the program to an estimated 347,000 uninsured Georgians, according to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
“There’s a lot of opportunity for the next governor to implement changes that are rooted in the realities of Georgians who for so long have been locked out of the ability to achieve optimal health,” said Leah Chan, director of health justice at the left-leaning Georgia Budget and Policy Institute.
Midterm Elections, a Looming Federal Decision
Georgians whose incomes are at or under the federal poverty level — $33,000 per year for a family of four in 2026 — and who complete up to 80 hours of qualifying activities a month are eligible for Pathways.
The future of the program rests heavily with the next governor, who will have to determine whether it’s fiscally sustainable past the end of the year.
The Jackson campaign did not respond to questions from KFF Health News. His campaign website says he plans to “use better technology” to “transform healthcare.”
Bottoms would “restructure” Pathways to cut through bureaucracy until Georgia fully expands Medicaid, said TaNisha Cameron, a spokesperson for her campaign.
“As governor, she will make meaningful improvements to Georgia’s eligibility and enrollment systems to ensure people can get enrolled and prevent people from being denied simply because of paperwork barriers,” Cameron said.
Bringing the program in line with federal law requires Georgia to offer exemptions to its work rules that it doesn’t now. For example, under the new federal Medicaid work rules as outlined, those who prove they are too sick to work wouldn’t be subject to the reporting requirements. Other groups can get exemptions, too, such as people with substance use disorder or caretakers for people with disabilities.
Georgia officials want the federal government to chip in more to pay for this expanded group of people who would qualify for an exemption. The state made a similar request for additional federal funding when it applied to create Pathways, but it was denied.
A state estimate projects an additional $1.4 billion in spending for this group by mid-2028. And state officials have signaled they may let the program expire at the end of the year if they don’t get the extra cash.
“The state will have no alternative but to make decisions that imperil health policy goals around personal responsibility and healthy choices,” state Medicaid agency officials wrote in their funding request to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.
CMS said it doesn’t comment on pending requests.
Carter Chapman, a spokesperson for Kemp, said the governor supports the request by the Department of Community Health, Georgia’s Medicaid agency, for enhanced funding and remains “committed, as he always has been, to ensuring Georgians have access to quality healthcare while maintaining fiscal discipline for the state.”
If the federal government grants the request, it could set a precedent for other states to draw down more federal money for limited Medicaid expansions, like Georgia’s, potentially putting the federal government on the hook for additional spending.
“It’s an attractive fiscal offer for states,” said Joan Alker, a health policy researcher and executive director at the Georgetown University Center for Children and Families.
That would reduce the incentives for states to fully expand Medicaid and might even encourage some to roll theirs back, policy researchers said.
But with Georgia’s work requirements serving as a model for the nation’s work rules, the chance of full Medicaid expansion in the state isn’t so far out of reach, said Laura Colbert, executive director of the consumer advocacy group Georgians for a Healthy Future.

A GOP Congressman Backed Medicaid Work Requirements. His Voters Might Be Exempt.
When U.S. Rep. David Valadao defended voting for a bill aimed at reducing Medicare spending by billions, the Republican noted his role in securing a key provision that will require some adult beneficiaries to work — a mandate he called “not an unreasonable ask.”
But the voters in his California Central Valley district, home to one of the most competitive House races in the nation, might get a pass from the Medicaid work rules in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which President Donald Trump signed into law last summer.
Starting in January, the law requires many nondisabled adults enrolled in Medicaid in 43 states and Washington, D.C., to work, volunteer, or go to school for at least 80 hours a month. But those who live in counties where a high number of people are out of work could get relief — one of several carve-outs in the law.
“Based on current numbers, every county in CA-22 would qualify for this exemption,” Valadao’s website says, referring to his district. “This waiver is important because it takes real-life situations into account, and if someone is trying to work but opportunities are limited, they won’t be required to.”
The congressman, who has said enrollees in Medicaid — the federal-state program covering the poor and disabled — should “put in a fair day’s work” if they can, declined an interview request. Valadao campaign spokesperson Paige Ash also declined to comment.
Valadao is among at least 21 Republican lawmakers running for reelection who voted for the 2025 GOP bill and represent counties that could qualify for a hardship exception, according to a KFF Health News analysis.
Roughly 6 in 10 residents in Valadao’s district are enrolled in Medi-Cal, the state’s Medicaid program. Researchers have estimated 60,000 more residents of his district could be without coverage by 2034 as a result of the One Big Beautiful Bill and the expiration last year of enhanced premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act insurance plans.
“It feels akin to an arsonist trying to take credit for helping put out a fire that they themselves ignited when all of this was avoidable pain from the outset,” said Miranda Yaver, an assistant professor of health policy and management at the University of Pittsburgh.
Valadao faces Democrat Randy Villegas in a district that was redrawn last year to lean more blue, and the two sides had each booked more than $16 million in advertising through Election Day, according to data compiled by AdImpact. Villegas and other Democratic challengers nationwide have made Republicans’ Medicaid vote a centerpiece of their campaigns, saying most enrollees already work, are disabled, or are caregiving.
The law allows states to apply for a short-term hardship exception for enrollees who live in counties where unemployment is at least 8%, or at least 1.5 times the national rate, whichever is lower. But it’s unclear how the Trump administration intends to implement that relief.
Some states have yet to submit their applications. Five Democratic-led states have asked the federal government to delay the work requirements, citing insufficient time to comply before the end of the year.
The press office for the federal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, which is implementing the new law, told KFF Health News in an unsigned email that states may submit unemployment data from a “reliable” source, including figures from their own labor departments. But the agency hasn’t said exactly what time frame of unemployment data states should provide.
Unemployment data can be reported in a variety of ways. It can be from the most recent month, or a 3-, 6-, or 12-month average. That data will determine how many counties — and how many people — might qualify.
Using July 2026 unemployment rates, which are not adjusted for seasonal swings, 95 U.S. counties would qualify for the exception, according to an analysis by KFF, a health information nonprofit that includes KFF Health News. Using the 12-month average, the number of qualifying counties jumps to 120.
“Which data is used matters,” said Jennifer Tolbert, deputy director of KFF’s Program on Medicaid and the Uninsured. “I think there’s a lot still unknown.”
Sixty-four counties have high unemployment rates that will most likely qualify them no matter what data is used. The vast majority of the counties have a Republican representative. CMS declined to say how long exceptions would last or which states have applied. Indiana, Iowa, and Missouri do not plan to seek the hardship exception, according to KFF’s Medicaid work requirements tracker.
Some states are waiting for answers. California is among those that have asked to push back the start date. In September, the state asked CMS for permission to use state unemployment data that it says is timelier than federal data. State officials are waiting for a response, as well as for details about how long exemptions could be granted, said Griselda Melgoza, a spokesperson for the California Department of Health Care Services.
While blue states like California are seeking exceptions to help minimize the fallout of the new Medicaid rules, Yaver said any exceptions to the work rules could serve Republicans politically in the future.
“I think that exemptions and strategic burden reduction will ultimately undercut the accountability,” she said. “Because voters will just not really see the full reach of the law.”

The call came late on a Wednesday afternoon in October, when the forecast cone stopped wobbling and started pointing steadily toward the Florida Panhandle. Tracie Hodson, who runs FavorHouse of Northwest Florida in Pensacola, decided to evacuate her domestic abuse treatment shelter.
By Thursday, her staff had relocated 15 women and 12 children. Some went north in Escambia County, away from the storm surge. Employees drove one family and another individual to a sister shelter in Panama City, three hours east. A woman who had nowhere else to go was placed, with her child, in a general community shelter. Then the staff went home and waited.
Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin at 8:30 p.m. on Friday, Oct. 9, as a Category 2 Storm with 105 mph winds. It killed at least four people, two of them in Florida.
On Saturday morning, FavorHouse’s shelter manager went to survey the damage. The buildings were still standing, but a tree fell across a long stretch of the privacy fence and clipped the back corner of the shelter, popping the soffit loose. The generator had quit roughly 18 hours into the outage, leaving spoiled food in four freezers and two refrigerators.
For the next 19 days, the shelter remained closed. FavorHouse’s outreach office had been running on internet-based phones; when the power and connection went, so did the hotline. Crisis calls were routed to Florida’s statewide domestic violence hotline and answered at Women in Distress of Broward County, on the other end of the state.
Hodson said, “We [had] just been a week not being able to provide the services that [were] desperately needed by our community members.”
What happened in Pensacola illustrates a growing concern among researchers, one Florida has almost no ability to measure: Climate change is simultaneously creating situations that can exacerbate domestic violence and weakening the systems survivors turn to for safety.
The Florida Panhandle has three certified domestic violence shelters. While FavorHouse was closed, the nearest was Shelter House in Fort Walton Beach, about 45 miles east—a drive Hodson put at an hour and a half to two hours in the days after the storm. The next closest shelter is in Panama City, roughly 140 miles away.
“We’re not really turning people away,” Hodson said during the closure. “We’re just not providing what we can and should until the shelter’s open again.”
Her injunction attorney kept working from her cell phone and appeared in domestic violence court that Wednesday, as she does every week. Outreach advocates remained in contact. The agency put people up in hotels where it was safe to do so and kept feeding them.
But for now, the shelter cannot offer its clients access to a secured, confidential building. Reopening required, among many other things, a temporary barrier where the fence had been; Florida requires that children at a certified shelter not be visible from the street.
Linda Parker, who is the president and CEO of Women in Distress of Broward County and has answered calls to Florida’s statewide domestic violence hotline since 2020, has seen how long that can actually take. After Hurricane Irma, which hit in September 2017 and took out her back fence, she said, it took nine months to repair. “You can’t stay closed for nine months.”
Parker’s organization has become a backup for centers across Florida. When a center goes offline, hotline calls are routinely routed to Broward. At least one Florida center a year temporarily hands over its hotline because of a tropical storm or hurricane, Parker said
Because moving residents to hotel rooms or general population shelters is often impractical, Florida’s certified centers try to shelter in place—and depend on generators to keep the power on.
Those generators are now eight or nine years old. FavorHouse’s failed after 18 hours. Parker now tells centers to have theirs inspected a week before an impending storm.
Storm Science
A preliminary analysis from Climate Central found that human-caused ocean warming added about 7 mph to Isaias’ peak winds and about 6 mph to its wind speeds at landfall, and that the sea surface temperatures the storm crossed were made at least four times—and in places up to 600 times—more likely by climate change.
Using NOAA’s hurricane damage potential estimates, Daniel Gilford, the Climate Central scientist who led the attribution work, calculated that roughly 36 percent of Isaias’ total damage is attributable to the seemingly small increase in its landfall wind speed—somewhere between $360 million and $1.1 billion, against damage estimates that range from $1 billion to $3 billion. Gilford cautions that the estimates are inconsistent across agencies.
Research on heat points in another direction: not at the shelter, but at the household.
In 2025, researchers analyzing over 150,000 domestic violence calls to New Orleans police between 2011 and 2021 found calls rose about 7 percent during heat waves lasting five or more consecutive days. The senior author, Anita Raj of Tulane University’s Newcomb Institute, told Inside Climate News that she expected something similar in Florida, with the differences coming down to policy and infrastructure—better-run shelters dampening the effect, more households without air conditioning amplifying it.
Raj is insistent about the mechanism. Heat does not make someone commit violence, but it can exacerbate a situation where violence has already occurred, raising the odds it escalates into something that requires a call.
In a separate 2025 study, Pin Wang at the University of Maryland and colleagues analyzed data from more than 400,000 women across 42 countries. The researchers found extreme heat was associated with an increased risk of intimate partner violence risk—with a stronger association than drought.

As demand for artificial intelligence surges worldwide, China is looking to its renewable energy sector for an advantage in the race to build the data centers that fuel the technology.
Its vast wind, solar and battery industries could help power those facilities with cheaper electricity and bring them online faster by reducing reliance on conventional grid connections.
Envision Energy, the world’s second-largest wind turbine supplier, offers a glimpse of China’s approach. In August, the company began operating a data center campus in Ulanqab, Inner Mongolia, powered by renewable electricity supplied directly to the site. Envision says the facility could become the world’s largest standalone AI data center, with plans to expand beyond 2 gigawatts of capacity. The company also says customers can lock in electricity rates 20 percent below grid prices for a decade.
The project highlights the contrasting strategies China and the United States are pursuing to meet AI’s soaring energy demands. The Trump administration has scrapped a requirement that AI data centers built on federal land be paired with clean energy generation. China is taking a different path, targeting renewable sources for more than 80 percent of the electricity used by new data centers in its major computing hubs.
“It’s a sign of how serious China is trying to pair two goals together,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the Brookings Institution’s John L. Thornton China Center. “China doesn’t want a trade-off between having faster data center build-out but sacrificing on the energy transition.”
By 2030, China aims to expand its AI computing capacity more than sixfold. That expansion is driving up electricity demand. China’s computing centers consumed about 170 terawatt-hours in 2025, accounting for 1.6 percent of the country’s total electricity use. Beijing estimated that consumption will reach roughly 800 terawatt-hours, or about 6 percent of the national total, by 2030.
The plan also calls for annual renewable electricity generation to rise from 4,000 to about 6,000 terawatt-hours, a roughly 50 percent increase. China has a track record of surpassing its clean-energy targets. Between 2021 and 2025, annual renewable electricity generation was roughly 20 percent higher than targeted.
U.S. data center electricity demand is also surging. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory estimated that U.S. data centers consumed 176 terawatt-hours in 2023, accounting for about 4.4 percent of the country’s total electricity use. Its 2024 report projected that annual consumption could reach between 325 and 580 terawatt-hours by 2028.
Energy research firm Wood Mackenzie projects annual additions of 13.2 to 16.4 gigawatts of gas-fired capacity from 2026 through 2035, depending on demand growth. That is more than triple the annual average added from 2023 to 2025.
That surge threatens to erode years of progress in cutting U.S. power-sector emissions— and the potential climate impact extends beyond the grid. A separate Sierra Club analysis, reported by Bloomberg, projects that emissions from new off-grid data centers alone could reach levels comparable to Mexico’s total annual emmissions by 2030.
While testifying before the U.S. House Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party in April, Chan described a divide in the AI race: the United States leads in large AI models and advanced chips, while China has an advantage in building power plants quickly and at scale.
China is adding generating capacity much faster, with renewables accounting for most of the growth. In 2025, it added an estimated 540 gigawatts of power generation capacity, more than 80 percent of that from renewable sources. During the same time period, the U.S. added 54 gigawatts, 60 percent from renewable sources.
David Fishman, a principal at the Lantau Group, an economic consultancy specializing in Asia-Pacific power and gas markets, agreed with Chan’s assessment of China’s ability to rapidly expand electricity supply.
“China can limit itself to renewable electricity for data centers because it already has such a strong ability to build regular electricity assets,” he said. “You can enjoy this luxury of saying, ‘We want green data centers.’”
This story is funded by readers like you.
Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.
Donate Now
Public opposition presents another challenge for data center expansion in the United States, with concerns about rising electricity bills emerging as an issue ahead of the midterm elections.
A recent Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll found that 72 percent of Americans opposed building data centers in their communities.
In China, data center construction has not sparked a comparable public backlash, Fishman said. Their expansion has not raised retail electricity prices, and many facilities are located far from major population centers. Data centers are also just one of several sources of growing electricity demand in the country.
“If it doesn’t affect your costs, it doesn’t affect your power prices, what is there to worry about?” he said.
Siting data centers away from major population centers is part of China’s national strategy. Launched in 2022, the “East Data, West Computing” initiative steers computing infrastructure toward less densely populated western regions with abundant renewable energy resources.
Inner Mongolia illustrates the appeal. China’s third-largest provincial-level region covers an area roughly 1.7 times the size of Texas and has one of the country’s lowest population densities. About 62 percent of its residents live in urban areas, leaving much of its countryside and desert sparsely populated.

Greg Casar, D-Texas, is pushing for votes on bills to tackle âprice gouging, that crack down on utility rates going up, that crack down on politicians profiting off their jobsâ â and though he acknowledged some might become law, âif Donald Trump vetoes them, then thatâs exactly the platform upon which we beat JD Vance or whoever else in 2028.â

Casar bristled at recent comments by Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, who said that Democrats should table bigger policy questions until the 2028 campaign, since Trump is still in the White House and likely to veto their legislation. The News
Americans are angry about war and prices, and a presidentâs second midterm is always difficult â but a series of decisions by President Donald Trump has made Republicansâ Senate majority ever-more vulnerable.
The mark Trump made on the midterms began in the summer of 2024, when he selected former Ohio Sen. JD Vance as his running mate. Since then, the presidentâs personnel and political decisions have reshaped the Senate battleground from what looked like an impenetrable red wall into a toss-up.
His decision to pick Vance opened up a special election in Ohio that will by the end of this week cost the GOP hundreds of millions of dollars and potentially a Senate seat. Trumpâs party-boss mentality in North Carolina, Texas, and South Carolina has further contributed to the yawning battleground.
He endorsed Rep. Mike Collins in Georgiaâs Senate race against Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff â a contest that never really got off the ground after Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp, whom Trump tried to take down in a primary in 2022, passed on the race. Ossoff is favored to win.
And party insiders blame Trumpâs tariffs and war with Iran for creating a volatile Senate map that has left seats in red states like Nebraska and Kansas vulnerable. Republicans could hold the chamber â or lose as many as a half-dozen seats on Tuesday.
âEvery negative for the GOP this cycle is a downstream effect of Iran,â said a person close to the White House. Republicans can lose up to three seats and still keep Senate control.
Trumpâs zeal on the campaign trail is undeniable and he helped direct huge sums of money into the midterms, albeit later than many Republicans would have liked. He spent the last weekend capping off a breakneck fall campaign schedule stumping in Iowa and Kansas, two places where the GOP was strongly favored to win a few months ago but now is struggling.
âPresident Trump has a 97% endorsement record and he remains the best turnout machine for our base voters,â said Republican National Committee press secretary Natalie Baldassarre.
Trump is hosting nearly 20 tele-rallies in the last days of the campaign, in addition to his almost-daily travel for rallies over the past month. The White House has sought to emphasize the administrationâs accomplishments on issues like the border, crime, and US investment and manufacturing, as they look to encourage low-propensity voters to turn out for Republicans.
âPresident Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,â White House spokesman Davis Ingle said.
But his moves to reshape the party in his image over the past two years also often showed little regard for conventional political risk assessment.
Trump created two special elections with decisions to put Vance as his vice president and Marco Rubio, a popular former Florida senator, as his secretary of state.
On Tuesday, Democrats are underdogs in Florida after nominating democratic socialist Angie Nixon to face appointed GOP Sen. Ashley Moody. The race is more competitive than expected but not a five-alarm fire like Ohio, where Vanceâs replacement, Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is in a precarious position.
The longtime preference of Husted, a former lieutenant governor, was to run for governor, according to multiple people familiar with internal party deliberations. He was instead appointed to the Senate and Vivek Ramaswamy ran for governor; Ramaswamy now trails Democrat Amy Action. A campaign spokesperson for Husted said that he âis completely focused on retiring Sherrod Brown once and for all this Tuesday.â
âPublic polls in the national media have gotten Ohio wrong every election cycle since 2016,â one Ohio GOP operative argued.

Tillis told Semafor afterward that Trumpâs backing might not have helped anyway: âIâm not sure that his endorsement would have helped me in a general election in North Carolina next year, to be quite candid.â
Trump quickly cleared the field for former RNC Chair Michael Whatley, avoiding a costly primary, but Whatleyâs candidacy crumpled against his Democratic opponent, former Gov. Roy Cooper.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said in an interview last summer that Tillis was âestablishedâ and âknew how to run and win in North Carolina,â while also praising Whatley as a candidate who could win with Republicans united behind him. In recent weeks, however, Republicans essentially ceded the race as the battleground map expanded to places like Texas.
Thune and many sitting GOP senators had hoped to convince Trump to back Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas. But Trump gave Cornyn the cold shoulder after the Texas Republicanâs remarks questioning Trumpâs viability heading into the 2024 election cycle.

Veteran lifestyle guru Martha Stewart has admitted she "really screwed up" by dressing as a homeless person for Halloween.
The 85-year-old US entrepreneur and personality has deleted a photo of herself wearing torn clothes and dirt on her face, holding a sign saying: "I am hungry help me!!"
She posted a statement on Sunday saying she was "distressed that my Halloween costume yesterday, which was intended to bring more awareness to the very serious subject of homelessness, has offended people, which was never my intention".
That was followed by a fuller apology. "It's hard to admit when you've really screwed up. My earlier statement didn't go far enough. I know many people are suffering economically. Wearing a costume like I did was insensitive and not funny. I am very sorry."
Stewart had captioned her original Instagram photo: "My QVC candles are perfect for Halloween!!!"
The post received a swift and sharp backlash.
"This sartorial take on a homeless person is a lot. Insulting? Demeaning? Confusing? All of the above," PR expert Molly McPherson wrote, external.
One person wrote on social media: "Why in the hell would you even think about wearing that as a costume?"
Another said: "Why would she do that? Who did she think would find that funny? Billionaires?"
Arguably the original lifestyle influencer, Stewart started a catering business in the 1970s and rose to fame in the 1990s when she started her own magazine, Martha Stewart Living.
She later became a billionaire, albeit briefly, when her media empire Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia was floated on the stock market in 1999.
But in 2004 she was sentenced to five months in prison after she was found guilty on a number of charges related to an insider trading scandal.
She has since attempted to rebuild her brand, starring in her own reality television show, expanding her food products and teaming up with rapper and friend Snoop Dogg for a television series.
In 2015, she sold Martha Stewart Living Omnimedia for more than $350m (Â£220m).
