The US midterms campaign is set to be the most expensive on record - with the total cost projected to reach nearly $12bn (Â£9bn), according to Open Secrets, an independent organisation that tracks campaign finance.
Most of the spending is driven by outside political groups - known as Super Political Action Committees (Super Pacs) - pouring large sums of money into some key races ahead of election day on 3 November.
The top individual donor is billionaire businessman Elon Musk, who has spent almost half a billion dollars backing Republican candidates, particularly in Texas where many of his companies are based.
BBC Verify has looked into the figures and where the money was spent.
How much has been spent?
There are rules on how much people, parties and political action committees (Pacs) can give directly to candidates.
But Super Pacs can accept unlimited contributions from individuals, corporations, labour unions, and other political committees. They can't give that money directly to candidates but they can spend it supporting them indirectly.
According to the latest Federal Election Commission, external (FEC) filings which run to mid-October, more than $9.5bn had been spent in this midterms cycle.
Pacs and Super Pacs make up more than half of that - at about $5.5bn - with their spending in the last couple of months almost doubling.
Candidates, parties and outside groups have to report their spending to the FEC, but the full totals won't be available until after the midterm elections.
However, Open Secrets has projected the total will be $11.9bn based on trends in past cycles.
This would be about 30% more than what was spent during the last midterm elections in 2022.
Which donors have spent the most?
The top 40 donors gave $2.4bn up until 14 October, according to the liberal-leaning think tank Brennan Center for Justice, external, which is a record high for that point in a midterms cycle.
"Spending in the 2026 midterms is shattering records, with more of the money coming from the wealthiest donors and groups this election," says Michael Beckel, a US campaign finance expert.
As well as individuals, organisations can also give to Pacs. For example, Geosor Corp and Fund for Policy Reform, both founded by the billionaire financier George Soros, have given a combined $102m to liberal groups.
Aside from Soros, former New York City mayor and businessman Michael Bloomberg has been the biggest Democratic donor, giving more than $60m.
Several billionaires including Jeff Yass, who runs one of the world's largest trading firms, and Richard and Elizabeth Uihlein, the owners of a US business supply company, have given over $100m this campaign to Republican causes, according to FEC filings.
But Musk has given by far the most of any individual, donating almost half a billion dollars as of October.
Musk has given most of this to a Super Pac he set up in 2024 called America PAC, as well as to the Republican-aligned Senate Leadership Fund.
Most of his money has been spent on the Texas Senate race, supporting Republican candidate Ken Paxton, who is running against Democratic candidate James Talarico.
America PAC's investments in the Texas race total more than $45m. It has also invested around $10m into both of the Senate races in Michigan and Ohio.
"Crypto companies have also been very active this cycle, with Ripple and Coinbase combining to give $63 million to fund Super Pacs promoting the crypto industry's interests," says Brendan J Glavin of Open Secrets.
What has the money been spent on?
Campaigns and political groups spend money trying to reach voters in a variety of ways - including hiring staff to do on-the-ground voter outreach and hosting campaign events like rallies. They also spend money to conduct internal polling.
However, the majority of funds are spent on advertising - especially on TV.
In this cycle, $11.15bn has been spent on advertising up until the end of October, according to ad tracking firm AdImpact, external.
"Traditional broadcast television remains the top beneficiary of advertising expenditures, though expenditures on digital ads continue to increase," says Beckel.
Similarly to Musk's spending, AdImpact tracked that most of the money has been spent on advertising in the Senate races in Michigan, Texas and Ohio, followed by Iowa and Maine.
Graphics by Tom Shiel.

9dca86bd4667.text: President Trump extolled his administration's Reflecting Pool project , dug up debunked claims of vandalism and applauded the new White House helipad in a Monday pre-Election Day speech. The big picture: Trump's deep focus on remaking the nation's capital has taken center stage as the clock ticks down to midterm elections. Driving the news: "The pool is now better and more beautiful than it's ever been before, and we're very proud of it," Trump said in Monday's speech, adding, "We went through a lot with vandalism." But Trump's own Justice Department dropped vandalism charges against former Olympian David Hearn , whose case was later killed by a judge after prosecutors acknowledged that faulty installation caused the damage to the Pool. Trump added the administration was "giving serious thought" to renaming the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to the "Trump Reflecting Pool," before later saying he was kidding. Throughout the speech, he held up printed images he identified as pipes, joints and other Pool materials. He also showed an image that appeared to show "8647" sprayed onto the base of the emptied pool, claiming "that was a Comey phrase" — a reference to his former FBI director and top foe. Zoom out: He also discussed his White House renovation projects, including the recently installed helipad and Scotts Miracle-Gro's lawn restoration after the UFC fight on White House grounds. Friction point: Trump's projects, including his D.C.-area arch and White House ballroom, have been broadly panned by Americans in polling. "This project should be a project that unites all Americans," Trump said Monday of the newly reopened Reflecting Pool, which stood empty for an extended period earlier this year. Zoom in: His pre-election pitch at times sounded more like a typical rally speech, where he touted his immigration policies and war with Iran while slamming Democrats as "a party that hates America." This is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime," he said. "The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history." He also reiterated his pitch to distribute $5,000 checks should Republicans win in the midterms. What's next: After inviting Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to speak, Trump then touted his planned " triumphal arch ," detailed plans for a "promenade" from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River and teased his golf course renovation . "We have a lot of great things planned for Washington, and I could get into the nation, but for that you don't have enough time," Trump said. He ended his closing argument by lauding a "golden age," saying, "We were laughed at like we were stupid people. We were laughed at by every ruler, every president, every prime minister, every king, every queen. But they don't laugh anymore." Axios' Josephine Walker contributed to this report. Go deeper: Trump to make midterm closing argument at Lincoln Reflecting Pool

8da482b9b1d3.text: By — Veselin Toshkov, Associated Press Veselin Toshkov, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/initial-results-suggest-iliana-yotova-wins-runoff-to-become-bulgarias-1st-elected-female-president Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Initial results suggest Iliana Yotova wins runoff to become Bulgaria's 1st elected female president World Nov 2, 2026 3:44 PM EST SOFIA, Bulgaria (AP) — Acting President Iliana Yotova is the apparent winner of Bulgaria's presidential runoff, initial results of the vote count on Sunday showed, as former interim Prime Minister Andrey Gyurov conceded defeat. According to the count by several polling agencies, Yotova received 58% of the vote. If confirmed by official results, she would become Bulgaria's first elected female head of state. Gyurov, backed by reformist pro-Western opposition parties, is said to be trailing at around 38%. Gyurov conceded defeat saying that "this is how the Bulgarian citizens have voted," and added that the results had to be accepted as they stood. Official results were not expected before Monday. The vote was the first major test for Prime Minister Rumen Radev's Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party, which endorsed Yotova. In April's parliamentary vote, the party won 131 of the 240 seats in Parliament, securing an outright majority. Observers note that a victory for Yotova will keep the presidency in the hands of the governing majority. Such a concentration of power could prevent the effective maintenance of checks and balances on policy decisions by institutions, they say. Yotova, 62, took over the presidency in January, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament, and was seeking her own elected mandate. She's expected to continue Radev's policy of keeping Bulgaria on its European path, while also supporting better relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions. After casting her vote on Sunday, Yotova said she voted for a Bulgaria that makes its own decisions and maintains a strong voice on the international stage. "I voted for national consensus through dialogue, for institutions that work for citizens, for a strong state with its own foreign policy in a strong Europe," she told reporters. The Balkan country joined NATO in 2004 and the European Union in 2007. While there is a broad consensus among the parties in parliament on the country's pro-Western path, widespread pro-Russia sentiment based on traditional historical and cultural ties with Russia has divided society, particularly since the start of Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Both Yotova and Radev have called for a diplomatic solution to end the war in Ukraine but remain evasive about possible Russian involvement in drone attacks in the Black Sea region. During a television debate between the two presidential contenders, Yotova advocated for a settlement involving both Ukraine and Russia, saying that "peace could come only through negotiations." She also proposed a security meeting involving all six Black Sea countries to sign a moratorium on hostilities. Bulgaria's presidency is primarily ceremonial. Although the head of state has no executive powers, and all major policies must be approved by parliament, direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces and can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors. Presidents in Bulgaria are elected for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 284b21fcef9e.text: By — Joshua Goodman, Associated Press Joshua Goodman, Associated Press By — Jim Mustian, Associated Press Jim Mustian, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/in-an-alaska-fishing-community-the-dan-sullivan-episode-takes-an-ominous-turn Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter In an Alaska fishing community, the Dan Sullivan episode takes an ominous turn Politics Nov 2, 2026 3:38 PM EST PETERSBURG, Alaska (AP) — In the sleepy Alaskan fishing community of Petersburg, nobody has seen Dan J. Sullivan for weeks. His rustic home stood dark a day after FBI agents visited friends who donated to his quixotic campaign to unseat the Republican senator with the same first and last name — Dan S. Sullivan. The only display of politics at his home was a yard sign from the League of Women Voters: "Stand Up for Democracy: Vote 2026." What may have begun as a ploy to harm the reelection prospects of Sen. Sullivan has taken a serious turn as President Donald Trump's administration weighs criminal charges over a campaign tactic known as ballot stacking. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. "It just seems like such a waste of our taxpayer money," said Sharon Hunter, a Petersburg resident who, with her husband, donated $1,000 to Dan J. Sullivan, a former elementary school teacher. FBI agents knocked on her door Saturday during a round of interviews with the campaign's dozen contributors. "I'm a bit incredulous about their whole angle," Hunter said, "because they're targeting a person who's been a real contributor in this community." Recruiting candidates to draw votes away from an opponent has been a part of Alaska's quirky politics for years. This time around, the state's open primary and ranked choice voting systems add another wrinkle, making it easier for lesser-known candidates to play spoilers when no contender secures a majority. The tactic has drawn fresh scrutiny as the incumbent Sullivan fights off a serious challenge from Democrat Mary Peltola, a former U.S. representative, in a race that could determine control of the Senate. 2 Sullivans vie for 1 Senate seat A building sits along the ocean Saturday in Petersburg, Alaska. Photo by Joshua Goodman/AP Peltola has denied any role in the alleged chicanery as she has sought to distance herself from a New York Times article published last week that linked a group backing the former congresswoman to a Democratic operative trying to recruit decoy candidates. "This is Alaska. We're not in the business of tricking each other up here," Peltola told supporters at a rally in Anchorage last week. Dan J. Sullivan's entry into the race has drawn scrutiny since June, when the Alaska Division of Elections tried to remove him from the primary ballot, determining he had not filed his candidacy as a Republican in "good faith." That decision was overturned by state courts. To avoid any confusion, state officials identify Dan S. Sullivan on the ballot as a Republican and the incumbent. Dan J. Sullivan repeatedly said he entered the race on his own accord and had no contact with Peltola's campaign — "zero, none, zilch," he told The Associated Press in June. He answered "no" when asked if any Democratic operatives had contacted him to run. "This is my choice," he said at the time. A federal lawsuit brought by the Republican Trump administration to revive efforts to undermine the former teacher's candidacy — and challenge a potential Peltola win by blocking certification of the election results — was dismissed on Sunday by a federal judge. The Justice Department quickly appealed. The AP's efforts to reach Dan J. Sullivan since the Times article have been unsuccessful. Several of the donors the AP interviewed said they have not spoken to him in quite some time. The senator, meanwhile, is seeking to ride the controversy to a third term. "My costume is the real Dan Sullivan – not the fake guy," he quipped to trick-or-treaters on Saturday night. The FBI comes to Little Norway The controversy has thrust Petersburg, a fishing community of 3,000 residents known as Little Norway for its late 19th-century settlers, into the center of a federal investigation and a crush of media attention. It's the type of small town where everyone seems to know everyone else's business, and more than a dozen residents said they liked and admired Dan J. a67930aa21e4.text: The top Senate GOP super PAC has nearly tripled its spending on streaming and social media platforms this election cycle to more than $200 million, Axios has learned. Why it matters : In a record cycle for ad spending, more political money is shifting to streaming, where super PACs have greater freedom to target voters, bargain and experiment — but platforms have more power to set the rules. In some states, streaming and social media have swallowed half of the Senate Leadership Fund (SLF) budget, according to a source familiar with the group's spending. SLF's $200M+ total for the 2026 cycle (up from $71M in 2024) includes tens of millions of dollars funneled through the SLF-linked Texas PAC and its affiliated nonprofit One Nation. The other side: The top Senate Democratic super PAC declined to provide a dollar figure for their spending on streaming. "Senate Majority PAC invested more this cycle in digital communications than any previous cycle, running digital campaigns in 12 states," SMP communications director Lauren French told Axios. Zoom in : Streaming and social platforms offer campaigns the power to target more specific audiences compared to traditional broadcast, and make it easier to measure the impact. "Its way more surgical than a linear broadcast buy," Zack Roday, managing director at Think Big, told Axios. But platforms can also set their own rules around which types of ads they want to accept. Some, like Netflix and TikTok, don't allow any candidate or issue ads . Republicans have complained about restrictions on ads that include transgender issues on Disney-owned platforms. Between the lines: Super PACs often pay multiple times what a campaign pays for ads on broadcast TV and radio because of laws ensuring candidates get the lowest rates. Online, super PACs can negotiate directly — and use their fat budgets and sprawling election maps as leverage. SLF works with platforms like SiriusXM, Paramount, Hulu, YouTube and others to lock in discounts based on their overall spending plans, according to the source. Groups can also experiment with different lengths and formats for ads online, breaking the 30-second broadcast mold. What to watch: Streaming ads can also be trickier for outside tracking. While Meta and Google provide public data on political ad buys, not every platform provides that kind of visibility, Streaming buys aren't covered by the same FCC filing requirements as political ad reservations on broadcast TV and radio. Broadcast filings can offer a preview of a group's targets months in advance, but streaming reservations are much harder to see. Although AI is changing the game, and there is a growing industry of companies offering better tracking tools. Super PACs still have to report independent expenditures to the FEC through 24- and 48- hour reports. Zoom out: Strong grassroots fundraising has helped Democratic candidates crush Republicans in dollars brought in directly to candidates. The GOP is hitting back with cash-flush committees and super PACs fueled by ultra-wealthy donors. In addition to super PACs moving more money to streaming, the National Republican Senatorial Committee jumped on a court decisions to coordinate ad buys with campaigns — giving them access to the candidate rate. It also allowed NRSC to negotiate with streaming platforms on behalf of multiple campaigns. The bottom line: It's just the beginning on maneuvering on streaming and coordinated buys. "That is definitely going to be the story of 2028," Kenny Day, senior vice president at IQM corporation, told Axios. He said the Supreme Court decision on coordinated spending "was too late for either party to really take advantage of the allowance of coordinated spending" in the 2026 cycle. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to show that the more than $200 million total included money spent through Texas PAC (not that it excluded that spending).

A court in South Africa has found a man guilty of stealing more than $500,000 (Â£372,822) in cash from a farm owned by South African president Cyril Ramaphosa, in a case that mired the head of state in an impeachment saga.
Imanuwela David was found guilty of theft on Monday, as well as conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal at Phala Phala farm in the Limpopo province in 2020.
Froliana Joseph, a cleaner at the property, was also found guilty of conspiracy to commit housebreaking with intent to steal.
Her brother, Ndilinasho Joseph, was acquitted on all charges.
David was accused of breaking into the cattle farm in February 2020 and taking $580,000 (Â£432,000) in cash from a sofa on the property. David then went on a spending spree, buying a range of cars including three Mercedes - among them one for his girlfriend - a Porsche, two Volkswagens as well as diamond-encrusted Rolex watches and a house.
David told the court he had made the money through businesses including diamonds and Bitcoin, claims the court rejected. The court also found that David was the only one of the two convicted who had any of the stolen cash in his bank account.
Pre-sentencing will take place on 13 November.
There have been many twists and turns in what is known as the Farmgate scandal.
The theft was largely unknown until 2022 when it was brought to light by Arthur Fraser, South Africa's former intelligence chief and an ally for the former president Jacob Zuma, when he claimed that Ramaphosa hid the theft from the police and tax authorities.
Ramaphosa admitted the theft took place but denied any wrongdoing.
An independent panel that same year found Ramaphosa could have questions to answer over the burglary. MPs voted against establishing an impeachment inquiry.
In May this year, the constitutional court ruled that parliament had acted unlawfully by shelving the panel's report, and in July Ramaphosa blocked the parliamentary inquiry through a provincial court.

Climate negotiators head to Turkey next month for the United Nations annual climate summit, just two months after an alarming U.N. report said the world has a vanishing chance of limiting global warming to safe levels.
The report’s projections will likely ripple through discussions at the event, known as the Conference of the Parties or COP, including one of its more urgent messages: In order to bring planet-warming gases under control, countries have to slash methane pollution, fast.
Because methane is more powerful over a shorter period of time than carbon dioxide—about 80 times more over 20 years—cutting methane emissions represents an expedient way to claw the world back from its current trajectory. But measuring methane, especially from livestock, its primary human-caused source, continues to stir controversy. Two new reports on methane say measurements of the gas are being manipulated and underestimated.
In a new analysis published Oct. 29 and commissioned by Greenpeace International, researchers dive into a method for measuring methane known as “global warming potential*,” or GWP*. Their findings underscore the concerns of many scientists who have said that if rich, livestock-heavy countries use GWP* to measure their livestock emissions, they can continue emitting vast quantities of methane and misrepresent the total emissions in reporting their progress toward global climate goals.
“Proponents of GWP* will tell you methane is part of the natural carbon cycle, we just need to keep it stable,” said Sophie Nodzenski, a campaigner with Greenpeace. “We argue that methane levels are already too high. Methane is the climate emergency brake. It disappears so quickly from the atmosphere and is so warming—if we acted on methane right now, we could see results within the next 15 years.”
Under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, greenhouse gas measurements have been standardized as carbon dioxide equivalents, based on their GWP, typically over 20- and 100-year time frames (GWP20 and GWP100, respectively). This has helped make different greenhouse gases more comparable.
Carbon dioxide, the most abundant greenhouse gas, persists and accumulates in the atmosphere over centuries. But because methane’s impact is speedy and brief, causing an initial burst of warming and then degrading after about 12 years, scientists have argued that GWP100 doesn’t accurately reflect its warming power.
About 10 years ago, scientists at the University of Oxford developed GWP*, in which emission rates of methane and other short-lived climate pollutants are equated to single pulses of carbon dioxide. This measurement reflects that methane doesn’t have the same cumulative effect as carbon dioxide and also that the methane emitted from cow belches originates from vegetation that originally removed carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. It assumes a steady climb in emissions won’t cause additional warming because methane degrades relatively quickly while methane sinks—mostly involving molecular processes that naturally break down the gas —mean emissions can remain stable.
Climate scientists say the science underpinning GWP* is legitimate and represents another tool to more accurately understand planet-warming emissions and how they behave. They worry, however, that the method is being used to justify weakening efforts to cut emissions from livestock and have warned against using it to measure emissions, especially as the livestock industry, including in the United States, has embraced it.
The industry has called for a “split gas approach,” underpinned by GWP*, to “better reflect the distinct warming behaviours of long- and short-lived GHGs.”
Industry groups did not respond to requests for comment from Inside Climate News.
But earlier this year, 42 prominent climate scientists warned that using GWP* threatens to undercut essential methane reductions because its calculation allows industries or countries to set “no additional warming” targets. That effort followed an open letter to New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, also signed by top climate scientists and bearing the same warning.
Last year, New Zealand, where the economically critical livestock industry accounts for nearly half the country’s greenhouse gas emissions, became the first country to set a “no additional warming” target based on GWP* accounting principles.
But critics and the new Greenpeace report say that applying GWP* to reflect progress toward the global climate goals enshrined in the Paris Agreement is potentially deceptive. They maintain it allows countries with historically high methane emissions to claim major reductions even for minor cuts, and in some cases report “negative emissions,” “climate neutrality” or “no additional warming.”

The report, based on modeling by the consultancy group Cerulogy, finds that these countries, which include two beef powerhouses, Brazil and the U.S., could cut actual methane by just 0.6 percent in 2030 compared to their 2020 emissions, yet report a 30 percent reduction under GWP*.

Before there was the other Dan Sullivan, there was the other Mike Doyle.
Four years ago, when longtime Pittsburgh Democrat Mike Doyle retired from Congress, a left-wing legislator named Summer Lee won the primary to replace him. Republicans nominated a local politician from the suburbs to face her who had a fortuitous name: Mike Doyle.
Some voters were perplexed. The new Doyleâs lawn signs called him âthe right Mikeâ without explicitly identifying him as a Republican â a moniker that would be a non-starter in the safely Democratic seat. Local Democrats got worried calls, asking why Lee was running against their beloved liberal congressman. The Democrat Doyle called an emergency press conference to clarify that he was not the Republican Doyle: âMy name is on the ballot, but itâs not me.â
Lee won, albeit by a smaller margin than other Democrats in her district had in the past. Nothing else came of the story. There was no federal investigation of the Doyle scheme; no demands not to seat Doyle if he won; no statement from the governor saying that he might not certify the election.
All of that has unfolded in Alaska this cycle. The clandestine Democratic effort to recruit a candidate who shares the name of the stateâs incumbent Republican senator could have major implications for what happens after Tuesday.
The plotâs exposure damaged Democrat Mary Peltola, knocking her off-message, and now threatens her partyâs chances of winning control of the Senate. President Donald Trumpâs administration is investigating, and also sued to block the certification of the results should Sullivan lose â though a federal judge tossed out the suit over the weekend. Those efforts, along with the announcement of investigations into candidates within 60 days of the vote, show how the Trump administration is jettisoning unwritten norms at the Justice Department.
The Alaska mess is weighing heavily on Democrats who hope to win control of Congress tomorrow. Victory in either chamber would mean a two-year license on oversight powers, empowering Democrats to subpoena the Trump administration and its allies in the private sector. There is a thirst for vengeance among some Democrats that is testing their public stance that they must restore standards blown up by Trump.
Thereâs also a shared sense, among most Democrats, that following those standards has gotten them nothing, while Republicans have benefitted from bending the rules.Â
âDonald Trump and [House Oversight Committee Chairman] James Comer have basically written a playbook on how to politicize investigations and attack political enemies and weaponize government,â said Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is in line to lead the House Oversight Committee in a Democratic majority. â[Attorney General] Todd Blanche? His whole job is just to grift for the president.â
The argument over which party first used âlawfareâ to get what it wanted is an old one. Democrats have long celebrated the Watergate investigation as an example of the Constitution and US legal system working as designed. Republicans are more likely to call the episode a coup against a president whoâd just won a landslide.
But the current debate begins, like so many irritating conversations, with the 2016 election. For all of Hillary Clintonâs errors, like telling coal miners that their jobs would vanish if she won, Democrats largely believe that she would have won the election against Trump had the FBI not abandoned its â60 day ruleâ and announced an 11th hour investigation into emails found on Huma Abedinâs laptop. Some believe that Barack Obama acted too timidly when Republicans refused to co-sign a letter warning of Russian interference in that campaign.
Nobody has ever accused Trump of acting timidly. Ten years on, his Justice Department is still probing the origins of the Russia investigation into his first campaign. When Joe Biden replaced Trump, he kept on the US attorney who was investigating his son. When Trump replaced Biden, he sacked the prosecutors whoâd worked on post-Jan. 6 investigations.
Democrats felt like suckers. Biden publicly promised that his Justice Department would act independently. Privately, he was resentful of Attorney General Merrick Garlandâs choices to hold off on investigating Trump until November 2022, after Republicans were more or less united in denouncing any Trump probe as âlawfare.â
This is on many Democratic minds as they watch the Justice Department in Alaska â even though itâs not the only race where one party meddled in a way that might confuse voters. In Maine, a conservative PAC is sending out mail for a left-wing spoiler candidate for governor. In Ohio, a conservative PAC is doing the same for a socialist Senate candidate who could threaten Democrat Sherrod Brownâs chances. In Nevada, a conservative PACâ¦ okay, you get the point.
âTheyâre obsessed with meddling in elections,â Garcia said. âWe have to put in place new rules and a new standard to get things back to a place where we donât have the president trying to rig elections constantly.â In Pennsylvania, when I asked Gov. Josh Shapiro how Democrats should respond to Trumpâs Justice Department, he was hopeful they would be the âparty of law and orderâ â by showing that this was not the way to use the governmentâs bottomless resources.
âI said every single day to our team and to the public that I enforce the law without fear or favor,â said Shapiro, referring to his six years as state attorney general. âThat is not the case in the Trump administration.â

Mario Alberto Morales made his first court appearance on a felony charge of aggravated assault with a deadly weapon for striking Miguel Parra Hernandez with an unmarked SUV on Oct. 10, as Morales chased the 48-year-old construction worker through a parking lot. A grand jury indicted Morales, 33, on Friday. During Monday's hearing, Judge Matthew Peneguy set bond at $30,000. Prosecutors had asked that bond be set at $75,000, according to the Harris County District Attorney's Office. Morales is one of just a few federal officers who have faced criminal charges over their actions on the job during President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown. Other encounters have come under investigation. READ MORE: An ICE officer is charged with assault for striking a man with a car in Houston ICE has asserted that Parra Hernandez ran in front of Morales' vehicle, an account that prosecutors say is contradicted by video. Surveillance camera video shows Morales' vehicle drive over a median and strike Parra Hernandez as he runs away. David Lindenmuth, Morales' attorney, has said his client was "truly a good man" and did not commit a crime. Parra Hernandez broke his leg and is recovering at a rehabilitation facility while in federal custody, according to Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare. Morales had worked as an ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations officer for a little more than a year, Lindenmuth said. He unsuccessfully ran for Congress this year and previously served in the Army. Morales was charged with a misdemeanor in 2013 for stealing four DVDs, according to Harris County Court records. Those charges were dismissed under a plea deal in which he paid a $270 fine. US President Donald Trump has notified Congress of his intention to remove South Africa and Rwanda from a preferential trade programme, from 1 January 2027.
The African Growth and Opportunity Act (Agoa) allows eligible African countries to export thousands of products to the US duty-free.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement that an annual review had found that both countries were engaging in practices inconsistent with the programme's eligibility requirements.
He added that the Trump administration had additionally notified the two countries of the decision.
The Trump administration cited barriers to US trade and investment, as well as concerns over national security and foreign policy interests in the region.
In Rwanda's case, Washington also raised concerns about human rights, political pluralism, the rule of law and workers' rights.
The move comes barely a week after Rwanda's defence ministry was hit with sanctions by US Treasury for its alleged role in the armed rebellion in eastern DR Congo.
The US Treasury said Rwanda's defence ministry directed thousands of troops to fight alongside M23 rebels in eastern DR Congo, providing weapons, equipment, logistics and training.
For South Africa, the US additionally pointed to corruption.
"The Trump administration is working to ensure our African partners take the necessary steps to meet the eligibility criteria," Greer said.
The announcement comes amid strained relations between Washington and both countries, with the proposed termination threatening their access to preferential trade arrangements with the US.
Last year, Trump accused South Africa of white genocide in a meeting with President Cyril Ramaphosa at the White House and launched a US refugee pathway for Afrikaners.
US Ambassador to South Africa Leo Brent Bozell III said it was regrettable that South African policies led to its termination from Agoa.
"This was a predictable and preventable outcome resulting from the rejection by South Africa's government of real concerns raised by the US," he wrote on X.

273290382ee2.text: By — David Fischer, Associated Press David Fischer, Associated Press By — John Funk, Associated Press John Funk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/evidence-suggests-parts-of-jet-broke-off-before-florida-crash-ntsb-investigator-says Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Parts of a Learjet may have broken off midair before Florida crash that killed 9, investigators say Nation Updated on Nov 2, 2026 5:35 PM EST — Published on Nov 2, 2026 2:31 PM EST WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. (AP) — Parts of a business jet likely started to break off even before it slammed into the ground and erupted in a ball of flames in South Florida, killing all nine people on board, a federal investigator said Monday. Video recorded by passersby captured the Bahamas-bound Learjet's rapid nosedive Sunday afternoon before it exploded in Greenacres, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as shocked residents looked on in horror. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site and little remained of the plane. READ MORE: Palm Beach plane crash footage isn't AI-generated, despite social media claims "Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire," Anthony Blackmon, who lives near the crash site, told NBC affiliate WTVJ. "I've always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today." Federal investigators outline the probe but decline to speculate Watch Monday's National Transportation Safety Board briefing on the plane crash in the player above. National Transportation Safety Board member Tom Chapman said during a news conference Monday that investigators found evidence the aircraft started breaking up before it hit the ground and that debris from the aircraft could be spread far and wide. "We do have some indication that the aircraft was breaking up before impact," Chapman said. "We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site." Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said key components of the jet's tail may have been lost during the turbulence or as it nose-dived. "If that happens you cannot control an airplane at that point. And that very well could explain the missile-like profile just before it hit the ground," said Guzzetti, a former NTSB and the Federal Aviation Administration investigator. Weather conditions will be a major focus of the investigation, Chapman said. Rain pounded the region on Sunday, and one of the pilots reported icing conditions at a high altitude in communications with air traffic control. Weather radar maps from the time of the crash that FlightRadar24 combined with the plane's flight path seem to show it flying directly into a storm cell that was rapidly expanding upward. But Chapman said investigators still have to determine what the weather conditions were at 35,000 feet. Chapman said the plane was originally equipped with a cockpit voice recorder that investigators hope to recover. "We have a lot of work to do on scene," NTSB investigator Timothy Monville said at the news conference. "This will be a several-day process, and the biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway." Mother identifies one of the pilots The jet began its journey at the Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas with two crew and seven passengers, Chapman said. Authorities have not released the names of the people who died and the Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office declined to discuss the death investigation, which is ongoing. Camila Corteleti told the New York Post and New York Times that her daughter, 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, was one of the pilots. She earned her pilot's license in 2023 while a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton Community High School in Florida, local news reports said at the time. Her pilot's license showed she had the rating to fly that model of Learjet but not to be in command of the flight. Her father, Allan Filgueiras, told The Associated Press he wasn't prepared to speak about the crash. A man who was driving close to the scene as the plane crashed suffered leg wounds, Monville said, but he didn't know the extent of the injury. Palm Beach County Mayor Sara Baxter asked for sympathy for the crash victims. "Please keep them in your thoughts and prayers," Baxter said. Pilot reported turbulence and ice, then the jet fell rapidly Police work near the scene of a plane crash in Greenacres, Florida, on Monday. Photo by Rebecca Blackwell/AP The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (11,000 meters) when the pilot started to report problems. The pilot said ice was accumulating on the jet and that turbulence was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (210 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net. "We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence," the pilot told controllers. The situation rapidly deteriorated. The pilot requested permission to climb another 2,000 feet (610 meters) and then quickly declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude at an alarming rate. "We're descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we're descending 10,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed. "We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed. Moments later, the pilot said: "We're going to crash into the ground." Video shows the plane banking sharply to the right before crashing and exploding. Some area residents are still not allowed to return home Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel G. Flores said at the news conference that the county "doesn't have a clue" when residents who live near the crash site will be able to return to their homes as investigators continue to comb the area. Massachusetts prosecutors have given their clearest indication yet that they plan to retry Lindsay Clancy for the murder of her three children in 2023.
At a hearing on Monday, Judge William Sullivan scheduled a 16 November hearing where he plans to rule on a handful of motions that could determine how a retrial would proceed, including a request to dismiss the first-degree murder charges.
Clancy faced a weekslong trial on those charges over the summer. It fell apart in early September after a 12-person jury failed to reach a verdict.
If there is a retrial, Judge Sullivan said, it could happen as soon as March 2027.
The prosecution did not say on Monday whether Clancy would face the same charges or amended charges in the event of a retrial.
When the parties meet again later this month, they will hear the judge's rulings on the motions argued in court on Monday, and potentially will discuss dates for a retrial, Judge Sullivan said.
Kevin Reddington, Clancy's attorney, pushed the judge for a spring trial.
"I am not going to have this woman sit incarcerated for the next year or two or three," he said. "I want a date and I want it this spring."
But prosecutor Jennifer Sprague said she wants to hear Judge Sullivan's rulings on Monday's arguments before the prosecution commits to a new date or specifics for a potential retrial.
When the judge asked for more details on how prosecutors planned to proceed with a potential retrial, Sprague responded: "This would be a retrial - as to what that looks like will depend".
But that appeared to frustrate Reddington.
"Why do we not know if the next trial is going to be murder in the first degree or a lesser charge, why do they need to wait for the motions? I need to know logistically."
Clancy was charged with three counts of first-degree-murder, which is the intentional and premeditated killing of another person.
Prosecutors could decide to bring lesser charges against Clancy in a retrial. For example, second-degree-murder charges, apply to unlawful killings committed with malice or extreme recklessness, but without prior planning.
Despite Sprague's statement in court, District Attorney Timothy Cruz has not yet confirmed that Clancy will face a retrial and has not announced future plans for the case.
Much of Monday's conversations in court focused on the one holdout juror, also known as Juror Doe, and the defence's investigation into him. Juror Doe disagreed with the other jurors, who appeared to want to find Clancy not guilty by way of insanity. The lack of agreement led to a hung jury and mistrial.
In some of the most fiery moments of the three-hour hearing on Monday, Reddington requested a plethora of evidence including the holdout juror's phone and phone records.
Heather O'Connor, the attorney who represents Juror Doe, said she was in court because Clancy's defence team has "combined several allegations" to try to argue that a mistrial should not have been declared, she said.
That is among the motions Sullivan said he will rule on in a few weeks.
Clancy does not deny killing her children, but her defence team argues she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time. Prosecutors claim the killings were intentional.

58fac3d53604.text: By — Marc Levy, Associated Press Marc Levy, Associated Press By — Mike Catalini, Associated Press Mike Catalini, Associated Press By — John Hanna, Associated Press John Hanna, Associated Press By — Calvin Woodward, Associated Press Calvin Woodward, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/voters-on-the-left-and-right-fear-the-america-theyve-known-is-slipping-away Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Voters on the left and right fear the America they've known is slipping away Politics Nov 2, 2026 2:14 PM EST The stakes in Tuesday's elections are so high that Shane Dunn voted for the first time in his life, at age 65. After a career as a cook up and down the East Coast, Dunn moved to the Philadelphia suburbs and voted last week in Levittown. "I was always a busy man," he said. But now, "I'm learning what's going on within our country and this is actually what brought me out." Democrats got his vote. "It feels great, to put my word in," he said, patting his "I Voted" sticker. Voters across the United States are getting their word in as they determine control of Congress, governors' offices and more in the final two years of Republican Donald Trump's presidency. What many see is that the America they've known is slipping away. They see lawlessness from those who create laws, politicians stirring hate among neighbors, billionaires ruling the roost and a culture that doesn't speak to how they live. Not to mention those crazy gas prices. Voter angst is evident on both sides In dozens of Associated Press interviews with people casting advance ballots, the angst was palpable, most sharply from Trump's opponents but also from many supporters. "I saw my vote today as trying to put the brakes on just the madness," said Arthur Horner, 59, who runs a tariff-slammed food importing and marketing company. He voted Democratic in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. In Sioux City, Iowa, cattle rancher Elizabeth Marlett, 61, left the courthouse stewing about processed food, her son's struggles to get veterans' benefits and what she sees as society's leftward lurch. "Family values are going by the wayside, and they need to be brought back," she said. "Our liberties have been stomped all over. Religion has been stomped all over." She voted Republican. The anger stirred by a cursing president who abides no slights is too much for some. "He's just destroying us," Democrat Linda Markle, 72, said outside a library in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. "I am so afraid for this country." "All people do now is just hate each other," she said, and Trump "seems to have given them the courage to go ahead and be like that." 'He's kind of going a bit crazy,' a Trump supporter says Republican Chris Smith, 27, a Harrisburg software engineer who voted for Trump in 2024, sympathizes to a point. "A lot of people hate him for various reasons, and I can understand why," he said, noting that "I think he's kind of going a bit crazy on a lot of things." But Smith likes Trump's manufacturing push and voted Republican because he considers the party more fiscally responsible. In Ohio, independents Lori and David Wilkinson have voted for Republican George W. Bush for president in the past, and David recently praised Republican Gov. Mike DeWine in a letter. WATCH: Poll gauges voter enthusiasm for both parties a week before election Trump? "He's the worst president in United States history," David said at the Wayne County election center. "You get up every day, and you're like, 'What's he going to do now?'" Also voting there was Trump supporter Therese Mennell, who understands the distaste. "There's that kind of arrogant vibe about him that people don't like, and sometimes I shut him off because of the way he talks," the retiree said. "But, I mean, he's doing the right thing. He is saving our country." Despite his unpopularity in polls, Trump repeatedly asked supporters to pretend he's on the ballot, hoping to motivate otherwise reluctant voters. That cuts both ways. A family voting tradition is handed down Brothers Samontae Mwangi, 20, and Gathenya Mwangi, 19, voted for the first time in Topeka, Kansas, with their grandfather, Lynn Henderson, 68, a retired tire worker and former Marine. Henderson's mother died recently, and he wanted his grandsons to have an event to remember him by. All three hoped for Democratic victories. "It really could change, make a difference, I feel, if a lot of people vote," Gathenya said. Denise Wunder, a retired sandwich shop manager whose top issue is illegal immigration, saw the stakes differently. "I think Trump is kind of our last hope, because otherwise this world's going to go to hell in a handbasket," she said outside the Topeka center. "Yeah, he says stupid stuff, but, you know, so do we." In Nanuet, New York, independent Primrose D. Sullivan, a nurse who voted Democratic, singled out the billionaires allied with Trump. "I don't begrudge any of our wealthy people, Jeff Bezos or, you know, Elon Musk," she said. "But I do have a certain problem with them wanting more and more and doing things that really don't help humanity." In Scottsdale, Arizona, David Lee, 63, described his conservative upbringing and past Republican votes before explaining his turn toward Democrats. He considers Trump's immigration enforcement lawless. "Nobody wants open borders, but you're treating these people without due process, sending people to countries they don't even belong to," he said. "There's no more rules." Trump supporters interviewed by the AP signaled tolerance for surging gas prices from the Iran war. "Iran has been killing Americans for 50 freaking years," said David Stouffer, 59, a mortgage bank branch manager and three-time Trump voter in Harrisburg. "Yeah, I'll suffer with some higher gas prices in the interim until they get that nonsense figured out." "He's made the tax cuts real," he added. "He has secured the borders." Two days of hearings on a challenge to Australia's landmark social media ban for children will begin at the country's highest court on Tuesday.
In a major test of the world-leading policy, a digital rights group will argue that the ban for under-16s robs children of their right to free communication. A separate challenge launched by platform Reddit will be jointly heard.
Introduced last December, the ban is a key part of sweeping changes the Australian government has spearheaded in recent years on online safety.
Supporters say the ban protects children from harmful content but critics say it is too blunt an instrument and efforts should focus on improving online safety.
The constitutional challenge in Australia's High Court was filed by the Digital Freedom Project a few weeks before the ban started on 10 December last year. The group is lead by New South Wales parliamentarian John Ruddick.
Two teens who originally spearheaded the case, Noah Jones and Macy Neyland, have since withdrawn as plaintiffs though Jones is still expected to attend Tuesday's hearing.
Speaking about the legal challenge last November, Jones told the BBC that there were bad things online but a blanket ban for under-16s was not the right answer.
"We shouldn't be using the resources and money of these social media platforms to try to avoid fines from our government," he said.
"They should be using this money and resources to try to get rid of the predators and harmful content out there."
Reddit also launched a High Court challenge to the ban, arguing the policy has serious implications for privacy and political rights.
Communications Minister Anika Wells last year said the government would not be "intimidated by legal threats."
"We will not be intimidated by big tech. On behalf of Australian parents, we will stand firm," she said last November.
Under the ban, ten platforms - Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Reddit, Snapchat, X, Kick, Threads and Twitch - must take "reasonable steps" to ensure no one under 16 years old can access its site.
Platforms risk fines of up to A$99m (US$70m, Â£52m) for serious or repeated breaches, but since the ban started, no company has been fined.
The eSafety Commissioner - the body tasked with enforcing the ban - has launched several investigations into alleged non-compliance by Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok and YouTube.
WhatsApp and online gaming sites like Roblox and Discord were not included in the ban, nor were educational platforms like YouTube Kids and Google Classroom.
In the first few days of the ban, Meta - which owns three of the banned platforms - said it had closed about half a million accounts.
Some children said they were booted off their accounts in the days before and when the ban started - but many have said they were able to easily circumvent the age checks which included uploading credit card details, photo IDs or a selfie.

8855caef2d80.text: By — Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Fatima Hussein, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/health/what-to-know-about-the-affordable-care-acts-open-enrollment-period Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter What to know about the Affordable Care Act's open enrollment period Health Nov 2, 2026 1:53 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — People heading into the Affordable Care Act open enrollment period with plans to sign up for insurance should expect a variety of changes in 2027, including higher premiums and fewer coverage options. The sign-up window for the marketplace, also known as Obamacare, starts Sunday in most states and runs through Jan. 15. Big changes to the exchange include expiring financial assistance, rising rates, potential delays in working with a broker, new restrictions on immigrants, and stricter enrollment checks. Financial help, including premium tax credits and cost-sharing reductions, is now restricted for many groups of people who were previously eligible. Across the board, healthcare experts predict less coverage and higher prices, with the average price of health insurance purchased through the marketplaces expected to rise by 13% in 2027, according to analysis of new CMS data by the healthcare research nonprofit KFF. Increases are driven by multiple factors Cynthia Cox, a vice president and director of the ACA program at KFF, said the increase is primarily driven by rising healthcare costs, hospital market concentration, and potential factors such as the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022 and bans surprise billing, or the rising availability of GLP-1 drugs. The people who will be most affected by the new increases are those who do not qualify for a subsidy. "They may or may not be able to afford to continue to keep their coverage into next year," Cox said, adding that "a lot of them have already moved into bronze plans, which are the cheapest plans." READ MORE: Affordable Care Act enrollment shrank dramatically in many states over the past year, new federal data shows A CMS fact sheet about open enrollment that was distributed Friday says "Americans using HealthCare.gov will have robust access to low-cost plans." The price of ACA insurance has skyrocketed for many people during Trump's second term after Republicans opposed extending COVID-era subsidies that had helped offset the costs of health insurance for most enrollees during Democratic President Joe Biden's administration. That resulted in 1.2 million fewer people signing up for coverage in the exchanges. Nearly 20 million people in US are actively enrolled in ACA plans As of February, roughly 19.2 million people in the United States were actively enrolled in ACA marketplace health plans, according to the Department of Health and Human Services website. The number of enrollees grew during the COVID-19 pandemic when enhanced subsidies became available through the American Rescue Plan Act and Inflation Reduction Act, both signed into law by Biden. New regulations starting in 2027 will also limit tax credits for certain lawfully present immigrants, which could result in an additional 1 million uninsured individuals over time. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has been removing ACA enrollees from the program as part of the ongoing campaign against what it characterizes as waste, fraud and abuse. In September, Vice President JD Vance and other officials in the Republican administration announced plans to remove 760,000 ACA enrollees from public healthcare exchanges, alleging the individuals were fraudulently enrolled in the program or simply did not exist. Vance said the discovery and canceled subsidy payments for hundreds of thousands of people from the exchanges, part of an administration-wide crackdown on fraud, would result in $2.2 billion in cost savings. It's unclear how many more people will drop off of ACA coverage in 2027, Cox said. But with higher premiums, immigration eligibility changes and the anti-fraud efforts, "I think there's going to be fewer people enrolled in this market, but it's going to be harder to understand why." Ukrainians have grown weary of the relentless alerts blaring from their phones and echoing through their streets, day and night, warning of Russian drones and missiles.
On Sunday night, the system delivered something to make them sit up and take note â a succession of more extreme threats that quickly escalated to impending nuclear strikes, chemical attacks and combat on the streets.
But many in the country did not take them seriously and doubted the veracity of the messages.
Sofia Kochmar, 34, a mother-of-one living in the western city of Lviv, said she was initially concerned but quickly questioned the authenticity of the alerts.
"The first thing I saw was the word 'nuclear' and that made me pretty nervous and scared. So my first thought was that something nuclear was actually flying toward us."
"But then the notification mentioned 'street fighting in Kyiv', and I thought, wait, no, that's impossible."
The alerts included some messages written in Russian, and one included a link to a Telegram channel apparently owned by a hacker group.
Within 15 minutes, Ukraine's Air Force issued a statement saying the alert app had been compromised and clarifying there was no radiation threat. But it took more than an hour to issue "all clear" messages.
Anastasiia Romanytska, a 29-year-old ballerina living in Kyiv, said she does not have the alert app installed but friends forwarded her the warnings.
"My first reaction was, 'Is this some kind of joke?' But then my body reacted as if I was under stress. My heart started racing, and my stomach tightened up."
"Still, somehow I immediately realised that it wasn't something serious. Or maybe I just really wanted to believe that."
There are a number of apps delivering phone notifications of air raid warnings, with maps showing areas under threat, all using the same data as the official government-backed app.
Yevhen Baliutov, a cybersecurity expert at Kyiv School of Economics, told the BBC it was clear to him the Ukrainian alert system was hacked by Russians, saying many Ukrainians had clicked a link included with the alerts leading to a Russian Telegram channel, potentially exposing them to further disinformation, phishing attempts or data breaches.
"This is a war, so it's no surprise that Russia will try to hack, will try to send us fake news, will try to manipulate, and will use that for their propaganda."
While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Baliutov said it was also logical that Ukraine would have responded by launching a cyber-attack on the Russian emergency alert system. Both sides have similar capabilities in cyber warfare, he added.
Kochmar said after the initial concern, Ukrainians quickly turned to joking about the incident.
"All our work group chats immediately blew up. Everyone started messaging each other, discussing what was happening. And what I found fascinating was how quickly we turned the whole thing into a joke."
Although the impact of this incident had been limited, it illustrated the weakness of a crucial system, Baliutov said.
"It's very dangerous for Ukraine and for our people. When developing such applications, we need to consider security from the very beginning, without skipping essential security measures. When millions of people rely on a service, we cannot afford to take shortcuts with security."
The authorities already faced the challenge of maintaining public alertness after four and a half years of war with ceaseless attack warnings sounding sometimes hourly. Now they must reassure people the systems in place to protect them are robust, trustworthy and should be followed.

8334e0a464ae.text: The world seems convinced the end is near — and social media is amplifying that belief, convincing people to stock up on food, water, generators and other items. Why it matters: Online chatter is fueling viral predictions of societal collapse amid growing unease about the future. But you're probably not going to die tomorrow. What they're saying: Michael Mills, a researcher at the University of Kent who has studied doomsday prepping for more than a decade, told Axios that modern doomsday fears aren't necessarily about a specific apocalyptic scenario. "It's an overall reaction to uncertainty in most cases," Mills said. He noted that whereas Cold War-era survivalists were often focused on nuclear conflict, modern preppers worry about terrorism, climate disasters, geopolitical threats and emerging technologies. He described the modern mindset as a "multifaceted concern with uncertainty." State of play: Viral posts have repeatedly urged people around the world to stock up on food and water, following similar recommendations from various governments and warnings from former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino. The situation has gotten so buzzy that President Trump was asked about it in an interview Monday. He said Americans don't need to stock up because the U.S. is "in good shape. We're strong. We have a great military and we will not have those kind of problems." Separately, conservative commentator Tucker Carlson — a man with 17.9 million followers on X alone — published a lengthy post Sunday evening alleging that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pressuring Trump to launch renewed attacks on Iran after the midterms, potentially with a nuclear weapon. For what it's worth, Carlson has been predicting similar doomsday scenarios for a while, and he's been wrong before. And the Pentagon's newly reported plan calls for U.S. military bases to prepare to operate without outside support for at least 90 days, terrifying some people into asking , "What's the government know that they're not telling us?" The big picture: Worries about financial insecurity , skyrocketing health care costs , a lack of rainy-day savings and younger generations' perceived inability to buy a house all contribute to the feeling that life is not okay. Then you've got AI , which could cut thousands of jobs, enable a cyberattack or help engineer a dangerous, and potentially deadly, biological disease. And then there's the geopolitical situation: wars, genocide and the possibility of global warfare as China continues to threaten Taiwan and rumors abound that the U.S. and Israel will reignite the Iran war with a fresh round of attacks. Zoom in: Political uncertainty can also fuel doomsday prediction culture, particularly around major elections . Mills described the prepper movement as historically right-leaning, with fears increasing during the Obama and Biden administrations and subsiding among some preppers after Trump's 2016 victory. During elections, "where it can often seem that everything is at stake... we don't know which way those contests are going to go and so naturally that uncertainty kind of flares up," Mills said. Reality check: Preparing for a catastrophe doesn't make you a conspiracy theorist. Governments commonly warn people about potential disasters, like advising them to evacuate before a hurricane. Mills distinguishes ordinary emergency readiness from prepping, which typically involves preparing for disasters lasting weeks or months, sometimes longer. The bottom line: Nobody knows what catastrophe, if any, might come next. But feeling prepared and stocking up for a couple of days without power can make sitting in the dark a little less scary. 8af800fbd3c8.text: By — Sarah Raza, Associated Press Sarah Raza, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-promised-farmers-15-billion-in-weeks-before-midterms Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration promised farmers $15 billion in weeks before midterms Politics Nov 2, 2026 1:25 PM EST SIOUX FALLS, S.D. (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration has made $15 billion worth of promises to agriculture producers in the last few weeks before the midterm elections, initiatives intended to help offset higher costs for diesel and fertilizer that farmers have endured largely due to his tariffs and the war in Iran. Whether that will motivate more voters to turn out in agricultural states where traditionally Republican seats are now seen as competitive is unclear. It may explain his increased attention on rural areas, including visits Sunday to Iowa and Kansas, two days before the election. A look at the Republican administration's pledges to farmers: Whom these efforts will help Besides the more than $15 billion worth of payments and initiatives announced by Trump's Department of Agriculture, the agency plans $13.8 billion in safety net program payments for eligible producers for the 2025 crop year, offsetting shortfalls for farmers who grow key crops such as corn, soybeans, wheat and rice. Of the $15 billion, more than half will go toward an $8 billion one-time payment plan for farmers buffeted by soaring diesel prices. The USDA said it will release more details about the payments this month. It is not clear when the payments will go to farmers, who rely on diesel for trucks, tractors and combines. Gregg Ibendahl, a farm management specialist at Kansas State University, said he estimates the payments to "more than cover the increase in fuel costs," and that the money could help with high fertilizer prices. At least $5 billion was announced in guaranteed loans for ranchers and fishermen. An additional $1.8 billion in payments is for producers and landowners who participated in conservation programs, $573 million will go toward fertilizer manufacturing projects and $57 million is for expanding meat processors. For specialty crop producers, $86.6 million in grants will be awarded to innovative projects. On Thursday, the agency said it would purchase up to $472.5 million in agricultural commodities to support producers and give to charitable programs. The money will primarily come from the USDA and doesn't need immediate congressional approval. The USDA also announced other efforts, such as expanding sales of a diesel normally used only for off-road use, helping ranchers by making cattle sale data more transparent and strengthening wolf management policies to protect livestock. Why farmers are struggling It has been a frustrating year for farmers. Increased costs for fertilizer and fuel have made it difficult to turn a profit. Last year, tariffs drove up expenses for other equipment that farmers use, and the trade war with China resulted in a near boycott of U.S. agricultural goods. On Friday, diesel was averaging $6.32 per gallon, down slightly from its peak in September but 70% higher than the price a year ago, according to motor club AAA. Filling up a 100-gallon tank now costs $260 more than it did one year ago. WATCH: Farmers struggle with crops as climate change makes weather less predictable "That input side risk, I think, is the thing that really has hurt farmers this year, as well as the fact that there has been a lot more uncertainty about what's going to happen in the world," Ibendahl said. He said he expects these ad hoc payments to be a big help for farmers who otherwise would not make a profit this year, but they do not address the broader issues driving up prices. "It's hard to go to your lender in the next spring and say, 'OK, well, we're looking pretty good this year, but it's all because of these extra temporary government payments, so how much can you make me a loan (for) next year for my crop?'" he said. Alexandra Middlewood, an associate professor of political science at Wichita State University, said she has heard mixed reactions from farmers, who are happy their business will survive this year but see these programs as one-time bailouts rather than a long-term solution. What farmers may vote on Rural voters, including farmers and those who rely on the agricultural economy, have been an instrumental voting group for Trump. Michael Smith, a political science professor at Emporia State University, said many rural voters like the president, but some of his policies have hurt the agriculture industry. Immigrant deportations have threatened the agricultural labor force, and cuts to foreign aid and SNAP food stamps hurt the market for agricultural products. "Some people who admire Trump really just admire the person, the man," he said. "But it doesn't mean they necessarily like his policies. Well, Trump himself isn't on the ballot this year. His policies are." Cost of living and access to health care are top issues for rural voters, Middlewood said. She added that there is a perception the administration has not done enough to address these issues, even as Trump boasts at campaign rallies about a booming economy. Middlewood, who is based in Kansas, does not expect frustrated rural voters to shift to the Democratic Party, given how long the state has been a Republican stronghold. But some voters may decide to sit out of this election or vote independent, which would hurt Republican candidates. "Independent voters make or break elections," she said. "And so that's really what it's going to come down to this year is those independent voters and who they're breaking for." A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy.
