Supermarkets across Europe have been hit by a suspected cyber-attack affecting their fridges and freezers, and raising concern about the vulnerabilities of internet-connected hardware from industrial machinery to humble domestic appliances.
Smart devices which are connected to the internet can include fridges, central heating, and even washing machines.
And while that makes them easier to control remotely, in theory, any device which goes online can potentially be exploited by malicious actors.
However, that doesn't mean hackers can easily take control of it, and big brands generally go to great lengths to make sure their tech is secure.
Exploits have been found before in some devices. In 2015, researchers demonstrated how a vulnerability in a Samsung smart fridge could allow them to intercept internet traffic.
But there's no evidence domestic appliances are being targeted in the cyber-attacks which targeted supermarkets in November.
Ciaran Martin, former chief executive of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) says manufacturers needed to do more to make connected devices secure.
"There's a lot more that we need to demand of big tech to give us safer devices and products in the first place," he said.
He advised consumers to keep devices updated and enable multi-factor authentication wherever possible.
"I know it's a pain, but it only takes a few seconds," he said.
Since April 2024, UK law has required manufacturers of certain consumer smart devices to meet minimum cyber security standards, including requirements around passwords and security updates.
The NCSC said it was working with international partners and industry to understand the supermarket incidents, but it was unaware of any impact on the UK.
However, researchers from UK Cyber Defence have identified more than 800 refrigeration and building-control interfaces associated with British retailers that can be accessed over the public internet.
That doesn't necessarily mean they can be hacked, but it could leave them exposed to attackers exploiting weak passwords or software vulnerabilities.
The government has already held talks with senior food retailers about cyber resilience, following earlier attacks on supermarkets.
Helen Dickinson, chief executive of the British Retail Consortium, has said cyber incidents are a major concern for retailers, with businesses working alongside the NCSC to share intelligence and strengthen their defences.
It would not be the first time that hacks have raised concern about impact on food supply.
When UK supermarkets M&S and the Co-op were targeted by ransomware hackers in May 2025, the retailers struggled to stock some shop shelves with fresh deliveries.
Customers across the UK complained of empty shelves in the days following the attack.
Tom Hegel, a researcher at cyber-security firm SentinelOne, said retailers must be clearer about responsibility.
"The question retailers need to answer is who owns the security of that equipment, not just who repairs it," he said.
He said internet connectivity can make everyday technology more convenient, but security needed to keep pace.
"Once an attacker can operate those controls, legitimate functions such as defrosting become tools for disruption," he said.
"Changing a setting can destroy physical stock, not just interrupt a computer system."
Could cars, power plants and water supplies be vulnerable?
Outside of the home, connected tech is used to remotely manage industrial machinery and vehicles.
Cyber security expert Ken Munro pointed to a 2015 demonstration in which researchers remotely hacked a Jeep through its internet-connected entertainment system, prompting improvements in vehicle security.
"Fortunately, the vehicle industry woke up to this and fixed the problem," he said.
Mobile connections are also widely used to monitor equipment in power plants and water networks, allowing engineers to manage systems remotely.
Munro said UK utilities were generally good at securing these connections, but standards varied around the world.
His biggest concern was smaller, poorly funded utility companies which may still be relying on older, vulnerable equipment.
Without proper protections, "any factory or equipment" connected to the internet - ranging from carmakers to electricity or transport infrastructure - could face similar risks, said Olivier Daloy, a cybersecurity expert at Zscaler.

cf5ec3840d74.text: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to mandate that California separate ballots of more than 20,000 voters the government suspects are "likely" non-citizens. The big picture: A federal appeals court rejected the administration's bid to set aside mail ballots last week, erecting another roadblock in the DOJ's pre-election quest to demand the state root out claims of voter fraud in the final days of the midterm elections. Driving the news: "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," the DOJ wrote in an application filed to the high court. "The only way to preserve the district court's ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now," the application, signed by Solicitor General D. John Sauer, continued. The DOJ's initial lawsuit came after the administration threatened California officials with emergency court action unless it probed potential ineligible voters over 48 hours and set aside ballots. Catch up quick: A federal appeals court and a federal judge stymied the administration's bid. U.S. District Judge David Carter cast doubt on the government's voter lists in a late October order denying the administration's request for a temporary restraining order, citing the "vagueness" of the government's "descriptions of its procedures and the unreliability of its similar claims in other states." And in last week's 2–1 ruling, a federal appeals court found that granting the request "would provoke catastrophic change, upending the administration of the election." What they're saying: "We will continue pursuing every available legal avenue to protect the integrity of our elections and ensure federal law is enforced," Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter said in a statement shared to X. The California Secretary of State's office did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

13c8a9a936b9.text: By — Steven Sloan, Associated Press Steven Sloan, Associated Press By — Hillel Italie, Associated Press Hillel Italie, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/kennedy-center-names-2026-honorees-as-trump-renovation-battle-moves-show-offsite Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Kennedy Center names 2026 honorees as Trump renovation battle moves show offsite Arts Nov 2, 2026 1:11 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The Kennedy Center said Monday that Paul Anka, David Foster, Andy Garcia, David Mamet and Barbara Mandrell would be recognized at this year's Kennedy Center Honors, which will be held away from the iconic performing arts venue for the first time as President Donald Trump battles with a federal court over his plans to renovate the building and add his name to it. All of the nominees have had substantial careers in their respective fields. Mamet is among the most acclaimed playwrights of his time, known for his hard-boiled dialogue in "Glengarry Glen Ross" and "American Buffalo" and other works. Mandrell is a member of the Country Music Hall of Fame whose many hits include "Years" and "Sleeping Single in a Double Bed" and Foster is among the most successful producers of the past 50 years, working with everyone from Chicago to Natalie Cole. Anka has written or co-written such iconic songs as "My Way" and the theme to the "Tonight" show when Johnny Carson was host. Garcia's acting credits include "The Untouchables," "The Godfather Part III" and the HBO film "For Love or Country." Several are either friendly with Trump or have been outspoken in support of conservative politics. Mamet told Fox News last year that he was once a "brain-dead liberal" who "discovered my conservative beliefs." Anka is a longtime friend of Trump who once rewrote "My Way," originally written for Frank Sinatra, with MAGA-themed lyrics. Foster has performed for Trump in the past. READ MORE: Kennedy Center Honors to be held at Capital One Arena amid fight over adding Trump's name The Kennedy Center Honors were established in 1978 and have been given to a broad range of artists. Until Trump's first term, presidents of both major political parties traditionally attended the annual ceremony, even when they disagreed politically with a given recipient. Prominent liberals such as Barbra Streisand and Warren Beatty were honored during the administration of Republican George W. Bush, and a leading conservative, Charlton Heston, was feted during the administration of Democrat Bill Clinton. Trump skipped the awards during his first term but has been far more involved with the Kennedy Center since returning to the White House. He fired the institution's board of directors and replaced them with loyalists who named him chairman. He personally announced last year's honorees and hosted the show that honored them. His administration has spent much of this year locked in a legal battle over whether and how to honor Trump, with the president insisting his name be added to the building in some form. As that plays out, the Kennedy Center has closed with its stages absent of performances for months. This year's honors program will be held on Dec. 7 at Washington's Capital One Arena. "We are proud to honor this year's class and to continue a tradition that has defined the Center for nearly 50 years," Trump said in a statement. Italie reported from New York. a539e2237f16.text: By — Amna Nawaz Amna Nawaz By — Maria Ramirez Uribe Maria Ramirez Uribe Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/watch-zelenskyy-confirms-ukraine-hacked-back-after-russias-cyberattack-of-its-emergency-alert-system Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter WATCH: Zelenskyy confirms Ukraine hacked back after Russia's cyberattack of its emergency alert system World Updated on Nov 2, 2026 4:47 PM EST — Published on Nov 2, 2026 1:06 PM EST Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed that his country retaliated against Russia by hacking its emergency alert system. "We only respond on their attacks," Zelenskyy said in an interview with PBS News' Amna Nawaz. The cyberattack, the Ukrainian leader said, was a response to Russia seemingly hacking Ukraine's emergency alert system, which notifies residents of imminent threats. "They attacked our system," he said. "It was a cyberattack." READ MORE: Ukraine and Russia both report fake emergency alerts after cyberattacks target apps as limited ceasefire ends Ukrainian authorities said on Sunday that users received false warnings of an imminent nuclear threat on their emergency alert mobile app. The alert system was suspended but is now back up and running. SUPPORT PBS NEWS: Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass "When it was very clear … that it's their personal attack against our people, civilians," Zelenskyy said. "Of course, we responded." Russian authorities on Monday said hackers gained access to their emergency mobile app and sent fake emergency alerts. Here are other key takeaways from his interview with PBS News. Zelenskyy describes his relationship with Trump as 'emotional' When Nawaz asked Zelenskyy to describe his relationship with President Donald Trump in one word, Zelenskyy paused. "Emotional," he said. Trump has previously described Zelenskyy as "not a good guy," and has said he shouldn't be the Ukrainian president and doesn't want an end to the war. WATCH: Ukraine less reliant on U.S. as Trump-Zelenskyy rift deepens, former ambassador says Following the release of an American imprisoned in Russia, U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff described Putin as a "humanitarian." Putin has been indicted for war crimes by the International Criminal Court. WATCH: American imprisoned by Russia released as Witkoff meets and praises Putin "Sometimes we need to be pragmatic in this war," Zelenskyy said. "Who is an enemy? Who began this war? Putin. Don't find good words to describe him. I'm not sure that it will be helpful." Zelenskyy also criticized Trump's deal with Russia to import tons of Russian diesel to the U.S. "If you are really about money, business and pragmatism, so don't speak that it will have influence on the price in the United States," Zelenskyy said. "No, it's not true, it doesn't work." WATCH: Ukraine disputes Trump's claim of energy ceasefire as Russian diesel deal draws fire Experts say it's unlikely the deal will reduce global diesel prices in the near future. The Ukrainian president told Nawaz the pragmatic thing to do is to support Ukraine. "We have to support Ukraine," he said. "Because it has to be strong, because otherwise Putin will go further to Europe and to the different parts of NATO countries." Zelenskyy has asked Trump to reduce limits to Ukraine's use of Starshield Zelenskyy said he has asked Trump several times to reduce limits to Ukraine's use of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink satellite internet service. The system is funded by the Pentagon and operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Starshield, which is a key component of Ukraine's military communications network, has geographic restrictions. It can't be used to carry out attacks inside Russia. It can act defensively and in the Russian occupied territories of Ukraine. Zelenskyy said if given the opportunity, Ukraine would use the system to identify and attack missile launch sites inside Russia. He said Ukraine would not use Starshield to carry out massive attacks on Russia or energy sites due to the likelihood of civilian casualties. Lifting Starshield limits would mean Russia wouldn't "have opportunity to use each day ballistic missiles against us," Zelenskyy said. "Because we will block their launches." The Ukrainian president said Trump seemed open to the reduction of limits. "He said that he will try. It doesn't depend on him," Zelenskyy said. "He said that it depends mostly on SpaceX. He said that he's supportive, and I was very thankful." In mid-October, Starshield was partially disabled. The details of what happened are unclear. WATCH: How Starlink disruptions affected Ukraine's battlefield operations Musk said limits to Starshield's speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and Trump. Trump has said he didn't order the restrictions and doubted that Musk was to blame for the disruption. Asked who he thought was to blame for the disruption, Zelenskyy said he's unsure whether Musk can act alone. "I'm not sure that he can do it with Starshield because it's military. It's government version," Zelenskyy said. "I'm not sure that he could do it personally alone without any representatives from American government." Asked whether he believes Musk supports Ukraine and wants it to win the war, Zelenskyy said "I don't know." He said he wanted to speak with Musk following the Starshield disruptions but "they didn't connect with us." See more of our interview with Zelenskyy on Monday's PBS News Hour. 2c2923437d0a.text: By — Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Lindsay Whitehurst, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-administration-asks-supreme-court-to-sideline-20000-disputed-california-mail-ballots Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump administration appeals to Supreme Court to sideline 20,000 disputed California mail ballots Politics Updated on Nov 2, 2026 4:37 PM EST — Published on Nov 2, 2026 12:53 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump's administration appealed to the Supreme Court on Monday in its push to sideline thousands of disputed California mail ballots the day before the pivotal midterm elections. The emergency appeal came after a divided appeals court rejected the request to set aside ballots from some 20,000 people the federal government suspects may not be citizens. It also came just hours before another federal judge ruled against the administration's efforts to make last-minute changes in California's election. Educate your inbox Subscribe to Here’s the Deal, our politics newsletter for analysis you won’t find anywhere else. Enter your email address Subscribe Form error message goes here. Thank you. Please check your inbox to confirm. The federal government says those ballots should not be counted until the voters' status can be verified. California officials say the list is highly unreliable and likely includes many people who are U.S. citizens. The Republican Trump administration has prioritized identifying noncitizen voters this year, despite them being rare. READ MORE: Analysis: More than 40% of names on DOJ list of alleged noncitizens not on California's voter rolls A district court judge had previously denied the Justice Department's request and warned that the demand could disenfranchise citizens in Tuesday's midterm elections to determine control of Congress. Also on Monday in Washington, Chief Judge James Boasberg ordered the Trump administration to stop making its demands, finding they violated the U.S. Constitution. "The Executive Branch has likely violated the Constitution's Elections Clause, which commits authority over election rules to the states and Congress alone," wrote Boasberg. At the high court, the Justice Department asked for a "limited injunction" that would direct California to set aside the ballots while the case plays out. "Once California commingles the challenged ballots with lawful ones, there is no way to get the challenged ballots back," Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote. Voting has been underway in California, a largely Democratic state, since early October. All of the state's roughly 23 million registered voters are mailed a ballot. Hundreds of thousands of ballots have already been processed. California election officials have said that finding and setting aside the challenged ballots now would be logistically impossible. California Attorney General Rob Bonta, a Democrat, said the appeal "reeks of desperation and is another attempt to undermine our elections and trample on the rule of law." Lower courts have sided with the state, with a district judge warning that segregating ballots would "wreak havoc" on the midterm elections and erode trust in the democratic process. "If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger," wrote U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, who was nominated by President Bill Clinton, a Democrat. A 2-1 appeals court panel upheld his order, with one judge appointed by Trump and another appointed by President Joe Biden, a Democrat, voting in favor. The third judge on the panel, also appointed by Trump, argued in a dissent that California's unwillingness to separate the ballots encourages the "violation of federal law." The Justice Department has sought to move the case along quickly, unsuccessfully asking an appeals court to intervene early. Trump's administration has racked up a series of wins in emergency appeals before the Supreme Court in his second term, but the justices previously rejected the president's push to restrict mail ballots ahead of the midterms. Associated Press writer Sophie Austin in Sacramento contributed to this report. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. 03cfeb7d032b.text: Cyberattacks are wreaking havoc on an unlikely target across Europe: supermarket refrigerators. Why it matters: Hackers are turning everyday, internet-connected equipment into physical hazards, spoiling food and causing costly damage. U.S. supermarkets use similar technology, and the Pentagon is already investigating suspected cyberattacks involving refrigeration systems at six military commissaries. Driving the news: Suspected cyberattacks sent refrigerator and freezer temperatures soaring at dozens of European supermarkets overnight, spoiling food and threatening costly losses. Grocery chains Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt reported incidents affecting stores in Belgium and Luxembourg, while Swedish chains ICA and Coop reported similar disruptions, per Reuters . A Belgian company that operates Delhaize's refrigeration systems said hackers switched the units into defrost mode. Here's what to know. Supermarkets hacked in Europe Supermarkets in Belgium, Estonia, Finland, Ireland, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and Sweden reported cyberattacks or IT disruptions, forcing some stores to discard spoiled food. Dozens of stores were affected, including an ICA supermarket in Sweden that said hackers set its refrigerator and freezer temperatures to 122°F, per ABC News . Authorities haven't shared who specifically is behind the attacks, per NBC News . Empty refrigerated shelves at a Proxy Delhaize supermarket in Maleizen, Belgium, following a refrigeration outage. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images Flashback: The incidents follow similar attacks in France last month, when hackers seized control of hundreds of refrigeration units, causing fires and spoiling food. It's unclear whether the attacks are connected. What they're saying: France's finance minister Roland Lescure said at the time that the attack "touches the heart of our food security." "It was a wake-up call for everyone," he said. How fridges get hacked How it works: Hackers aren't opening up each individual fridge and setting new temperatures. Instead, they target computer systems that control the temperatures of multiple refrigerated units remotely. Many stores use internet-connected controllers — small computer-like devices, sometimes with touchscreens — that allow maintenance workers to remotely monitor temperatures without having to visit every store. Hackers can exploit software flaws or stolen login credentials to change temperatures or activate defrost functions. Case in point: Danish manufacturer Danfoss said it identified security flaws last year and had long recommended customers install updates, according to The Guardian . In the Netherlands, some affected refrigeration systems used default passwords and were connected to unsecured networks. A supermarket manager discards spoiled food following a refrigeration outage linked to suspected cyberattacks across Europe on Nov. 2 in Belgium. Photo: Wiktor Dabkowski/Bloomberg via Getty Images The cost of hacked refrigerators Spoiled food: If temperatures rise overnight, the stores end up finding ruined meat, dairy and frozen products the next morning. In some French supermarkets, the soaring hot temperatures lasted for six hours, per Reuters. Spoiled food becomes unsafe to sell. Overheating and fires: Refrigerators can also overheat and cause fires. French prosecutors confirmed that the October attacks caused fires and food losses. Supermarkets lose money: Some stores lost more than €130,000. Two markets in the French region of Alsace reported combined losses of €270,000, per The Guardian . Intermarché's parent company estimated its nationwide losses in the tens of millions of euros. Yes, but: Not every attack causes extensive damage. In Estonia, a refrigeration company said technicians responded to the breach within minutes and halted any massive losses, per AP . Fridge attacks in the U.S. Zoom out: Many U.S. supermarkets use refrigeration technology similar to that found in Europe. Danfoss markets refrigeration monitoring and management systems in the U.S. Copeland, a U.S.-based refrigeration technology company, sells controllers that manage the grocery store display cases and walk-in refrigerators. What we're watching: The Pentagon is investigating whether cyberattacks caused freezer malfunctions at at least six U.S. military commissaries in August.

57b88ed6349c.text: By — Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press Hanna Arhirova, Associated Press By — Volodymyr Yurchuk, Associated Press Volodymyr Yurchuk, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/a-brief-ceasefire-between-russia-and-ukraine-opens-a-perilous-escape-window-from-khersons-riverside-kill-zone Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter A brief ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine opens a perilous escape window from Kherson's riverside kill zone World Nov 2, 2026 12:38 PM EST KOZATSKE, Ukraine (AP) — A white towel on her gate and a white rag in her hand were Ukrainian Nataliia Diadiuk's only ways to tell Russian drone operators she is a civilian. When a brief ceasefire kicked in on Oct. 27, she had a moment of respite. The 53-year-old is one of a handful of residents left in Kozatske, a riverside village located in the kill zone of Ukraine's Kherson region less than 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from a Russian-controlled area. READ MORE: Ukraine and Russia both report fake emergency alerts after cyberattacks target apps as limited ceasefire ends "I really want silence," Diadiuk said, fighting back tears as she stood on an empty street lined with abandoned houses. "And I want to see the people who left, all of them. People left for both sides." Diadiuk's life has been reduced to basic survival: rainwater to drink, firewood gathered around town for heat, a radio she tries to tune in to for news, and the remnants of humanitarian aid that had not reached her in two years until the brief ceasefire that ended Sunday night just days after it began. Going out means dodging every kind of weapon, including mines scattered everywhere. The neighbors she mentions are more often the dead than the few still living nearby. A team from The Associated Press gained rare access to a so-called red zone to see firsthand what life in the kill zone looks like, a visit made possible only because of a brief, localized ceasefire tied to the humanitarian aid mission in the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky. People walk next to damaged buildings, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the frontline city of Kherson, Ukraine, Oct. 28, 2026. Photo by Reuters stringer Oleshky has drawn the world's attention, but civilians are trapped in many more places on both sides of the front line. During the mission, Ukrainian regional officials, police, the Ukrainian Red Cross Society and volunteers, with the facilitation of civil-military cooperation specialists, used the rare window of time to reach people on their side of the river, some of them cut off for nearly two years. In all, 180 people were evacuated from riverside communities and the city of Kherson, including 23 children, the regional administration said. About 140,000 people remain in the Ukrainian-held part of the Kherson region. Before the war, the whole region, now nearly 70% under Russian control, had about 1 million residents. The riverside is designated a red zone, the highest level of military danger. With the ceasefire over, residents will again face drones, artillery, glide bombs and airdropped mines. Still, many refuse to leave. Some cannot afford to start over, and others will not abandon the places where they grew up. Life is grim in the kill zone On the road to Diadiuk's village, burned-out cars sit abandoned where they were hit, alongside wrecked ground robots that Ukrainians try sending down roads too dangerous for people. A relic of peacetime still stands on that road: "Thank you for keeping the roadside clean." In the village, many houses are reduced to burned walls. Glide bombs have left craters, and the tail fins of shells stick out of the asphalt like flowers. Mines dropped from drones lie everywhere, some petal-shaped, others improvised and wrapped in foil or plastic, so every step must be taken with care. Thick vegetation swallows the ruins of empty houses. What Diadiuk finds hardest to bear is the howling of the dogs left behind in the houses, surviving much as she is. "Even for the sake of these, I can't leave them," she says, pointing to two thin dogs that never stray far from her. But she shares what little food she has with other dogs as well. A woman walks on a street covered with an anti-drone net, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in the frontline city of Kherson, Ukraine Oct. 30, 2026. Photo by Nina Liashonok/ Reuters Isolated and forced to fight for survival every day, she has lost track of time. "I turn on my phone only to see what day it is," she says. She charges it with solar panels. Diadiuk collects rainwater, strains it through gauze, treats it with chlorine and boils it. "The water here is more or less all right," she says. "There are a lot of dead lying in the houses, so it's good water only in a manner of speaking." Why people stay The village's ordeal began in the first days of Russia's full-scale invasion, when it was occupied. After Ukrainian forces liberated it, Kozatske gradually came under siege by drones as the war turned increasingly technological. "Before, I'd just open the door and walk out," said Oleksii Shavokin, 54, who lives a little farther down the street. "Now I open it a crack, stick my ear out and listen to the sky." His house burned down in early 2023 after a mortar attack, he said, but he patched it up and stays on there. He lives off old humanitarian aid and eggs from the hens he still keeps. "I ration my food so it lasts. I'm used to it," he said. "Now I eat once a day, in the evening, and that's quite enough." He has lost 30 kilograms (66 pounds) from a weight of close to 100 kilograms (220 pounds). READ MORE: Evacuees fleeing Oleshky reunite with family at the Ukrainian-Belarusian border Many of the people he knew were killed by strikes, and others left. He decided to stay. "I value life, but where's the guarantee a car won't hit me somewhere else?" Shavokin said. "Wherever it's written for you, that's where you'll lose your life, or go on living. And still, I

Fighting has resumed in Ukraine's Kherson after a six-day truce brought quiet to the front-line region for the first time in years.
The ceasefire - the longest since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 - allowed hundreds of people trapped in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky and its surroundings to be evacuated.
On Monday morning, local authorities confirmed that strikes had resumed, saying Moscow had hit a medical facility in Kherson city centre. They also said a 62-year-old woman and a 73-year-old man were injured when a Russian drone attacked the car they were travelling in.
Ukraine also accused Russian forces of using the humanitarian ceasefire to strengthen their military positions, rotate units and deliver ammunition.
"The enemy used the humanitarian pause to set up their positions," said Ukraine's General Staff, adding they had recorded rotation of Russian units, expansion of anti-drone equipment on the roads, and delivery of ammunition.
The Kremlin appeared to corroborate this when spokesman Dmitry Peskov said it was "reasonable to assume that the Ukrainian army also used this period for the necessary regrouping".
"It is a completely standard practice in such situations," he added.
The ceasefire had been brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump. Both Kyiv and Moscow thanked her repeatedly, though no details of her involvement were shared.
An unusual show of cooperation came from Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova and her Ukrainian counterpart Dmytro Lubinets. The pair oversaw the ceasefire, travelled into Oleshky and were filmed speaking to residents together. They publicly thanked each other for their work, often highlighting that no violations of the ceasefire had been observed.
Both Lantratova and Lubinets called for the initiative to be repeated elsewhere, and Ukraine repeatedly said it would be prepared to observe similar ceasefires on a national level too.
But many have questioned whether this will lead to more cooperation and further truces.
In fact, the Kremlin swiftly dismissed the idea even as the ceasefire was under way, calling Oleshky "an isolated case" which would not affect the "settlement process" â a euphemism for the stalled peace talks. "There are no similar plans or initiatives," Peskov reiterated on Monday.
And although last week the guns fell silent in Kherson region, elsewhere in Ukraine Russia's air strikes continued, killing scores of civilians and destroying crucial infrastructure.
The decision to observe an unusually broad and comparatively lengthy ceasefire in and around Oleshky was therefore a notable exception.
The ceasefire's observance appears, at least in part, to have been linked to Melania Trump's reported involvement. By violating the truce, Moscow would have risked undermining its own efforts to cultivate the crucial relationship with her husband, US President Donald Trump.
Some commentators have argued that Trump himself would be interested in presenting the Oleshky ceasefire as a foreign policy achievement scored days before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
"I totally get why our official representatives need to 'play along' with the US first lady on Oleshky," said Artyom Sheynin, a prominent figure on Russian state TV.
"I understand why it's so important to create a 'success story' ahead of the elections for the US president, whose wife 'achieved a ceasefire' in Oleshky."
Kyiv, too, had its reasons to be fully compliant. Although relations with the US and its president are often fraught, Ukraine continues to rely heavily on US intelligence and US-made Patriot air defence missiles to counter Russian aerial attacks. Ahead of another tough winter of war, continued American support is essential to protect Ukrainian skies from Russia's assaults.
But though the ceasefire may have been born out of political calculation rather than purely humanitarian compassion, it also resulted in hundreds of civilians escaping.
There were emotional scenes when hundreds of Oleshky residents arrived in northern Ukraine on Saturday. Many were met by tearful relatives they had not seen in years. To the journalists waiting, the evacuees told of years of hunger and hardship in a destroyed town.
The hundreds of residents who decided to stay behind will receive monthly humanitarian aid deliveries, Lantratova said, adding that decision too was the result of Melania Trump's mediation.
Yet the troop rotations and resupply efforts show that neither side is expecting Oleshky to be a blueprint for lasting respite in the future.
As Kherson came under fire again, Ukrainian drones hit several energy facilities across four Russian regions. In Samara, residents reported hearing explosions and seeing black plumes of smoke rising into the sky as an oil refinery was hit for the fifth time in a month.
If the truce brought a rare moment of relief to Oleshky, it has done little to alter the wider trajectory of a war that grinds on for now.

Dutch authorities have offered a record award of â¬2m (Â£1.7m/$2.24m) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers, one of Europe's most-wanted men.
The 35-year-old, who is also known as Bolle Jos (Chubby Jos), was previously accused of being "one of the key players in international cocaine trafficking" by Dutch police.
Commenting on the decision to increase the reward ten-fold, Dutch justice minister David van Weel said it was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order".
Dutch prosecutors said capturing Leijdekkers was their "highest priority" and any information shared would be kept secret.
He is listed by Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, as among their most-wanted fugitives.
In January 2025, Dutch police said he was believed to be living in Sierra Leone and going by the name Omar Sherrif.
Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of President Julius Maada Bio and other officials have previously emerged.
Dutch prosecutors have demanded his extradition but Sierra Leone has refused to cooperate, prompting the EU to cut some aid to the country.
West Africa is a major transit point for cocaine trafficking from Latin America.
In 2024, a court in Rotterdam sentenced Leijdekkers in absentia to 24 years in prison after finding him guilty of smuggling â more than seven metric tons of cocaine.
Several other police investigations in the Netherlands are ongoing.
Leijdekkers has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
Dutch authorities estimate he has made tens of millions of euros from â cocaine smuggling, and accuse him of money laundering and involvement in the use of extreme violence.

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.
The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.
“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”
Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.
Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.
“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.
The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.
Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

- Published
The impacts of over-foraging natural spaces, particularly in protected areas, can damage habitats, a Devon charity has said.
The Woodland Trust said unsustainable harvesting of plants - and particularly fungi - could put wildlife under pressure.
Joe Middleton, site manager for the Woodland Trust, said he had seen commercial mushroom pickers "wiping out everything on the path edges they can find".
Under Section 4 of the Theft Act 1968, it is "perfectly legal to forage for fruit, foliage, flowers, and fungi on any land, provided they are wild and collected strictly for personal use", but "foraging becomes criminal theft if you pick wild plants for commercial sale or reward without permission".
Middleton said: "I have seen commercial pickers, dropped off in mini buses with bags for life, laden heavy with mushrooms and they are going through and they are wiping out everything on the path edges they can find, trampling the forest floor."
The majority of mushrooms are not edible to humans, so picking them can be potentially dangerous.
In the autumn they are an essential source of food for animals such as deer and badgers, all the way down to things that live in the soil such as worms and woodlice.
Middleton said: "If we start decimating the population, it takes their food source away.
"They can't just get up and move, a lot of our wildlife is dependent on this fungi. We just need to be a bit more sustainable in what we are doing."
Entering private property without a landowner's consent to forage is a civil rather than criminal offence. However, foraging is heavily restricted or illegal in local Sites of Special Scientific Interest (SSSIs) or protected areas like Woodland Trust sites.
Using ingredients from local areas is very fashionable on social media at the moment.
John Dobson, from the Refectory restaurant near Ugborough, said he thought there were other factors too.
He said: "The rising cost of ingredients; they're getting really, really expensive, so I think that could be encouraging people to go out and source things from other places. There is also a lack of education about the impact."
Dobson added he made sure to forage responsibly, only taking a third of what he found, and doing so with any landowner's permission.
Middleton said foraging was a great way to connect with nature, but he wanted to encourage people to enjoy woodlands without taking any of it home with them too.
He said: "We've gone a long way from Victorian times in terms of taking everything we see and pinning it and netting it.
"Now we are in a technological age. We can just use our phones, take great pictures; we can look without touching - particularly in a protected place."

The UK government's ambition of achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2050 could be undermined by its new deal on AI data centres, according to BBC research.
During Wednesday's Budget speech, Chancellor John Healey said data centres would be allowed to build onsite power generation while they wait for a grid connection.
BBC File on 4 Investigates has discovered that four planned "hyperscale" data centres - including three in the south of England - are already considering using gas-fired power to meet their electricity needs, creating more CO2 than the cities of Manchester, Liverpool and Southampton combined.
Labour MP Toby Perkins, who chairs the Environmental Audit Select Committee, said a substantial increase in the use of natural gas "can't be the future".
"Government absolutely shouldn't be in the business of just saying anyone who wants to bring it here, can do whatever you like to power it, because that is not acceptable," he said.
The government said data centres were "essential to Britain's economy" and that its new Data Centre Covenant set clear expectations for developers to pay a fair share of the costs they impose on the energy system and deliver benefits for local communities.
Data centres are warehouses full of powerful computer servers used to run a vast range of digital services, including streaming, banking and public services and have been part of the British landscape for more than two decades.
But a new generation of data centres due to come on stream in the next few years will operate on a much larger scale to cope with the growing computing demand needed for increasingly sophisticated artificial intelligence technology.
They will consume considerably more energy than their predecessors at a time when the National Grid is already struggling to meet demand.
Ofgem, the energy market regulator, says data centre developers are seeking connections totalling 72 gigawatts. The peak electricity demand across the whole country last year was 45 gigawatts.
Such is the demand for access to the already under-strain national electricity grid, some data centre developers have been told they could be waiting up to 10 years for the system to be upgraded to provide them with a connection.
Nathan McWhinnie, head of market intelligence and oversight at Ofgem, said: "In a lot of places, the grid is at capacity. I think sometimes it's easy to forget the scale of the demand of these connections. These projects are sometimes the size of cities."
In last week's Budget, the chancellor announced a British Data Centre Covenant, requiring operators to invest in local communities, create jobs and protect water supplies in return for priority grid connections.
But he also said that where grid connections were unavailable, developers would be permitted to generate their own power on-site.
BBC File on 4 Investigates has discovered that four data centres are already looking at using gas-fired power stations to meet their electricity needs.
If continuously running at full capacity, our calculations show they would require 1.3 gigawatts of power and could produce an estimated 4.1 million tonnes of carbon emissions a year. This could be more than the cities of Manchester, Liverpool and Southampton combined.
Oliver Hayes, head of campaigns at environmental charity Global Action Plan, said: "If we're powering by gas that means local communities are going to have huge gas turbines on their doorstep, and they are going to be generating a huge amount of local air pollution and a huge amount of noise and they will be using a huge amount of water from the local water supply."
The developments already considering on-site gas vary in scale.
At Acre Slough, west of London, developers say they could use gas engines with a generating capacity of up to 49.5 megawatts while waiting for a National Grid connection, something they expect could take at least 10 years.
At Wapsey's Wood, next to the M40 in Buckinghamshire, a proposed 200-megawatt gas power station could operate until sufficient grid capacity becomes available, currently not expected until 2040.
"It would be a disaster for us environmentally," said Buckinghamshire independent councillor Ed Gemmell, who also leads the Climate Party.
"If allowed, it sets a precedent that we could be getting gas-fired power stations all over the country and that would make it extremely difficult for us to hit any of our environmental and net zero targets."
Is it time to press pause on AI data centres?
An increasing number of large AI data centres are waiting in the UK energy supply queue - but will meeting that demand derail the road to net zero?
3 November
Quest Park has proposed building a data centre on the site of a quarry pit next to the planned Universal theme park in Bedfordshire. It would have a power load - the total amount of electrical power drawn at any given time - of 1 gigawatt, the equivalent to 200,000â250,000 average UK homes.
David Kohler, director of Quest Park, has previously told the BBC the company's energy mix was still a "work in progress" and that incorporating renewable power was "sensible" but had to be "feasible".
He said creating 1 gigawatt of solar electricity would require an area equivalent to 15% of Bedfordshire, and that wind power was "intermittent and expensive".
He said the company was considering alternative technologies that did not rely on gas combustion.
In Cardiff, a data centre developer is also seeking permission to build a temporary energy centre that has turbines with a maximum generating capacity of 49.9 megawatts.
Planning documents say it could operate for up to five years if the site cannot secure an electricity grid connection quickly enough. Developer Curtis Hall has described the turbine plan as a "worst-case scenario".
All four projects say they intend to connect to the national grid when it can meet their electricity needs, reducing their reliance on fossil fuels.

North Korea has denied claims that it was behind the record $6.3bn (Â£4.7bn) hack of cryptocurrency exchange Binance, calling the allegations "absurd rhetoric".
Kim Yo Jong, a top Democratic People's Republic of Korea official and the sister of leader Kim Jong Un, said on Tuesday that the accusations are another "sinister attempt" by the US to damage Pyongyang's public image.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Secret Service and cyber analysts have said North Korea orchestrated the hack, which has been described as the largest in history.
This is the latest hack to be linked to North Korea, which has been accused of relying on cyber-crime to help finance its sanctioned economy.
Blockchain analysts and the FBI have said the attack was led by state-backed hacking group TraderTraitor.
The FBI has called on industry partners to help block transactions involving cryptocurrency accounts linked to the group.
"The US has made a trite provocation of linking it with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea again," Kim Yo-jong, the director of North Korea's General Affairs Department, said in a statement.
"It is a grave political provocation against the DPRK that the US misleads the international public opinion as if all the cyber crimes in different parts of the world are our deeds," she said.
But Pyongyang has been blamed for a number of major cyber attacks in recent years - accusations that it has denied.
The TraderTraitor unit, which is also known as the Lazarus Group, was blamed for a then-record $1.5bn hack of crypto exchange Bybit in 2025.
Pyongyang has systematically built its cyber operations, recruiting promising students from universities and sending them to hacker units overseen by North Korea's intelligence agency, research groups like the S Rajaratnam School of International Studies think tank have said.
The country has consistently denied such claims.
Kim Yo Jong said "it is the consistent policy stand of the DPRK government to resolutely oppose all sorts of malicious acts in cyberspace".
The BBC has contacted Binance for comment. Since the hack, the crypto giant has largely focused its public statements on the technical nature of the breach and its response to protect users.
The company said last week that initial checks indicated that an engineer's laptop had been compromised, enabling an attacker to make unauthorised withdrawals.
Trading in major cryptocurrencies on Binance has since resumed after the exchange worked with issuers to freeze assets impacted by the hack.
A net $5.27bn has been withdrawn from the exchange since transactions resumed on Sunday, according to data posted on Tuesday by Binance. It also said the level of transactions has now stabilised.
The company has repeatedly said it would cover all of the losses linked to the attack and that it has so far covered around 95% of the assets stolen in the breach.

Scientists have picked up signals from the smallest scale of nature ever explored â 100 billion times smaller than an atom.
A world so small that some physicists have nicknamed it the zeptoverse.
The research, led by scientists based in Cambridge, was obtained from an experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC).
This vast machine at the European Laboratory for Particle Physics (Cern) on the Swiss-French border smashes atoms together to break them apart and discover what is inside them.
The result is important because it could help researchers develop a new, more complete theory of how the Universe works.
'Knocking on the door' of the zeptoverse
Dark matter makes up a large part of our cosmos, and yet researchers have struggled to detect it.
Scientists know it is there because its gravitational force influences normal matter, but in all other respects it has remained completely invisible.
So in this experiment, particles were smashed together at high energy and scientists studied the material that was thrown out - the shrapnel of collisions.
One of these is a sub-atomic particle - smaller than an atom - called a beauty quark.
The particle is unstable and exists for just one and a half trillionths of a second before breaking down into other forms - decaying.
Despite its short lifetime, researchers managed to detect it interacting with other tiny particles at a scale of a billion-trillionth of a metre.
Some theories suggest that at these scales particles are more sensitive to dark matter and it could influence how the quarks interact and break down. So, detecting activity in this tiny world could help scientists detect dark matter.
"We're knocking on the door of this zeptoverse," Dr Harry Cliff, of Cambridge University who led the analysis of the data, told BBC News.
He said this sub-atomic dance provided researchers with a ringside seat to the behaviour of possible new particles.
"And what we want to do now is go in and explore and find what new particles are waiting there. And to do that, what we need is more data," Cliff added.
The 28 countries involved in the project have agreed a Â£150m upgrade to this detector at the Large Hadron Collider (LHCb), which would increase the frequency of these decays tenfold.
"With that we can probe inside the zeptoverse and see what's waiting," Cliff said.
But earlier this year the UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) agency, the government body in charge of research funding, announced that it was withdrawing its share of the money for the planned upgrade.
It did so as it announced cuts to several other particle physics and astronomy projects, including Jodrell Bank's iconic Lovell telescope.
Although this research was led by scientists based in Cambridge, because of the cuts, Prof Tim Gershon, who leads the LHCb international collaboration, told BBC News that the UK's full involvement in the research would be in doubt.
"The UK is at risk of not being involved and making really major discoveries," he told BBC News.
"But I think the biggest long-term impact comes from the fact that the UK won't get the benefits from training young people who really are our greatest product."
Among those early-career researchers is Dr Mary Richardson-Slipper, who is part of the team that made the zeptoverse discovery. She is reconsidering her future in light of the physics cuts.
"I love being here in the UK, but I am looking at jobs abroad because that seems to be where there are more opportunities at the moment," said Richardson-Slipper.
She added that "lots" of her fellow researchers working in fundamental physics had already moved.
The cuts are being made despite an overall record increase in the science budget.
Prof Brian Cox, TV presenter and particle researcher at the University of Manchester, who is not part of the research team, described the result as "important".
But he condemned the recent decision to cut UK funding for the Cern project.
"It would be extraordinary to walk away from UK scientific leadership at this moment, damaging the future research programme and seriously damaging our hard-won international reputation," Cox said.
The UKRI told BBC News that it remained a fully engaged member of Cern as its second largest funder at around Â£175mâ¯per year.
A UKRI spokesperson said: "We sought independent advice and have taken forward an exciting portfolio of new infrastructure investments, which include projects in clean energy, medical imaging and cultural heritage.
"However, as usual, there were more exciting applications for funding than we were able to support."

Greenpeace has dropped nine boulders off the east coast of England to create a barrier that disrupts bottom trawling by fishing vessels.
The environmental campaigners' ship, Arctic Sunrise, sailed off the Norfolk coast to release the rocks without a licence over the weekend before mooring in Great Yarmouth.
Bottom trawling involves dragging weighted nets along the seabed to catch fish, although it can harm underwater vegetation.
Greenpeace claimed it had "effectively closed 116 sq km (45 sq miles) of the Southern North Sea Marine Protected Area (MPA) to bottom trawling". The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) said "activities at sea should be carried out lawfully".
When asked if they had permission to drop the boulders, Greenpeace said this was a "last resort" for it, and it did not have a licence.
It said that after years of meeting with politicians and the government to try to protect marine protected areas, progress had been "at a glacial pace".
A Defra spokesperson said: "We have strict legislation in place to protect our marine environment while supporting sustainable fishing and coastal communities.
"All Marine Protected Areas are safeguarded by legislation, with damaging fishing activities banned in more than 100 sites, and we are also considering further restrictions where there may be benefits in doing so.
"Activities at sea should be carried out lawfully and with due regard for the safety of other sea users."
Greenpeace added that bottom trawling could leave harbour porpoises, external, marine mammals which are found all over the UK's coast, with low fish stocks to feed on.
They added that the noise pollution of trawling disrupted the porpoises' ability to hunt and that the MPA had been designated to protect the animal.
In 2022, activists dropped 18 boulders off the coast of Cornwall.
After this, the government body responsible for managing coastal waters, the Marine Management Organisation (MMO), said: "As England's marine regulator, we are very disappointed that Greenpeace has chosen to take this action to drop boulders to form a barrier, as we don't believe it is justified or will help protect our marine environment."
Greenpeace said that, external after dropping the two-tonne boulders, it had called "the authorities to tell them the coordinates of each placement, and they update maps to inform other vessels".
The Southern North Sea MPA covers an area stretching from north of Dogger Bank (due east of Tyneside) to the Straits of Dover in the south.

The US has launched strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials have told CBS, the BBC's US partner.
Iranian state news agency IRNA reported several explosions on the island on Monday.
The US officials described the strikes as limited and said they were in response to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) firing upon a US aircraft.
The BBC has contacted US Central Command (Centcom), the part of the US military responsible for operations in the Middle East, for comment.
It comes ahead of the US midterm elections, which will determine whether the Republicans or Democrats control Congress.
Trump has been facing falling polling numbers and pressure from within his party to end the war, which began when the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Earlier on Monday, he told reporters that he was in "no rush" to ramp up strikes on Iran.
"One way or the other, we will do something, but there is no rush. We crippled them financially," he told news outlet Axios. "They have no money, no gasoline and their people are getting very tired of it."
He also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe", a site linked to Iran's nuclear programme, in an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterm elections.
This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump added.
There has been mounting speculation in the last few days that the US may resume significant strikes in Iran again after the midterms. But asked by a reporter on Monday if that was the case, Trump said "no".
Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi told IRNA earlier that "very intensive" talks to try and end the war are under way with the US via mediators.
He also said Tehran was prepared for both diplomatic and military scenarios "more than ever before" and that it was up to the US to choose between a "wise path" of negotiation or the "mistake of military aggression".

The US Supreme Court has rejected a last-minute request by the Trump administration asking it to intervene in California's midterm election vote count.
The justice department wanted 20,000 ballots to be set aside that it alleged may have been issued to non-US citizens in the state.
Two lower courts had already rejected the request. State election officials had questioned the federal government's claims - saying the process used to identify alleged non-citizens was inaccurate.
The Monday ruling comes on the eve of the midterms, which will determine which political party controls the US Congress for the last two years of President Donald Trump's second term.
The Supreme Court announced its decision in a one-line order, saying it was denying the justice department's request for an injunction.
"The application for injunction pending appeal presented to Justice Kagan and by her referred to the Court is denied," it reads.
Its means rulings made in lower courts will stand and essentially ends the Trump administration's bid to disqualify the ballots.
California is the most populous state in America with some 23 million people on its voting register. As of Sunday night, more than six million mail-in ballots had already been received, according to the California secretary of state's office.
The justice department sent letters to the California secretary of state and Los Angeles County Registrar last month, demanding they set aside the ballots of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration "believe" are "likely" non-citizens, according to court documents.
About a week later, armed officials from the Department of Homeland Security delivered letters to county officials and employees across California threatening criminal charges if they didn't sequester those ballots.
In a 22-page brief reviewed by the BBC, the justice department maintained that ballots cast by non-citizens could "debase or dilute valid votes".
On Friday, a federal appeals court declined the government's request to segregate the ballots.
California election officials have questioned the accuracy of the government's claims, and have said the list of names the government has provided is riddled with inaccuracies.
They have expressed concern that eligible voters could be disenfranchised and said segregating ballots whilst voting is underway is unfeasible.
The attempts are a part of a years-long campaign by Trump and his administration to fight alleged voter fraud that they believe is widespread, despite research showing that it is extremely rare.
President Trump has repeatedly claimed that Democrats steal elections by allowing immigrants to vote illegally, and he blames much of it on the so-called "mail-in" or postal voting that is permitted in many Democratic states.
Last week in a scathing ruling, district judge David Carter said the government's move in California was indicative of an "ongoing pattern of attempted election interference" on the part of the Trump administration.
The judge added that "never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the executive branch".
With additional reporting by the BBC's David Willis

Two people have been arrested after a volunteer for Australia's right-wing populist party One Nation was allegedly assaulted with a baseball bat.
A man, 37, and a boy, 14, were arrested on Sunday night after an incident outside the volunteer's home in Torquay, about 100km (62 miles) south-west of Melbourne.
The man was charged with assault offences and remanded in custody while the boy was issued with a caution. The volunteer was hospitalised with non-life threatening injuries, police said. He remains in a stable condition.
One Nation's Victorian leader Warren Pickering claimed the attack happened after the pair "interfered with" election signs on the volunteer's property.
Police haven't provided any detail about a motive, but Pickering said the alleged assault was "un-Australian and unacceptable".
"Political violence or intimidation of any kind against anyone is unacceptable in this country," he said.
"If you don't like someone's politics, you vote accordingly. You don't assault them."
On Tuesday, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson visited the injured volunteer at University Hospital Geelong where he is recovering, praising his "resilience" and "belief" in her party.
"He wants to go right back out there and put the signs up," she said outside the hospital.
The party has said the man has serious injuries, and shared a photo of him with severe swelling and bruising to his face.
Victorian Premier Ben Carroll described the attack as "shocking".
"Whether you're wearing a red, a blue, an orange, or a green T-shirt, they are volunteers," he said.
"They are out there doing what they believe is right, and no one should be coming under attack."
The alleged attack comes during a state election campaign in Victoria, and amid a reckoning in the country more broadly over the tone of political debate, after the attack on Federal MP Helen Haines last month.
Police have not detailed a motive for the incident - which left Haines needing both of her legs amputated - but politicians, law enforcement, and experts have said heated public discourse is heightening the threat of political violence in the country.

Price, Associated Press By — Samy Magdy, Associated Press Samy Magdy, Associated Press By — Cara Anna, Associated Press Cara Anna, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/u-s-strikes-iranian-targets-in-strait-of-hormuz-u-s-official-tells-ap Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter U.S. strikes Iranian targets in Strait of Hormuz, U.S. official tells AP World Nov 2, 2026 9:59 PM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — The United States has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, a U.S. official said Monday, on the eve of crucial midterm elections. Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island. The official, who wasn't authorized to comment publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity, said that "Iranians using surface to air missiles against U.S. assets" had been targeted. The strikes appeared to be limited as opposed to a return to full hostilities but followed President Donald Trump previously saying the U.S. would not launch new strikes on Iran before Tuesday's midterms. The unpopular war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress. The region is on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran, and the new strikes, which were reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal, are certain to raise fresh concerns. Backchannel negotiations also are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the more than 8-month-old war that's rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran. The Trump administration was last known to have carried out attacks in early September, but thousands of U.S. troops remain in the waters off Iran to maintain a naval blockade aimed at preventing tankers hauling Iranian oil from getting to the global market. Plus, a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are on their way to the Middle East. Before the strikes were confirmed, U.S. Vice President JD Vance offered measured optimism that a deal could still be struck. Vance sent a letter to Iran's security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, but the White House has offered scant details. Trump told reporters that letter was focused on assisting Iran with "medical supplies and various things." "We've had a number of good conversations with the Iranians," Vance told reporters Monday when asked about the letter. "I actually just spoke with the president of the United States about an hour ago about this. Look, the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement. We're going to keep on working at it." FILE PHOTO: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and President Donald Trump and hold a press conference after meeting at Trump's Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida, on Dec. 29, 2025. Photo by Jonathan Ernst/Reuters Netanyahu pushed Trump for strikes in a weekend call Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes on Iran after the U.S. elections, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter. A return to full-scale war with Iran could help Netanyahu to form an emergency government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week's elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran. The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress, with Qatari mediators holding two rounds of talks last week with Iranian officials. The two officials said the mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran's ports. They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American, and in one case Israeli, officials. One official said Netanyahu was working with senior officials in the U.S. administration to persuade Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign and that the president does not appear to have made a decision. Netanyahu pressed for strikes during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it. Other U.S. allies in the Middle East are warning against more strikes, saying that would destabilize the region and could lead Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen to step up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, a third regional official said. Iran-backed militias in Iraq could also get involved. The Israeli government did not immediately comment. The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Trump's discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call. Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman said he spoke by phone Monday with U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth about "the latest regional and international developments" and the Houthis' continued attacks on Saudi Arabia. Trump downplays scale of Iran conflict Oil prices dropped sharply Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts in the Iran war appeared to show signs of headway. Trump noted the drop in a speech in Washington on Monday, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47 billion. "I don't know if you even call it a war, because we haven't been doing any fighting for months," Trump said. Foxâs $22 billion acquisition of Roku is poised to clear Justice Department scrutiny and move forward under a consent decree, according to people familiar with the deliberations, despite efforts from a right-wing ally of President Donald Trump to hold up the deal.
Itâs unclear what a consent decree would entail, or what terms are being considered. Itâs possible the DOJ could change course, the people said. Fox declined to comment.
Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward also declined to comment on the deal. âHowever, we can affirm that this DOJ under President Trumpâs leadership will continue to prioritize affordability for all Americans across our economy,â he said in a statement.
The deal, which would unite Foxâs content empire of news and sports with Rokuâs dominant connected-TV operating system, had worried rivals who fear that Fox will favor its own content. Rokuâs free, ad-supported channel also competes for viewers and content with Tubi, which Fox owns. Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch has said his âexpectationâ is to run the two businesses separately while selling advertising across them.
Semafor first reported in September that antitrust regulators were widening the inquiry into the deal, days before the two companies confirmed the deeper probe, known as a âsecond request.â That enhanced scrutiny came in part because of pressure from Newsmax majority owner Chris Ruddy, who bills himself as a Trump confidant and has had a long-running spat with Fox owner Rupert Murdoch, Semafor later reported.
Rohanâs view
Ruddy, briefly a reporter for Murdochâs New York Post in the 1990s, has been feuding with Fox for more than a year over streaming access to his media assets.
Murdochâs camp has previously dismissed Newsmaxâs efforts as a bid to âsue their way out of their own competitive failures,â and Murdoch himself has dined with Trump more than once. But itâs clear that Ruddy has been a headache for the Murdoch clan. Investors have fretted about the possibility that Foxâs deal for Roku could get tied up as a result of Ruddyâs efforts.
Those worries were exacerbated after Fox ousted business anchor Maria Bartiromo following an internal investigation into allegations she leaked internal network information and communications to the Trump administration, a claim her lawyers have disputed.
But if the deal goes through, itâs more evidence that the Murdoch name still carries a fair amount of weight in Washington.

4b2061e9dec8.text: Republicans don't know if they'll lose big or small on Tuesday, but they're already bracing for an epic blame game. Why it matters: Privately, Republicans acknowledge it's not a complicated version of Clue. The leading suspect: Mr. President , in the Oval Office, with an assortment of weapons — and one war. Returning Republican senators are unlikely to blame President Trump publicly. There's a price for that. And don't expect Trump to shoulder the responsibility. But do expect departing GOP lawmakers to take shots at Trump or his team, and Trump to fire back at Senate Republicans, whom he's never been shy about torching. The irony of Trump's second midterm: With Republicans privately resigned to losing the House, Trump can still credibly claim victory if they hold the Senate. "It's Donald Trump's midterms. He gets all the credit if we win. He gets all the credit if we lose," one national GOP strategist told Axios. The Iran war: From Alaska to Maine, Trump's decision to go to war with Iran — and the resulting spike in gas and diesel prices — has become a major political liability for Republican Senate nominees. "It's not tariffs … it's the war, it's gas prices, it's diesel," Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton said at a closed-door fundraiser in September, Axios reported last month . Tariffs: Trump's trade policies have compounded Republicans' affordability problems, particularly in farm country, where producers have faced higher costs and uncertainty over export markets. "We need to end this tariff war now," former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) , the GOP Senate nominee, said in an October campaign ad, breaking with Trump over his tariffs on Canada. Bad candidates: Trump's preferred nominees are also drawing blame, GOP strategists tell Axios. Paxton in Texas and Sen. Darline Graham in South Carolina have forced Republicans to spend heavily defending races that should have been easier — and where the party had other options. Complacent incumbents: Sens. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Cindy Hyde-Smith (R-Miss.) are facing accusations of "arrogance" and "laziness" from Republicans frustrated that their once-safe seats have become late-breaking battlegrounds — exactly the complacency NRSC Chair Tim Scott warned against. Weak governors: Underperforming gubernatorial nominees in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio threaten to drag down Republican Senate candidates. Vivek Ramaswamy, for example, saw his polling crater in the final weeks . Recruitment failures: Republicans couldn't persuade Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp to run for Senate, and in New Hampshire settled for their second-choice Sununu — former Sen. John Sununu — instead of his brother, former Gov. Chris Sununu. Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) landed marquee candidates in Alaska, Ohio and Iowa — though Michigan and Maine proved more difficult. MAGA money: Trump's political operation amassed an enormous war chest, but some Republicans complain the money arrived too late to rescue vulnerable candidates. Distractions: Trump's focus on D.C. construction projects, the Kennedy Center, Sen. Jon Husted's (R-Ohio) backside and the SAVE Act has frustrated Republicans desperate for a closing message focused on the economy. "Reflecting Pool presser was an interesting choice for closing message," another national GOP strategist said of Trump's Monday news conference.
