15ae37afd710.text: Data: AdImpact; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Republicans on the ballot this cycle have all but stopped mentioning President Trump in their campaign ads , according to an Axios analysis of broadcast advertising data from AdImpact. Why it matters: Trump has tried to make the 2026 midterms a referendum on his presidency. His party has run the other way. The big picture: Ads from both parties in Senate, House and gubernatorial races have shifted from a heavy focus on Trump during the primaries to a much greater emphasis on the economy in the general election. Both parties have also leaned much more heavily into health care, with a noticeable increase among House Republicans. By the numbers: The drop-off is steepest among Republicans, and especially in House races. Trump appeared in 66% of House Republicans' primary ads but shows up in just 3% of their general election ads. In Senate races, Republican ads mentioning him fell from 77% to 22%. Governor's races saw the same shift: Republican ads mentioning Trump fell 34 percentage points. Democrats have also pulled back from Trump, though less dramatically. Trump appeared in 45% of Democratic primary ads, but just 18% of their general election ads. Zoom in: Republican candidates are mentioning some of Trump's signature issues less than during the primaries. The share of Republican ads mentioning immigration has dropped 20 percentage points in Senate races and 14 points in House races. Ads referencing law enforcement fell from 11% of Republican Senate primary ads to 6% in the general election, even as their mentions of crime increased. Data: AdImpact; Chart: Erin Davis/Axios Between the lines: Candidates often lean on the country's most prominent political figure in primaries, then pivot to policy issues in the general election. But this year's drop-off stands out given how hard Trump has pushed to tie himself to the midterms. He has urged voters to pretend he's on the ballot and essentially demanded ads running during the Republican midterm convention in September feature him. Of note: In this analysis, primary ads are broadcast ads that aired before a race's primary. General election ads aired between the primary and Oct. 26. The trends may be even more pronounced in ads running through Election Day. The bottom line: Most Republicans have been too scared to tell Trump how unpopular he is, Axios reported . But their ad receipts don't lie.

e142c8051889.text: The Pentagon's former top military planner is under federal investigation and may face a court-martial for allegedly leaking to reporters from the Wall Street Journal and New York Times, according to three sources familiar with the controversy. Why it matters: Former Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was fired by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last week after being accused of misconduct as part of the department's war on leaks. Sylvia failed four polygraphs and admitted to the incidents during two interviews on video that lasted more than a total of two hours, according to details from an internal Pentagon report shared with Axios. "The president has no tolerance for leakers, so Sylvia's termination is the first step in the accountability process, not the last," one of the sources said. Zoom in: Starting in the fall of 2025, the sources said, Sylvia gave information without authorization to reporters Michael Gordon of the Wall Street Journal and Greg Jaffe of the New York Times. Neither reporter is suspected or accused of doing anything illegal, improper or unprofessional in their reporting. Journalists often rely on confidential sources in reporting on issues that involve institutions where insiders aren't authorized to speak publicly. The report states Sylvia admitted to more extensive contacts with Gordon in 2025 and 2026, when the general allegedly shared classified information about Ukraine and Iran with the reporter. The Justice Department is investigating that. Only one discussion with Jaffe appears in the investigative report, concerning Hegseth's unexplained purging of military leaders. Sources said the unauthorized communication by Sylvia potentially violated the Uniform Code of Military Justice's prohibition of "conduct unbecoming of an officer." Behind the scenes: Sylvia allegedly admitted to first disclosing information to Gordon in the fall of 2025 when the two met in the Pentagon and discussed unspecified information about Ukraine, the sources said. After the Wall Street Journal and other outlets were barred from the Pentagon, Sylvia met Gordon at the Silver Diner in Arlington, Va., to give information about a book the reporter was planning to write, the report said. "Major General Sylvia relied on notes he took while reviewing a classified secret report to orally brief Gordon on assistance to Ukraine," said the report, which emphasized that Sylvia didn't receive clearance to discuss the sensitive information. A separate legal analysis of Sylvia's conduct alleged that the general also discussed "munitions stockpiles and high-level interagency discussions with Iran" that were classified, according to a source briefed on the document. Then, "sometime in June or July," Gordon sent Sylvia a message on the encrypted app Signal, the report said. "Sylvia is unable to recall exactly what was in that message" the report said. "But he believed it had something to do with Iran. He stated that he did not respond to the message and instead deleted it." While deleting the message, Sylvia allegedly told military investigators that "he believed he deleted the entire message thread with Michael Gordon. This erased Signal messages and Signal phone calls that would have been recorded in Signal on [Sylvia's] personal phone." Sylvia "indicated multiple times he was comfortable with what he told Gordon about Ukraine assistance," the report said without elaborating. The intrigue: Sylvia's case has led to some friction in the Pentagon after the Joint Staff initially issued a positive statement about the general immediately after he was terminated. The Joint Staff retracted its statement after senior Defense Department officials sent word that Sylvia had been fired for allegedly leaking. A source familiar with the investigation said the Joint Staff should have known better. "You don't get four polygraphs deep without the head of the Joint Staff being briefed at some point. Why wasn't he flagged, what red flags flared up?" the source said. "Their first statement, they gave him a farewell — you know, 'We wish you well in your future endeavors' — and had to retract that information after the truth came out," the source said. "So there's a level of culpability within the Joint Staff that I think is a critical part of this they need to answer for." What they're saying: The Joint Staff declined to comment and referred questions to the Justice Department. The New York Times and Wall Street Journal declined to comment. Sylvia could not be reached for comment. The Defense Department referred Axios to a statement by Assistant Defense Secretary Sean Parnell, who said last week that "classified information is not personal property. Leaking it for personal, political or professional gain is a betrayal of the trust placed in those responsible for keeping it."

8dd6b4aba466.text: Data: AP via The New York Times and Axios research; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios The first votes counted Tuesday night will almost certainly look redder than the final result, and control of the House and Senate could take days to settle. Why it matters: Early leads can create false impressions of who's winning and suspicion when those leads vanish. Election night is really election week. By the numbers: AP didn't call control of the House until seven or eight days after Election Day in each of the past three elections . The Senate was settled by 10:44pm on election night in 2018 and at 12:06am the next morning in 2024 . In 2022, it took four days , and in 2020, it wasn't called until Georgia's January runoffs , two months later. State of play: Republicans hold 53 Senate seats . Democrats need a net gain of four for a majority. The red head start: In every national election since 2018, the House and Senate votes counted by 9pm ET were 4 to 9 percentage points more Republican than the final result, an Axios analysis of AP and Edison Research vote counts found. It's mostly geography. Fast-counting Florida and other right-leaning states report first. At 9pm on election night 2022, Florida accounted for 40% of all Senate votes counted nationwide. By 11pm, more House races had been called for Republicans than Democrats in all four elections, including 2018 and 2020, when Democrats won the House. The tilt fades, slowly. At 6am Wednesday, the national House count was still 2 to 3 points more Republican than the final, largely because California, Washington and Oregon count for days. Data: Axios research; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Zoom in: Each state tilts its own way, depending on which ballots and which counties it counts first. States that count early and mail ballots first tend to start bluer than they finish. States that count Election Day votes first start redder. Ohio, Nebraska, Texas, Kansas and Iowa start blue. Sherrod Brown and Bernie Moreno were tied at 9pm in 2024 with half of Ohio's votes counted. Moreno won by 4. Independent Dan Osborn led Sen. Deb Fischer at 11pm in Nebraska with half the votes counted in 2024. Fischer won by 7. Beto O'Rourke led Ted Cruz at 9pm in 2018 with nearly half of Texas counted. Cruz won by 3. In 2020, Kansas Republican Roger Marshall was down by 8 points at 9pm, even though he'd eventually win by double-digits. Michigan swings both ways. Elissa Slotkin led Mike Rogers by 13 points at 9pm in 2024, trailed by 3 at midnight and won by less than half a point. Maine starts red and counts slowly. In 2020, Susan Collins led by 18 points at 11pm with 16% counted. She won by 9. Alaska is the slowest and starts out redder. In 2020, Sen. Dan Sullivan led by 28 points at 6am ET with 37% counted. He won by 13. Election-night results include Election Day ballots and some early and absentee ballots. The rest are counted in the following days. Rural mail often goes through Anchorage, and weather can slow it, with domestic ballots accepted up to 10 days after Election Day if postmarked on time. If no one wins a majority of first choices, Alaska will run its ranked-choice tally on Nov. 18. Data: AP and Edison Research via The New York Times; Chart: Andrew Pantazi/Axios Watch the clock (all times ET): 6pm — The first votes: Parts of Indiana and Kentucky close, giving us the first House returns. 7pm — The red head start: Polls close in the key Senate states of Georgia, South Carolina and most of Florida and New Hampshire. Fast-counting Florida gives Republicans an early boost in House races. 7:30pm — North Carolina and Ohio close: Watch for early Democratic leads in Ohio that could shrink as more votes come in. 8pm — Four more key races: Maine closes, along with most of Michigan, Texas and Kansas, the rest of New Hampshire and Florida's Panhandle. 9pm — Peak red mirage: Iowa, Minnesota and Nebraska close, along with the rest of Michigan, Texas and Kansas. Historically, the national House count looks most Republican between 9pm and 11pm. 11pm — The West Coast: California, Oregon and Washington begin reporting, bringing millions of votes and pivotal House races into the picture. The early Republican tilt should begin fading. About 1am Wednesday — Alaska: The last polls close, and initial results are expected. Election-night results include Election Day ballots and some early and absentee ballots, with others counted in subsequent days. The bottom line: Early leads aren't necessarily predictive. The closer the race, the longer voters may have to wait to learn who won.

9882cdfeb770.text: Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/live-results-nevada-governor-midterm-election Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Live Results: Nevada governor midterm election Politics Nov 3, 2026 5:00 AM EST WASHINGTON (AP) — Nevada voters will elect leaders for federal, state and other offices on Tuesday. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied: When do polls close? Polls close at 7 p.m. local time, which is 10 p.m. ET, but state law requires polls to stay open until all voters in line by poll closing time have cast their ballots. What's on the ballot? The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare winners in races for governor, U.S. House, mayor of Henderson, lieutenant governor, attorney general, secretary of state, statewide ballot measures, state Supreme Court, state Senate, state Assembly, controller and state treasurer. How many people voted in the last midterm election? About 1 million votes were cast in the 2022 U.S. Senate race in Nevada. How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot? About 80% of all ballots cast in Nevada's 2022 election for U.S. Senate were cast early or by absentee ballot. The latest advance vote totals for Nevada can be found in the AP's advance vote tracker. When are early and absentee votes released? Every Nevada county is expected to release at least some early in-person or mail voting results at the start of the night. About half of the counties are expected to release all or almost all mail voting results. Nearly every county is expected to release all or almost all in-person early voting results in the first update. About half of counties are not expected to release any in-person Election Day results in the first update. READ MORE: Nevada is set to have one of nation's premier races for governor as Democrats seek to reclaim seat In both Clark and Washoe counties, the first vote update of the night tends to include all early in-person voting results and partial mail voting results, before any in-person Election Day results are released. How long does vote counting usually take? The first results of the 2024 general election were reported starting at 12:54 a.m. ET on Nov. 6, about three hours after polls closed. The state reached 50% of votes reporting less than 10 minutes later, at 1:02 a.m. ET, and 90% of votes reporting at 8:26 p.m. ET later that day. When will the AP declare a winner? The Associated Press does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it's determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why. How do recounts work? Recounts in Nevada are not automatic, but a candidate may request and pay for one regardless of the vote margin. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome. -- Camille Baker and Robert Yoon, Associated Press A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. 099d9934667b.text: The 2026 midterms will offer the first test of voter sentiment on the AI race, offering a window into how a niche policy debate is transforming into a wedge issue ahead of a presidential campaign cycle. Why it matters: The results will reveal whether explicitly campaigning on AI regulation — or aligning with tech moguls like Elon Musk — is a winning political strategy or a liability for 2028. One thing is already clear: Candidates increasingly can't afford to have half-baked AI agendas. Here are three major questions about the future of AI politics and policy and the races we're watching on Election Day for answers. 1. Did AI break through? A different kind of AI political spending has emerged in the midterms. Instead of supporting or opposing candidates based on their AI positions, some groups want to make AI policy itself a campaign issue. Guardrails Alliance, a pro-regulation advocacy group, recently launched ads targeting Republicans and Democrats over their positions on AI in Arizona, Montana, North Carolina and California. The organization backed Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, who said AI was the most important issue heading into Election Day, tying it explicitly to jobs and affordability. Democratic group Tomorrow Together also launched ads against Republicans' AI track record in Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona and Pennsylvania. Meanwhile, competing AI groups Public First and Leading the Future spent more than $50 million through affiliated super PACs in nearly 50 races, but their TV and digital ads largely avoided the very issue they're trying to influence: AI. These races could offer an early test of whether explicitly campaigning on AI is a viable political strategy heading into 2028. 2. Did Elon Musk help or hurt candidates? Elon Musk's political spending, involvement in DOGE and ties to the Trump administration have made him both a powerful political backer and a target for Democratic attacks. He was the biggest donor in the midterms by far, contributing more than $400 million. Races we're watching include: Texas' 10th District: Republican Chris Gober, who represented Musk in connection with DOGE, faces Democrat Caitlin Rourk. Kansas' 1st District: Democrat Lauren Reinhold has leaned into her experience with DOGE, criticizing Musk's influence over the federal government in her challenge against Republican Rep. Tracey Mann. Ohio Senate: Republican Jon Husted has benefited from spending by Musk's America PAC in his race against Democrat Sherrod Brown. Texas Senate: Musk-affiliated spending has made the contest between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton another test of the billionaire's political influence. These races could help answer whether Musk's money helped elect Republican allies or gave Democrats a useful target. 3. How loud will the AI safety movement be in the next Congress? A handful of candidates aligned with stronger AI safeguards could help determine whether the next Congress has a more vocal bloc pushing back against the industry's efforts to limit regulation. Races we're watching include: Michigan Senate: El-Sayed wants a new Cabinet-level federal agency to regulate AI and a ban on super intelligence. He has used Musk's political involvement to attack Republican Mike Rogers, who has benefited from Musk-affiliated political spending. Colorado's 8th district: Democrat Manny Rutinel sponsored the nation's first comprehensive AI bill. California's 11th district: Democrat Scott Wiener's AI transparency legislation was at the center of a regulatory fight that divided the industry, offering a preview of battles in Washington. Minnesota's 2nd district: Democrat Matt Little would add another voice to the push to ban data center construction and nondisclosure agreements at the national level. These are some of the races that will help determine the size and influence of the AI safety movement's congressional coalition, an important indicator of where the fight over AI regulation is headed in 2027 and beyond. The bottom line: Many factors will shape the outcomes of races across the country. But competing AI factions will be quick to claim victories, explain away losses and draw lessons about what worked ahead of 2028.

7978f33b0338.text: Elon Musk is looking to shake up America's wireless industry, potentially bringing the first major new competitive threat in years to a business dominated by three companies. Why it matters: The cellular industry has seen enormous technological change, but relatively little disruption to its competitive structure. Musk has the money, spectrum and satellite network to attempt something different — though he faces daunting obstacles. Driving the news: SpaceX is assembling the pieces to become a major U.S. wireless carrier, potentially building its own terrestrial network and buying available spectrum. The moves are meant either to build the capability to bypass existing carriers or to bring them to the table for a deal that would allow Musk to strike a deal for wholesale access to their networks. Musk may have reason to move quickly while the current administration and its regulatory appointees remain in place, a reason some analysts have cited in the context of proposals for a merger between Tesla and SpaceX . What they're saying: Blair Levin, a former FCC chief of staff who now heads policy at Optimal Advisory, says Musk's financial resources distinguish him from previous challengers. "For the first time, there is an entity capable of scaring investors in the traditional big three," Levin told Axios. Unlike Dish, which faced serious financing constraints, SpaceX can draw on capital markets that have rewarded Musk's ambitious plans. The latest : SpaceX has held talks with EchoStar about acquiring Boost Mobile or gaining access to its network arrangements, according to a Washington Post report Monday. That could provide a quick route to customers and infrastructure, although approval of such a deal is far from a foregone conclusion if Musk's businesses are drawn into a regulator quagmire after the midterm elections. The Post reported that Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile have all rebuffed Musk's efforts to gain access to their networks. State of play: Musk also has a path to maneuver around them. SpaceX has agreed to multibillion-dollar spectrum deals , including a low-band variety useful for reaching customers indoors and supporting a traditional cellular network. The company could build its own network using towers and smaller rooftop antennas, though doing so would require substantial investment and time. The big picture: America's wireless industry has spent much of the past two decades consolidating. T-Mobile once played the scrappy challenger, shaking up the industry with aggressive pricing and the elimination of unpopular practices. But its 2020 acquisition of Sprint reduced the number of major nationwide carriers from four to three. Regulators tried to preserve a fourth competitor by requiring the sale of Boost Mobile to Dish Network, which planned to build a nationwide network. That effort never delivered the competitive alternative envisioned, leaving Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile firmly entrenched. The intrigue: Musk would be moving from a business where SpaceX enjoys enormous technical and economic advantages to one where the established players have spent decades building infrastructure, acquiring customers and learning how to serve them. In terrestrial wireless, the big three carriers have spent decades investing in towers, spectrum, indoor coverage and the countless small improvements that make their networks reliable. Building such a network isn't simply a matter of spending billions on infrastructure, Craig Moffett of MoffettNathanson said in a recent podcast interview. It also means catching up on decades of work filling in coverage gaps in stadiums, airports and other difficult locations. The catch: Even if Musk can assemble the necessary infrastructure, it's far from clear that becoming a nationwide wireless carrier would be a particularly attractive business. Moffett questions why SpaceX would want to enter an industry where even the established carriers struggle to earn attractive returns on their investments. Between the lines: Success will depend on fundamentally lowering the cost of providing service or creating something for which consumers are willing to pay extra. SpaceX has floated the idea of using Starlink rooftop equipment as small cellular base stations, potentially reducing some of the costs of building a traditional network. The political backdrop: Musk's plans come as Washington faces a potentially significant shift following Tuesday's midterm elections. While SpaceX is likely to face significant political and regulatory risks due to Musk's ties with Republicans, analysts aren't sure that will translate into opposing a wireless deal that adds competition to the market. The bottom line: Musk has repeatedly succeeded in industries where established players doubted his ambitions. But this time he's the outsider, trying to overcome the advantages of companies that have spent decades building the networks he wants to challenge.

8c82090c2887.text: Democrats are poised to romp in today's election — easily winning the House and, according to most forecasts, flipping the Senate too. Yet the party itself is less popular than the IRS . Even the GOP has a better brand. Why it matters: There's a difference between a blowout and a mandate. Confusing the two could tempt Democrats to overread the results and forget the serious credibility problem they still face heading into 2028. The big picture: Democrats have done a lot of things right to position themselves for a big night. They recruited candidates who've put red state Senate races that seemingly were beyond reach, within their grasp. Many of those candidates vastly outraised their Republican opponents. But polls across the board still show a lesser-of-two-evils election — or as one Republican tied to President Trump's political operation described it, a contest of which party voters hate more. Voters are more eager to disempower Trump than to empower Democrats. By the numbers: Just 29% of registered voters have a positive opinion of the Democratic Party vs. 38% who view the Republican Party positively, according to a pre-election NBC News poll . The same poll showed Democrats with a 7-point lead in the congressional generic ballot, 52 to 45. And nearly 6 in 10 voters who plan to back Democrats in the election said their vote is about stopping Trump and Republican policies — vs. 4 in 10 who said they were more motivated to help Democrats enact their policies, per an October CBS News/YouGov poll . Zoom in: Many Democrats say they're determined not to repeat the mistake they made after the last midterms in 2022. They defied predictions of a red wave and saw it as an endorsement of Joe Biden and their party — when voters actually were increasingly angry. The post-2022 takeaway ultimately laid the groundwork for Trump's return to the White House after the 2024 election. Democrats won the House in the 2018 midterms — and went on to impeach Trump the following year. This time, presumed House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) isn't talking about another Trump impeachment — his 100-day agenda is focused on affordability. Zoom out: Other Democrats warn that it's been easier to run against Trump when he's actually in office. Making him the face of the election didn't work in 2024, and it might not in 2028, either. At the Third Way gathering in South Carolina earlier this year, Democratic strategist Jim Messina told a crowd of operatives and party leaders, "We have no economic message. And if we don't get one, we're not going to win" in 2028. Flashback: The 2006 midterms also featured a Democratic uprising against an unpopular war and an unpopular president. Democrats flipped the House and Senate in a major rebuke of President George W. Bush. But the party that year had a net-positive party image of 4 points in NBC polling. Today, it's 23 points underwater. Two years later in 2008 — with anti-Bush and anti-war backlash still running hot — Democrats harnessed Barack Obama's talents and calls for "change" to win back the White House. But a midterm blowout in 2026, if it materializes, will offer no guarantee the party will find an equally talented standard-bearer in 2028. What they're saying: "It's not great for the Democrats ... for 2028," Bill McInturff, one of the pollsters who conducted the NBC survey, said of the Democratic Party's lousy image. "But I don't see it as a barrier for how well they can do in 2026 when midterms are about Trump and these economic numbers." The bottom line: Ultimately, many top Democrats believe it will take a new presidential nominee — and likely one who wins in November 2028 — to fully repair the party's damaged brand. Axios' Alex Thompson and Holly Otterbein contributed to this story.

As Grace Griffin and her husband were welcoming their long-awaited baby — a daughter — Griffin found herself worried about looming medical bills and unsure if their family could pay for the care they needed.
“This whole experience has me wondering (keeping me up at night, actually): Can we ever afford to have another child?”
— Grace Griffin, Calumet, Michigan
Grace and Daniel Griffin, both 26, knew money would be tight once they had their first child. So, even before the Calumet, Michigan, couple tried to conceive, they began crunching the numbers to figure out the cost of pregnancy.
“We wanted to save up enough to pay for those medical bills right away, if possible,” Grace said.
But the cost estimator she found linked to her UnitedHealthcare student plan asked for medical billing codes for each procedure Grace was likely to receive. That’s information she didn’t have.
So, she kept digging until she found the Summary of Benefits and Coverage information on the health plan’s website, which estimated out-of-pocket costs for a routine pregnancy and delivery at about $2,700.
“We thought, ‘OK, that’s doable,’” she said. “We should be able to save up that much and pay for that out-of-pocket.”
But, as the expenses piled up, it was clear the estimate wasn’t even close.
Early in the pregnancy, Grace met her $500 deductible, the out-of-pocket cost she had to pay before insurance pitched in. Her plan also required her to pay 20% coinsurance for in-network care. That meant that for every $100 billed for things like routine blood work and other needed care, she was on the hook for $20.
“When I started getting lab work is when we started realizing expenses would add up quickly,” Grace said. Routine blood tests to check iron levels or for gestational diabetes were a couple of hundred dollars every visit, she said.
In June, after what Grace described as a routine pregnancy and delivery, the couple welcomed their daughter. Then the Griffins received an “explanation of benefits” notice, which showed the hospital charged about $18,000 for the delivery, with the family on the hook for a sizable portion.
“I thought, ‘Oh no, it’s going to be a lot,’” she said. “Much more than we budgeted for.”
She was right.
In early October, Grace said, her family’s out-of-pocket expenses totaled more than $9,000, more than three times the general estimate published by her insurer for pregnancy-related costs.
Meanwhile, Grace and Daniel are scrambling to cover their bills.
For years, federal lawmakers have tried to remedy this issue, said Sabrina Corlette, a research professor and co-director of Georgetown University’s Center on Health Insurance Reforms. To make healthcare costs more transparent and accessible to patients, Congress required insurers to provide consumers with an individualized “advanced explanation of benefits” estimating what scheduled care would cost them. The rule, part of the 2020 No Surprises Act, was due to take effect on Jan. 1, 2022, but federal regulators have yet to make that happen, despite ongoing pressure from members of Congress.
“So, it’s basically 4½ years since this was supposed to be available, and I think it’s a source of a lot of frustration for a lot of folks,” Corlette said. “People have a right under the law to know these things.”
Meanwhile, she said, another change is pending. Beginning Jan. 1, long-standing maternity billing codes that bundle much of pregnancy care will be replaced with more detailed coding for prenatal care, labor, delivery, and postpartum care.
The change could make it easier to see what individual services cost, but Corlette said it’s not yet clear whether the change will make it easier for people trying to stick to a budget.
“I could see where it might be advantageous to the provider,” she said. “But I’m not sure I’m seeing benefits to the patient.”
Until out-of-pocket maternity expenses get easier to estimate, here are some tips to help you budget for the cost of pregnancy.
1. Enroll your baby before the clock runs out.
Ensuring your newborn has health coverage is one of the first paperwork responsibilities parents face in the whirlwind of bringing a baby home.
Birth creates what’s known as a special enrollment opportunity, meaning you don’t have to wait until the annual open enrollment period to sign up a newborn.
Many employer health plans require parents to request enrollment within 30 days of birth. Marketplace plans — for those who buy their own insurance rather than get it from an employer or the government — generally allow 60 days. Wait too long, and your baby may be left uninsured until the following year.
Michelle Critzer of Ventura, California, learned that lesson the hard way. She works as a sales rep and is the mother of a toddler and a newborn. Her second son, Hudson, was born in February 2026, and Critzer missed the enrollment deadline for him. Ever since, she’s been asking her insurer to make an exception — so far, without success.
“The way they set hard must-dos within 30 days of having a baby is actually insanity,” she said.
The family was able to enroll Hudson in a health plan through Critzer’s husband’s workplace, which has a 60-day enrollment window. But that coverage is not nearly as robust as Critzer’s insurance, she said. Still, she’s grateful to have Hudson insured while she continues pressing her own plan to enroll him.
2. Ask about must-know numbers, like your MOOP.
Budgeting for a pregnancy often begins with a tally of the expected expenses. The deductible is the amount you’ll pay before much of your insurance coverage kicks in.
After that, you’ll likely face copayments — fixed fees paid each time you receive service, regardless of the size of the bill.
Coinsurance is another expected expense, but, as Grace discovered, it can be especially tricky to estimate. Coinsurance requires the patient to pay a percentage of the cost for each service received.

A Few Miles From the US Capitol, Dozens Slept in Their Cars, Waiting for Free Care
TAKOMA PARK, Md. — Friday night lights took on a whole new meaning at a high school here in this suburb of Washington, D.C.
Instead of fans packing stadium bleachers to watch football, on this recent October weekend the gymnasium, hallways, and parking areas were jammed with people desperately seeking healthcare at a free pop-up clinic.
The 2026 election season has been punctuated by affordability issues, with polls showing high healthcare costs are a top concern among likely voters. The staggering toll of people struggling to get care was on full display here just eight miles northeast of the U.S. Capitol — in an area where census data shows the median household income tops $108,000 and about 94% have health insurance.
Dozens of people slept in their cars overnight outside Takoma Academy to secure spots for free health, dental, or vision care, according to clinic coordinators and interviews with patients.
Though clinic doors were scheduled to open at 6 a.m. Oct. 17, the first patients drove up shortly before midnight. By 4 a.m., three hours before sunrise, about 80 cars had arrived. Patients were given numbers representing their place in line when they entered the parking lot, and they had to be on site when they were notified by text message that it was their turn.
Kenys Bautista arrived at the school before midnight after driving 20 minutes from her home in Wheaton, Maryland. She wanted to be sure she got the medical and dental checkups that she had put off for three years because she didn’t have insurance or the money to cover the costs.
“It’s really sad that a lot of people like me had to sleep in their car just to see a doctor or dentist because we do not have health insurance,” Bautista said. She works as a payroll specialist for a small company but does not get any health benefits.
Bautista was one of 467 patients at the weekend clinic. Most received dental and/or medical care. Ninety-nine got vision exams, and many left with new eyeglasses, according to clinic organizers.
While most patients at the clinic were uninsured, 1 in 4 had health coverage, such as through Medicare or their employer. But many said just having coverage was not enough, because it left them with unaffordable out-of-pocket costs .
“I never thought I would need a clinic like this, but it’s gotten so expensive in the world,” Alma Walton said. She has Medicare, but routine dental care is not a standard benefit.
Walton, who lives in Camp Springs, Maryland, was 59th in line for care. She arrived around 1:30 a.m. “I wanted to make sure I could get in,” she said. She went to the clinic in hopes of getting a filling fixed after it cracked over the summer. She had postponed seeing a dentist.
Around 11 a.m., Walton was in one of the 30 dental treatment tents set up in the large gymnasium, having her filling replaced.
“You got here just in time,” John Renzi, a dentist volunteering at the clinic, told her just before he began drilling. “Any longer and this tooth would have been a goner.”
The clinic was organized by Remote Area Medical, a Tennessee-based nonprofit that says it has provided free healthcare to more than a million patients over its 40-year history. The clinics initially targeted rural areas, such as in Appalachia, traditionally home to some of the poorest and least insured communities in the country.
In recent years, the organization has branched out into urban and suburban areas — such as around the nation’s capital, Baltimore, and Philadelphia — where having insurance is more common. The clinics rely on doctors and dentists donating their time.
At the Takoma Park event, more than 300 dental, medical, and vision professionals volunteered along with members of the U.S. Public Health Service.
According to a survey by Remote Area Medical, nearly 40% of patients here said they had not seen a dental provider — other than one provided at a RAM clinic — in at least two years.
And nearly two-thirds said they did not have a usual place for seeking care other than a hospital emergency room.
Dana Bensinger, a nurse specialist working at the medical care clinic, said many patients had high blood pressure or diabetes. They were given prescriptions for a 90-day supply of pills and told to connect with community health centers or free clinics where they can get free or low-cost primary care.
“We have seen a lot of folks who lose insurance or are not able to keep it, and so they can’t get their prescriptions renewed,” he said.
Many patients at the clinic showed up to get a tooth extraction — and with it, relief from dental pain.
“We call it point-and-pull dentistry,” said Tom Ritter, a retired dentist who was triaging dental patients. “You point to the tooth you want out, and we take it out.”
The dilemma, he said, is patients often need multiple teeth extracted and the volunteer dentists have only limited time for each patient. “We have to spread the love around because we have a busy schedule.”
Michel Boudreaux, an associate professor at the University of Maryland Department of Health Policy and Management, said the RAM clinic, about 5 miles from his campus, highlighted the growing difficulty people with and without health insurance face.
“Even in this suburban county there are a lot of uninsured people struggling with affordability and insured people struggling with high deductibles and copays,” he said.
Boudreaux called it “disheartening” that people felt they had to sleep in their cars overnight for care.
Having a government job with benefits was once seen as way of immunizing one’s family from rising health costs.
Cheromie Johnson, who works for the District of Columbia, said that recent dental work left her with a $12,000 bill.

The number of buildings across the contiguous United States threatened by wildfires could almost triple by 2060, according to a new study, if the country continues to ignore the perils of climate change, mismanage its forests and build homes in places where large fires naturally occur.
The paper, published Tuesday in Nature Communications by researchers from the University of Colorado Boulder’s Cooperative Institute for Research in Environmental Sciences, combined different climate models with land-use patterns to estimate wildfire risk to structures across the lower 48 states.
On average, they found that 300,000 buildings could be damaged or destroyed by midcentury.
“It’s a call to action,” said Virginia Iglesias, director of Earth Lab at the University of Colorado Boulder and the paper’s lead author. “Not doing anything is always an option. Here’s what happens.”
On the current trajectory, a disproportionate amount of burned acreage will occur in the West, home to many fire-adapted ecosystems, where total burned area between 2023 and 2060 could exceed 1 billion hectares (over 2.6 billion acres).
Central U.S. grasslands, which evolved alongside fire for thousands of years, could also see a notable uptick in fire activity over the same time frame, burning as many as 111 million hectares (almost 275 million acres).
The East could see a five-fold increase in area burned by 2060, suggesting “a growing misalignment” between where people think it is usually safe to build and the “evolving geography of risk,” the authors wrote.
But larger, faster fires driven by climate change are only part of the story.
“Where we have built is driving a lot of the risk,” Iglesias said. The researchers modeled continued growth in fire-prone areas and found, somewhat surprisingly, high fire risk for “socioeconomically vulnerable” Western communities.
“There’s an association that we tend to make between wildfire and wealthy communities,” Iglesias said, referring to the influx of wealth to parts of the West where human development has increased alongside vegetation that has evolved to burn.
But with fast-moving fires increasingly pushing into urban spaces, she said that socioeconomically vulnerable communities “may not have the resources for mitigation. Insurance may be more precarious and recovery if a fire hits might be much more difficult, if not impossible.”
The paper’s approach—pairing land use with climate models—is necessary to understand how severe future fire risks may be, said Max Moritz, a cooperative extension wildfire specialist at the Bren School at the University of California, Santa Barbara, who was not involved in the study.
“I thought it was a really interesting, novel approach to trying to understand where things are headed,” he said. “We don’t have a lot of good scenarios to get a handle on how big the problem is … I think it’s a real contribution.”
Many of the recent urban conflagrations in the U.S., like the fires that tore through Los Angeles in the winter of 2025 and Boulder, Colorado, in December of 2021, were fueled by unusually powerful winds. Mortiz said climate models have a hard time accounting for this.
“These kinds of models—they don’t do wind,” he said. “Some of the places that are pointed out in papers like this could be even worse than we think.”
Both Iglesias and Mortiz noted that some states are already taking action to mitigate wildfire risks for homeowners. In some areas of California and Colorado, new homes will have to be built to specific fire codes depending on the severity of the fire risk they face. While some other states in the West have some level of protection in place, no region-wide or federal standard exists for homebuilding in the wildland-urban interface—where housing development abuts flammable grasslands and forests—and these regulations do not mitigate risks for older homes built before the standards were implemented.
Given the changes already underway at the state level, the paper’s authors considered a “business-as-usual” scenario as unlikely to persist. But they wanted to understand what would happen if the country did nothing to address the growing threat of wildfire to housing.
“If we decide to just keep doing things the same way, we’ll have a relationship with fire like we’ve been having until now,” Iglesias said.
As climate, land management and development trends continue to evolve, that relationship will put far more homes in harm’s way.
About This Story
Perhaps you noticed: This story, like all the news we publish, is free to read. That’s because Inside Climate News is a 501c3 nonprofit organization. We do not charge a subscription fee, lock our news behind a paywall, or clutter our website with ads. We make our news on climate and the environment freely available to you and anyone who wants it.
That’s not all. We also share our news for free with scores of other media organizations around the country. Many of them can’t afford to do environmental journalism of their own. We’ve built bureaus from coast to coast to report local stories, collaborate with local newsrooms and co-publish articles so that this vital work is shared as widely as possible.
Two of us launched ICN in 2007. Six years later we earned a Pulitzer Prize for National Reporting, and now we run the oldest and largest dedicated climate newsroom in the nation. We tell the story in all its complexity. We hold polluters accountable. We expose environmental injustice. We debunk misinformation. We scrutinize solutions and inspire action.

Republicans can lose up to three seats today and still keep the Senate majority. Any further losses, however, carry immense consequences.
Most in the party are already clocking North Carolina as lost to the Democrats. Losing the Senate would deprive Republicans of control over President Donald Trumpâs nominees â including lifetime judicial appointments.
And provided the House flips Democratic, Republicans could see a procession of impeachment trials for Cabinet members â and perhaps even the president.
âThe two oldest members of the Supreme Court are both Republican [appointees]. We want to make sure that if one of them decides to retire, or both, in the next two years, that President Trump can make an appointment that will get confirmed in the United States Senate,â Senate Majority Whip John Barrasso, R-Wyo., told Semafor on Monday amid a day of campaigning in Iowa.
Republicans can quickly table impeachment trials with a simple majority if they keep Senate control; just two years ago, a Democratic majority dismissed the impeachment of then-Homeland Security Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas. Next year, if Democrats claim the majority in both chambers, the GOP canât expect quick dismissals.
âWeâre going to need to be able to make sure that those are dealt with quickly in the Senate and are not allowed to be dragged out, which is what youâd have with a Democrat majority,â Barrasso added.
The national mood is poor, and Republicans are fighting it out deep in red territory. They are hoping a pair of eleventh-hour dramas in Alaska and Michigian â and their most battle-hardened incumbent â will help bail out their embattled Senate majority.
Republicansâ best pickup opportunity at the start of the cycle has faded away in Georgia. But GOP leaders see Democratic Rep. Haley Stevensâ surprise endorsement of Republican Mike Rogers as fueling their best chance in Michigan since their last Senate win in 1994.
Stevensâ endorsement âbrings more energy and more attention to that race, and itâs going to help in Michigan,â Barrasso said. âThat is going to be a positive influence for the Republicans in the race tomorrow, and in turn I believe is going to generate more turnout and more votes for Mike Rogers.â
The last batch of Michigan polls still show Democrat Abdul El-Sayed ahead of Rogers, though they wonât take into account Stevensâ stunning turn over the weekend. If Republicans somehow flip the Michigan seat, Democrats would have to net five pick-ups elsewhere, which would mean winning a majority of races in eight GOP-held states: North Carolina, Ohio, Texas, Maine, Alaska, Kansas, South Carolina and Iowa.
Alaska has been one of Democratsâ core focuses since the start of the year, and the race still looks close. Republicans are praying that enough Alaskans saw The New York Timesâ story on Democrat Mary Peltolaâs campaign allies working to recruit a spoiler candidate who might siphon votes from GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska.
âThe more people that know about the situation, I think the more itâs going to help Sen. Dan Sullivan. I believe he wins the race,â Barrasso said.
Asked if Peltola would be seated if she wins, Barrasso demurred: âWeâre not there yet. I believe Dan Sullivan is going to win.â He also predicted GOP Sen. Susan Collins would defeat Democrat Troy Jackson in Maine, holding a seat she has occupied since winning it in 1996.
Barrasso has been to Kentucky, Iowa, Michigan, Texas, and Ohio over the past few days. He said that Trumpâs rallies are critical to stoking turnout by the GOP base in a cycle thatâs typically brutal for modern presidents. âNobody can get out a crowd or energize a crowd like President Trump,â Barrasso said.

The News
OpenAIâs attempt to rebrand data centers and set a new tone for AI policy discourse after the midterms is landing with a thud in some circles, including with members of Congress.
The companyâs latest policy push is multi-pronged. It involves calling data centers âcompute campusesâ and seeking community input on their buildouts. It likens AI rules to speeding limits for cars, arguing that AI helps people in their daily lives, and pushing for global AI standards, as Axios first reported.
If initial reactions from AI safety advocates are any indication, AI and tech companies have a long way to go to convince both voters and Democrats, who will likely hold more power in Washington after Tuesday, that their efforts are sincere and not just an attempt at face-saving.
âIf they think they can change the AI debate with Orwellian name changes, they are setting themselves up for failure,â said Brad Carson, former Oklahoma Democratic congressman and co-founder and president of Americans for Responsible Innovation, a group pushing for AI guardrails.
âAI will be the number one issue in 2028,â Rep. Greg Casar, D-Tex., posted on X. âAnd anyone looking to OpenAIâs lobbyist for advice will lose.â
Still, OpenAIâs top lobbyist, Chris Lehane, is betting the companyâs refreshed positions â on data centers and AI policy that puts people in control of the technology â will be âdurable,â even if itâs in a âlonely position,â he told Semafor in an interview.
âPeople are going to wake up in November and December and January, and thereâs going to be hundreds and hundreds of state bills out there. So does Congress and the White House want to cede control of all of this?â he said, adding that OpenAI plans to push for a mandatory AI testing bill that can get 60 votes by connecting members across the aisle.
OpenAI still supports certain state AI laws as well, recently endorsing two frontier AI safety bills in California, he said.
He also said OpenAI spoke with Rep. Ted Lieu, D-Calif. on the AI âkill switchâ bill the Democrat proposed in July, and said he would soon have ânext stepsâ on making OpenAIâs products safer for teen users.
Lehane said OpenAIâs views are meant to offer an alternative to extremes around AI. He argued that embracing a middle path would avoid the US ceding ground to China by being outright opposed to data centers, echoing the White Houseâs argument for a light touch on AI regulation.
His argument isnât doing much to win over skeptics.
â[Lehane is] trying to get the best deal out of the Trump administration that he can before Democrats take over,â Alex Bores, the New York State assemblyman who became a top target of the AI industry in his run for Congress, told Semafor. âBut itâs nice to see him say this debate is about control, and that the American people need a stake in whatâs happening.â
Room for Disagreement
If Democrats want to get anything done on AI policy next year, theyâll need to work with Republicans â regardless of control of Congress. And that will inevitably involve moderation and compromise, as well as working with AI firms.
âIâd expect others to follow [OpenAIâs lead],â Joseph Hoefer, chief AI officer at Monument Advocacy, told Semafor. âThis is where the political calculus is inevitably heading. The industry had a good run making the case for a lighter touch, but the polling shows the limits of that strategy â¦ and a hands-off message gets harder to sustain when voters are asking whoâs in control.â
Hoefer said that for AI companies looking to buoy continued AI sector growth, âthe goal is to give lawmakers a case for AI investment they can defend back home.â

The Environmental Protection Agency late last week announced it would end a 20-plus-year effort to develop methods to monitor air pollution from factory farms, effectively shuttering the agency’s stop-and-start attempts to regulate the potentially pollutant-spewing facilities under the Clean Air Act.
The announcement came just days before the midterm elections and was characterized by the agency as a long-awaited reprieve for farmers, a historically important constituency for Trump and the Republican party.
When tens of thousands of animals are packed into one place, pollution from their waste is blown from ventilation fans or emanates from giant lagoons of liquid effluent. Livestock facilities emit fine particulate matter, ammonia, nitrogen oxides, sulfur dioxide and volatile organic compounds, all contributing to a toxic mix. Research has shown that emissions from these operations are a major cause of air pollution, causing nearly 12,700 deaths in the United States a year.
Strictly speaking, concentrated animal feeding operations, or CAFOs, are required to get permits under the Clean Air Act and report emissions of these pollutants under the Comprehensive Environmental Response, Compensation and Liability and Act and the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act. But through a deal crafted in tandem with the EPA and the livestock industry, they’ve been given amnesty from doing so for more than 20 years.
The arrangement goes back to the early 2000s when the agency attempted to prosecute CAFOs for exceeding limits on some of these pollutants. The industry pushed back, arguing there was no adequate way of measuring them. So the agency worked with industry groups to develop what was dubbed the Air Consent Agreement, through which the EPA granted thousands of CAFOs safe harbor from legal action in exchange for their participation in a study that was funded by the industry.
The goal of the study, the agency said, was to develop tools and models that CAFOs could use to “determine whether they emit pollutants at levels that require them to apply for permits under the CAA or submit notifications under CERCLA or EPCRA” and “produce a scientifically sound basis for measuring and estimating air emissions” from these facilities.
But since the adoption of the agreement in 2005, the agency has failed to produce any air “emissions estimating methodologies,” even prompting a 2017 report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General that faulted it for slow-walking the process.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration and Congress have also gutted reporting requirements for factory farms to report air pollutants under CERCLA, also known as the Superfund Act, and EPCRA.
“As EPA has been saying it’s proceeding with this plan, it’s been dismantling all of its own tools to regulate emissions,” said Tarah Heinzen, the legal director for the advocacy group Food & Water Watch, which has tracked the proceedings from the beginning and filed dozens of lawsuits attempting to push regulators to control pollution from CAFOs. “Now it has announced it has no intention, basically, of ever holding factory farms accountable under the Clean Air Act, either.”
In its Oct. 30 announcement, the agency noted that in the two decades since the study, known as the National Air Emissions Monitoring Study, was conducted, many farms have modernized their barns and manure systems.
“Good science requires good data, and these data are too old and too limited to support methods that farms could rely on,” said Abigale Tardif, the acting assistant administrator for the agency’s Office of Air and Radiation, in a statement. “We would rather tell farmers that plainly than issue numbers we cannot stand behind.”
Rob Brenneman, president of the National Pork Producers Council, which has long pushed for the decision, said in a statement: “This move confirms what farmers have long known: Every farm is different, and there is no one-size-fits-all model to apply to them.”
Heinzen noted that the agency’s decision simply means that this administration has no intention of regulating air emissions from CAFOs, but for now, the Clean Air Act still requires permits for facilities that exceed emissions thresholds. The amnesty granted to these facilities will no longer be in effect now that the agreement has concluded.
“There’s no EPA-issued methodology to estimate emissions,” she said. “That doesn’t mean that there aren’t good studies out there of emissions from different types of animal feeding operations that can be used.”
Heinzen pointed to California, which has models for livestock emissions that it uses to enforce its own air regulations. “We just don’t have one set of national emissions factors from EPA,” Heinzen said. “That does not absolve these factory farms from their obligation to comply with federal law.”
Still, under this administration, it’s clear air emissions from factory farms won’t be measured and monitored any time soon. “No one’s going to estimate anything,” Heinzen noted. “As EPA said in its press release, we’re certainly not about to try to enforce the law.”
The Air Compliance Agreement did not extend to methane. The U.S. livestock industry is the single-biggest source of methane in the country, but Congress effectively blocks livestock facilities from reporting methane emissions in annual spending bills.

With two years of his presidency remaining, Donald Trump, who has dominated American politics over the past decade and transformed it in remarkable ways, is facing potentially pivotal elections.
And the midterm elections on Tuesday that will decide control of Congress come at a difficult moment for his Republican Party.
Voters overwhelmingly say they are most concerned about the cost of living. Food and fuel prices have soared in part due to the president's aggressive tariffs and unpopular war with Iran, so it will be top of mind as many head to the polls.
Trump, who has faced record low approval ratings in recent months, has been campaigning hard, headlining dozens of rallies across the country.
He made his closing pitch on Monday in front of the Reflecting Pool in Washington DC, which has been the subject of a controversial renovation. Looking back at the midterms campaign, he said Republicans "gave this a very strong shot".
But ahead of the vote, high prices are a concern for voters on all sides - which helps explain why he has been campaigning in previously safe Republican territory, appearing in Iowa and Kansas during a final weekend blitz.
His party has also poured hundreds of millions of dollars of campaign advertising into these traditionally safe contests, such as the Senate race in Kansas.
"When they start spending hard American dollars on political advertising in a state that they should be winning, that's how you know that they think they're in trouble," Carrie Dann, the managing editor of the Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, told the BBC.
"The spending [in Kansas] is going to be far more than Republicans ever anticipated," she added. That points to a party that is approaching these elections on the defensive.
At many of his rallies, Trump has also made a plea to voters. "In this election, I'm asking you to pretend, please, that I'm on the ballot," he said last month. "Just pretend."
Of course, he is not on the ballot. But this plea - which he made again in Iowa on Sunday - gets to the heart of a critical question: Is he still an electoral asset for his Republican Party?
The answer to that is not as simple as it once was.
Trump returned to the White House as a formidable force following his crushing 2024 election win - and had the healthy approval ratings to match. Before that, during the previous midterm elections in 2022, his endorsement was courted by Republicans who saw it as vital to success.
Now, with the war with Iran dragging on and hitting many Americans in the pocket, his approval ratings have sunk. The price of a gallon of diesel - which was $3.75 before the war started in February - hit a record high of $6.52 in September.
"I literally just had my son drive across the country, and he called me in every state and told me the price of gas," one voter in Iowa told me. "And I was like - 'oh my gosh, this is horrible'."
Inflation has also ticked up from 3% when Trump took office to 3.7% today, and economists estimate it would have been lower without his sweeping regime of global tariffs.
There is concern among Republicans that this economic picture has left them vulnerable in typically safe races, in states such as Texas, Ohio and Kansas.
"The southern states, the midwestern states, the American heartland - that is where Republicans tend to thrive," said Stephen Hawkins, the global director of research at the pollster More in Common.
"But that is where the Senate races that are so interesting are playing out right now."
"Places where President Trump won by 10, 12, 15 points just two years ago in the presidential race are now states where Democrats have a very viable chance of taking a Senate seat," he said.
When I asked voters in Iowa, a state Trump won in 2024 that has been hit by soaring fuel and fertiliser costs, whether the president would make people more or less likely to back Republicans - the answer was revealing.
"With the current climate, I would think possibly less, believe it or not," Paul Ross told me outside a busy college football game. "As a Republican myself, I would think it might be detrimental."
"I think it definitely puts voters off, there's no doubt about that, and I do think it probably raises the Democratic side to a level that isn't always there, just because it's Donald Trump," added Zach Shimp.
"He's got us in the war," another voter, Rose Heming, said. "Prices and groceries [are] high - sky high - gas is sky high."
That is the story of this election. Many voters, including in solidly Republican states, are hurting financially and polls suggest they may want to make this known at the ballot box on Tuesday.
But it is too simplistic to think this backdrop of war, tariffs and soaring prices will usher in a thumping Democratic victory in the House, Senate and governors' races.
Many Republican voters are angry with the president, but not so angry that they would vote for a Democrat. It is a mistake to assume that Trump's weak approval ratings translate to increasing popularity for the other side.
In fact, final polls taken before the elections suggest Trump's approval rating is around 38%. That is low - but the same polls, including a national NBC poll released on Sunday, external, indicate that only 29% of voters view the Democratic Party positively.
Voter frustration is no guarantee of a willingness to switch sides on Tuesday.
"We like to stay out of people's business," Tim McKinnon, a Republican in Iowa who voted for Trump in 2024 told me last month. "And so [Trump's] world stage interventions time after time after time - we don't love it.
"We didn't expect him to necessarily be a perfect choir boy obviously," his wife, Michelle, added. "We voted for the underbelly of what he was standing for."
The Democratic Party cannot rely on voters like the McKinnons, who are frustrated with elements of Trump's recent agenda, to back them. They do not think Democrats will ever reflect their Christian, conservative

Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel has died after the 30-year-old suffered a serious injury during a Spanish second-division match.
The forward suffered head and chest injuries during a match against FC Andorra on Monday in a heavy collision with goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who was sent off for his challenge.
De Miguel's condition was described as 'stable but serious' on Monday but his health deteriorated on Tuesday morning, with the Spaniard dying at 07:00 GMT.
Reuters reported on Tuesday that police in Spain have opened an investigation for possible involuntary manslaughter following De Miguel's death.
Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry.
"Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true" Tenerife said.
"There are no words of comfort; there is absolutely nothing that can lessen this overwhelming sadness. We stand with his grieving family, with his loved ones, with all of Tenerife who mourn this cruel loss today."
'There are no words'
Tenerife and Andorra were drawing 2-2 seven minutes into stoppage time when the incident occurred.
Owono ran towards the centre circle to clear a long ball when his knee appeared to collide with De Miguel.
The striker lay motionless on the pitch as medical staff treated him before he was taken by ambulance from Tenerife's Estadio Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez to hospital.
Players from both teams were visibly distressed by the incident, with a number of De Miguel's team-mates in tears.
The referee showed Owono a straight red card before abandoning the match.
The goalkeeper, who had over 30,000 followers on Instagram on Tuesday morning, has since deactivated his account.
Spanish media, including Marca, reported De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest in the ambulance and was resuscitated by paramedics on the way to hospital.
Andorra, Tenerife's opponents on Monday, said: "With broken hearts and devastated, we want to send our most sincere condolences to the family of Jesus de Miguel, to all his team-mates, friends, and to CD Tenerife."
Former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, who co-owns Andorra, said: "I am sorry with all my soul. Rest in peace, Jesus."
De Miguel's former club, Castellon, said: "It's hard to find words when reality strikes in such an unfair way.
"We join with all our affection in the grief of his family and loved ones, whom we embrace in these terribly difficult moments and to whom we extend our most heartfelt condolences."
Javier Tebas, president of La Liga, said: "Today, we all share the terrible pain of an irreparable loss.
"My deepest condolences to his family, loved ones, team-mates and the whole club."
Real Madrid and France striker Kylian Mbappe wrote on his social media: "Much sadness, there are no words."
Inter Miami and former Barcelona forward Lionel Messi said: "There are no words. My condolences and lots of strength to all his family and friends."
The Spanish football federation announced following De Miguel's death that Tuesday's Spanish Cup fixtures had been postponed.
Two fixtures in the first round of the men's Copa del Rey were due to be played, while Espanyol were set to take on AS Celtas in the women's Copa del Reina competition.
A lower-league player with an eye for goal
De Miguel, who was born in Madrid, started his career at Leganes in 2015 and went on to play for eight different clubs in Spain.
After spells with Lugo Fuenlabrada and Internacional Madrid, he returned to Fuenlabrada before stints at Union Adarve, Navalcarnero and Unionistas.
He joined Castellon in 2023 and scored 16 goals as the club achieved promotion to Spain's second division a year later.
The Spaniard joined Tenerife on a three-year deal in 2025 and scored 11 goals in 29 appearances for the side.
De Miguel is survived by his daughter, Carla de Miguel Fernandez, who was born in 2025.

A spending watchdog has strongly criticised the lack of progress made by public sector organisations in tackling climate change.
Audit Wales says since a Welsh government "climate emergency" was declared, external in 2019, "decarbonisation" has become a lower priority for public bodies.
It says there are many examples of positive changes but the "collective ambition" for a net zero public sector in Wales by 2030 is unlikely to be met.
It has been estimated that it would cost at least Â£2.3bn to decarbonise Welsh council buildings alone.
The Welsh government said its 2030 ambition had "driven action and leadership, but it's clear that there is more work to do".
Net zero means balancing the amount of planet-warming "greenhouse" gases produced by human activities with the amount being actively removed from the atmosphere.
Effectively this means no longer adding to the total amount of these gases in the atmosphere to limit climate change.
In its new report, the spending watchdog said public bodies in all sectors recognise decarbonisation is important.
But it said: "Since 2022, financial and political pressures have caused decarbonisation to fall down the priority list.
"Public bodies told us their overall financial pressures mean they are struggling to invest in decarbonisation."
It criticised the Welsh government for not defining the "collective ambition" for net zero by 2030 as a "target".
"There are also no penalties or incentives to drive compliance. Some public bodies told us this had added to uncertainty around the level of priority to attach to carbon reduction."
On spending, it added that public bodies had made "limited progress" overall in understanding how much it will cost to decarbonise in the near or longer term.
"Where public bodies have estimated the longer-term cost, some described it as unaffordable."
Ann-Marie Harkin from Audit Wales said: "We can list positive examples, but not enough progress has been made overall, and we owe it to future generations to do better."
In 2017, the then-Labour Welsh government called for a net zero public sector by 2030, saying that public bodies were "uniquely placed" to influence emissions in areas such as buildings and transport.
The thinking was that if government-backed bodies made the switch and invested in infrastructure like electric vehicles and charge points, renewable power and heating systems, it would make it easier and cheaper for the public to follow suit.
The "collective ambition" does not require every public body to reach net zero individually by 2030 but it is meant to provide a shared direction of travel and an expectation that all public bodies contribute towards reducing emissions.
Responding to the report, a spokesperson for the Welsh government said: "A net zero public sector is a priority for Welsh government.
"We want to continue to support the decarbonisation of the public sector to lower emissions, energy bills and strengthen energy security.
"The 2030 ambition has driven action and leadership, but it's clear that there is more work to do on decarbonisation across and beyond the public sector in Wales."
The current Plaid Cymru government's ambition is for Wales, as a whole, to reach net zero by 2040 - which is ten years sooner than the current legally binding target for Wales and UK.

Spain's Transport Minister Ãscar Puente has resigned - six days after the high-speed train collision in which at least 69 people were killed and dozens injured.
He announced his decision in Congress, where he had appeared to give the circumstances of last Wednesday's crash near the town of Urda, south of the capital Madrid.
"A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year," he said, also referring to a deadly crash in January in Andalusia, southern Spain
The latest tragedy in Urda happened when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company.
Puente announced his decision at the end of a congressional session on Tuesday evening in which he had outlined new rail safety measures and been grilled by the opposition.
He said he had taken the decision immediately after the 28 October disaster.
Puente had been under mounting pressure as opposition parties and some allies of the government called on him to step down.
Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media soon after the crash revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the disaster.
Three tapes between Madrid's control centre and two train drivers appear to show that one high-speed train was given clearance to move even though another train had stopped on the track, about 25km (15 miles) ahead.
Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez has said that authorities will "get to the bottom of every last detail of this tragedy".

1201cf121c45.text: By — Josh Kelety, Associated Press Josh Kelety, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/escaped-tennessee-inmate-convicted-of-co-workers-murder-is-recaptured-in-missouri-officials-say Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Escaped Tennessee inmate convicted of co-worker's murder is recaptured in Missouri, officials say Nation Nov 3, 2026 3:54 PM EST A man convicted of murder who escaped from a Tennessee prison was recaptured on Tuesday in Missouri after troopers used roadside cameras and a helicopter to track him down after more than a week on the run, authorities said. READ MORE: Florida executed a prisoner who killed his cellmate in hopes of getting a death sentence. It's the state's 17th execution of the year Jacob Morley, who was serving a life sentence for killing a co-worker four years ago, was apprehended at around noon near Kansas City, Missouri, officials said. The Missouri State Highway Patrol says it learned Tuesday morning that Morley was possibly traveling west on Interstate 70. The vehicle was located using automated license plate readers and undercover officers traveling on a state highway in western Missouri. A Kansas City police helicopter also followed the vehicle, which made it into Carroll County, a small county in northwest Missouri, before it traveled off the road, getting stuck. Troopers took Morley into custody without incident ending a weeklong hunt. Morley, 28, escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tennessee's far northwestern corner on Oct. 25, after he slipped through a fence in his prison clothes. Surveillance video showed him stealing a truck from a farm near the prison, which he abandoned last week in Marion, Illinois. That is about 120 miles (193 kilometers) north of the prison. Morley was serving a life sentence for killing co-worker Cody Birchfield in 2022. Birchfield's body was found in a box under Morley's home after he had been missing for a few weeks. The two lived in Carter County, in eastern Tennessee. When Morley saw deputies at his home, he led officers on a chase that ended in North Carolina, authorities said. Morley was convicted of first-degree murder, aggravated burglary, tampering with evidence, vandalism and evading arrest. After his escape, law enforcement agencies searched buildings and other structures near the prison, which is in Tiptonville, about 90 miles (145 kilometers) north of Memphis in flat farmland near a bend in the Mississippi River. Prison officials offered a reward of up to $17,500 for information leading to Morley's arrest. Morley's escape is the latest blemish for Tennessee's prison system. Several violent attacks between inmates and by employees have been reported in recent years at Northwest Correctional Complex. A grand jury in July returned dozens of indictments for five inmate killings and other violent acts. Following the failed execution of Christa Pike in September, Department of Correction Commissioner Frank Strada resigned after less than three years on the job.
