Here's what that means Politics Nov 3, 2026 7:14 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check WASHINGTON (AP) — The Justice Department has escalated its investigation over an Alaska Senate candidate who shares a name with the Republican incumbent, sending letters advising a prominent Democratic attorney and others that they are considered targets of the criminal inquiry. The letter to attorney Marc Elias, who for years has represented Democratic presidential campaigns and the party itself in election-related challenges — and has himself been a target of President Donald Trump — is among numerous ones that have been issued, said the people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss an ongoing investigation. Target letters are sometimes issued to people the department intends to indict, but they do not necessarily mean someone will be charged. They come as the department has ramped up an investigation into a race headlined by two-term Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democratic former U.S. Rep. Mary Peltola. Also on the ballot is retired teacher Dan J. Sullivan, whose presence the Trump administration is investigating as a potential effort to spark voter confusion and steal votes from the incumbent Republican. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News A look at the latest developments: Criminal investigation has intensified in recent days The criminal investigation has been quietly unfolding for months but gained new steam after the New York Times reported last week that Peltola's campaign appeared to be involved in recruiting Dan J. Sullivan. The Justice Department has issued more than 100 subpoenas and has also sent letters ordering people to preserve records as part of the investigation, according to one of the people briefed on the probe. The FBI over the weekend has also paid home visits to donors of Dan J. Sullivan. READ MORE: FBI visits Dan J. Sullivan donor in candidate's hometown as Alaska Senate inquiry widens Alaska U.S. Attorney Michael Heyman told reporters in Anchorage on Friday that the new revelations led to a "significant surge of law enforcement assets to Alaska." He declined to say what specific crimes authorities were investigating. "I'm not making any assumptions on whether a crime has been committed or not," Heyman said last week. "That's why we are conducting that thorough investigation." Peltola has said she didn't know anything about the effort to put Dan J. Sullivan on the ballot. "I am not interested in tricking voters," Peltola said last week. Democrats, including the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, have also repeatedly denied that they were involved in any campaign trick. Dan J. Sullivan has long denied he was running at Democrats' behest. Recruiting spoiler candidates to siphon votes from the other major party is a practice that has been used by Republicans and Democrats alike for decades without drawing criminal scrutiny. But Trump's Justice Department says it takes the matter seriously. "Everybody agrees that there is a man running that doesn't want to run, that doesn't expect to be senator, that is only running to confuse Alaskan voters," Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Fox News. "And so that's why the Department of Justice has been fighting tooth and nail to stop this process." Blanche declined to discuss the target letters, saying he was not going to " confirm anything that has to do with an ongoing investigation." Please check your inbox to confirm. Elias is a fixture of Democratic politics — and longtime Trump target Elias has for years been a target of Trump's ire due in part to his role as general counsel for the 2016 presidential campaign of Trump's Democratic opponent, Hillary Clinton. During that campaign, he and his then-law firm paid for political research into Trump that ultimately led to the creation of a dossier of allegations on the Republican candidate's connections to Russia that contained salacious gossip, unverified rumors and discredited information. Trump has long been furious about the research, known casually as the "Steele dossier," and last year announced that he would sanction the Perkins Coie firm by revoking security clearances of attorneys at the firm. The punishment was blocked after a court challenge. Elias, who did not return messages seeking comment Tuesday, alluded to that history in a statement that said: "No one should be surprised that President Trump's Department of Justice is targeting me and my law firm on Election Day. This administration has repeatedly weaponized the DOJ against the President's political enemies despite zero evidence of wrongdoing, and we are the latest targets." What is the significance of a target letter? A target letter is a letter that the Justice Department sometimes sends to individuals whom it sees as at legitimate risk of indictment. The department defines a "target" as a person against whom it has gathered substantial evidence linking them to a possible crime and regards as a potential defendant. The Justice Department does not typically require targets of its investigations to testify before a grand jury in part because of constitutional protections against self-incrimination. - Published
South Africans are voting in highly contested local elections likely to see a haemorrhaging of votes for the country's former ruling party, the African National Congress (ANC).
This year's voting season has been marked by intense campaigns that have included politicians spinning cars, watching grannies knit and even wading through giant-sized potholes.
Leaders are campaigning to head South Africa's nearly 300 municipalities, responsible for basic service provision such as water, electricity and refuse collection.
For the ANC, the elections are a chance to prove it still has what it takes to govern. The party had a disastrous showing in the last national election, when it lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since 1994 when the racist apartheid system ended.
Support for the party has been dropping significantly over the years because of anger over high levels of corruption, unemployment and crime.
At its peak, in 2004, the ANC got 70% of the vote in the general election. Two decades later its share dropped to 40%.
Polls and pundits have predicted a further loss in these elections but President Cyril Ramaphosa has denied that his party was in a downward spiral.
"What I'm seeing here is that the ANC is going higher and higher and on the 4th [of November] we will show those naysayers," he told supporters at the party's final election rally on Sunday.
In townships like Alexandra, north-east of Johannesburg, the ANC has traditionally had a strong supporter base but poor governance and voter apathy are unravelling this support.
The BBC visited the sprawling township a week before the elections and spoke to residents to get their views. One of them was Sanele Ntombela, who is a first-time voter excited to make his voice heard.
We found the 18-year-old hanging out with his friends on a street corner. Most of his friends said they had no intention of voting and had not registered to do so.
They cited a lack of change and deteriorating delivery of basic services.
But Ntombela was looking forward to voting for the first time and thought it might lead to change.
"We face many challenges in Alexandra. There's rubbish everywhere and we struggle with electricity and water and many other issues," he said.
Just metres away, heaps of rubbish lay gathered beneath a streetlight pole covered in election posters from the different political parties.
On the other side of the street, drain water trickles through the many potholes that have gutted that part of the road.
The BBC also spoke to Zandile Mncube, who said she wouldn't vote, even though she is registered to do so.
The 33-year-old woman also cited poor service delivery and performance by local leaders for her decision.
"It makes no difference [whether I vote or not]. Things have gotten worse over the years," she said.
Alex, as the township is known, is a stone's throw away from Sandton, Africa's richest square mile, but the differences could not be starker.
Sandton is known for its skyscrapers, designer shops and well-maintained roads but in Alex, houses are sandwiched together and rubbish, either piled together or left strewn across the pavement, is everywhere. The stench of raw sewage and uncollected rubbish is heavy in the air, but residents appear used to it.
The issues plaguing Alexandra are not unique. A drive around Gauteng province reveals similar patterns of neglect and disrepair, especially in the townships.
South of Johannesburg, Soweto looks marginally cleaner than Alexandra, but residents also complain about service delivery.
Mduduzi Makhubo, 45, has lived in Soweto his entire life and he told the BBC of the community's daily struggles with accessing water and electricity.
"Every Monday we know we won't have water after 2pm," he said.
Makhubo is registered to vote and intends to use his vote to deal with the "arrogance" he says local leaders have towards residents and "change the status quo".
These areas offer a small, but important, glimpse into the state of South Africa's local governance.
Years of reports by the auditor-general have highlighted the dire state of most of South Africa's 257 municipalities.
A recent report only gave 39 clean audits - the highest ranking a public entity can achieve - between 2024 and 2025. None of Gauteng's three metro cities, Johannesburg, Tshwane and Ekurhuleni, featured in this list.
Earlier this year auditor-general Tsakani Maluleke said Johannesburg "needs ongoing attention".
"If we don't that, we are going to continue on this slide where financial health deteriorates [and] where service delivery continues to be compromised, which is what we are living," she told lawmakers.
The city has been labelled "effectively bankrupt" due to the dire state of its finances. Dirty streets, unstable electricity supply and persistent water issues have been common for years.
Experts the BBC spoke to agreed that all eyes will be on Africa's wealthiest city as well as the country's seven other biggest municipalities, or metros, particularly those in Gauteng when the results come in.
The expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done
Of South Africa's eight metros, only three are governed by a single party. In Gauteng, all three metros are governed by coalition governments, with the ANC the largest party.
But that might change.
Political analyst Melanie Verwoerd said the elections would be a "verdict ... and judgment" on the ANC.
"And the expectation is that the ANC generally in the country is going to [perform] the worst it's ever done," she said.
Several polls point to a continued decline in support for the party in Wednesday's election, contested by over 500 political parties.
One, conducted by Ipsos, put the ANC's support at 30%, down from the 46% it got at the last local elections in 2021.

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.
But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.
“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.
The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.
But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.
The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.
Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.
Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.
These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.
Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”
The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.
But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.
“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

54d5802999c0.text: Top party strategists may hate seeing one of their candidates gutted by a brutal ad. But they can still admire the hit. Why it matters: A record $11.6 billion has plastered political ads across screens of every size in the country during the 2026 midterms . Only a handful of those earned the grudging respect of operatives on both sides. 📺 Zoom in: Multiple Republican strategists singled out the "brutal" series of ads attacking Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kans.) over lawsuits against patients with overdue medical bills — some of whom were later arrested . Against the advice of his own team, Marshall released a self-directed ad answering the attacks. In Nebraska , an ad highlighting a past vote by former Gov. Pete Ricketts to pardon a man convicted of rape was singled out by both parties as one of the cycle's most damaging. Ricketts is expected to win re-election to the Senate. In Maine, an upbeat jingle hit Democratic nominee Troy Jackson for having children with his second cousin. "If he'll f**k his own family, he'll f**k yours too," the radio ad said (among other things). Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) called for the ad to be taken down. And in Florida , Rep. María Salazar (R-Fla.) turned on her own party leader, criticizing President Trump over ICE's aggressive enforcement tactics, saying some immigration policies had "gone too far." The intrigue : Even hardened operatives are dealing with a new frontier: AI-generated attack ads that can make up scenarios and put words in an opponent's mouth. In Michigan , a Republican-aligned super PAC used AI-generated imagery to depict Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed in a fabricated family photo and playing a game with cards referencing "Death to America" and 9/11. In Texas, GOP Senate nominee Ken Paxton's team used AI to depict Democratic candidate James Talarico defacing a Bible with a crayon and saying: "In the beginning God was non-binary, and he wasn't a Christian. And God said, 'let there be six genders,' and there were." 🤺 Between the lines: An attack ad helped spark this weekend's blowup in the Michigan Senate race. Rep. Haley Stevens' (D-Mich.) shocking decision to withdraw support from El-Sayed grew out of their public dispute over an ad she called antisemitic. El-Sayed ultimately disavowed the ad but said Stevens wasn't welcome at his events, and she endorsed former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) on Sunday. The other side: It's hard to imagine a bigger backfire than Vivek Ramaswamy's (R) ad featuring the estranged mother of his opponent for Ohio governor, Amy Acton (D). It could prove fatal for his gubernatorial bid, and Republicans worry it could hurt Sen. John Husted's (R) re-election chances too. The ad sparked immediate bipartisan backlash. Ramaswamy doubled down before pulling it off-air. One internal GOP poll had Acton's lead grow by 6 points after the ad ran.

'I'm not a quitter': Kim Kardashian on retaking the bar exam
Kim Kardashian has said she will retake the California bar exam with the aim of becoming a lawyer in real life, after playing one in the legal drama All's Fair.
The reality TV star and actress discovered she had failed the exam after the first series of the Hulu programme aired last year. She had previously studied law for six years.
"I'll take it again and let you guys know once I've passed. I'll be very vocal about that," Kardashian told the BBC's Annabel Rackham, adding: "I'm going to be a little more quiet about my journey until I get there."
She was speaking alongside co-star Naomi Watts ahead of the second series of All's Fair, which was roundly panned by critics despite breaking streaming records.

b298af581a6a.text: Tuesday on the News Hour, voters across the country head to the polls to decide control of the House and Senate in a midterm election widely seen as a referendum on President Trump and his administration. A look at the DOJ's efforts to change voter rolls and even block some results. Plus, as more Americans vote early, a new survey aims to better capture how and why they cast their ballots. Geoff Bennett: Millions of Americans from Anchorage to Atlanta are voting on this Election Day. Polls in some states are just now starting to close, but much of the country still has hours to go. And we will be here tracking it all. Amna Nawaz: The midterm elections will determine whether control of the House and the Senate will shift to Democrats. And many see the outcome as a nationwide verdict on President Trump. Our White House correspondent, Liz Landers, begins our coverage. Liz Landers: Across America this morning, early risers lined up before sunup... Woman: Polls are open. Come on in. Liz Landers: ... to make their voices heard with the cast of a ballot on this final day of voting. Kalyn Reeves, Georgia Voter: I'm here before work to do my civil duty. And I think it's important because this midterm election is a turning point. Liz Landers: In battleground states coast to coast from Maine to Alaska, contentious campaigns coming to a close as control of Congress hangs in the balance. Man: It's about a 50/50, I think. Liz Landers: All eyes were on Michigan after a weekend that turned the Senate race on its head. Republican Mike Rogers today lauded the surprise endorsement from Democratic Representative Haley Stevens and her criticisms of his opponent, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed. Mike Rogers (R): Here's somebody who said, I voted Democrat all the way down the list, except for one person who I think is too extreme for our state. That's country over party. Liz Landers: Some voters were swayed by the move. Paul Stocky, Michigan Voter: She elected to support the opposition, which is very rare. It never happens. So I got to believe that there's something there. Abdul El-Sayed (D): In the end, this is about what Michigan wants in its politics. I'm not running to be the first anything. I'm running to be the next senator for Michigan. Liz Landers: El-Sayed supporters say their vote was based on issues like affordability. Walletta Kemp, Michigan Voter: My little car that used to take $30 is now almost taking $50. It's ridiculous. Families shouldn't have to go through this. Liz Landers: President Trump mostly laid low this Election Day, but was optimistic on a call with "FOX & Friends." President Donald Trump: The inflation is solved. Liz Landers: The president dismissed voter anxieties about rising prices brought on by the war in Iran. President Donald Trump: I think the results are going to be better than you think. Liz Landers: A polarizing president playing an outsized role in voters' decisions tonight even without his name on the ticket. Patricia Witt, North Carolina Voter: I think President Trump is doing what needs to be done. Neil Jones, Maine Voter: The Republican Party has become the Trump party and I just don't feel comfortable for anyone associated with Trump. Liz Landers: The administration also taking unprecedented steps in combating what President Trump has falsely long decried as widespread voter fraud. For the first time, the Justice Department deployed election monitors in all 50 states to pursue -- quote -- "transparency for elections in an assertive and nondiscriminatory manner." In New York today, some voting machines were plagued with technical issues, impacting a key congressional race between Representative Mike Lawler and his Democratic challenger, Cait Conley. Officials assured that emergency paper ballots will be counted, though it's unclear when. The economy and the state of democracy have been named as the top issues for US voters, according to an election day poll.
The survey - officially called the Voter Poll - asks tens of thousands of the American electorate their opinions and motivations, and providing a breakdown by age, gender, education and other demographics.
Polling company SSRS collects data on behalf of a consortium of news companies, and the survey is a representative sample of American voters in the run up to the election, and includes exit polling of both early and on the day voters.
Here are some of the breakdowns from the 2026 voter poll. Like all surveys they are estimates; the numbers are also likely to be updated as more data arrives.
Economy ranked as top issue
Some 39% of those asked in the poll of more than 79,000 people said the economy was the most important issue, while 32% put the state of democracy top.
Following that, immigration was named most important by 14% of voters while healthcare, foreign policy and crime were ranked first by a lower share.
Data suggests the majority of US voters have a negative view of the state of the national economy.
Some 75% of those asked said the economy was in a "not so good or poor" state with 25% saying it was "excellent or good".
Looking at their own family finances, 44% of people said they were in a worse situation than two years ago, 38% said about the same and 18% said better.
Majority say Trump's policies 'worsened economy'
Almost two thirds (65%) of voters surveyed say US President Donald Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions in the US.
By contrast, 28% say Trump's policies have improved conditions and only 8% say the president has had no impact.
People were also asked whether expressing support or opposition for Trump was one reason for their midterm vote.
Some 43% said expressing opposition was a reason but a similar proportion (41%) said he was not a factor. Only 16% of those asked said expressing support was a reason for their vote.
Nearly 40% unhappy with state of the US
Almost four in ten of those asked (38%) said they were angry at the way things are going in the US at the moment, with a further 37% saying they were dissatisfied.
Only 18% said they were satisfied, and 7% of respondents felt enthusiastic.
So taken together, there is a majority telling pollsters SSRS they are not happy about the current state of the country.
Inflation has caused hardship for most Americans
As well as broader issues, pollsters also asked about inflation and the impact of rising prices on people's lives.
Almost eight in 10 voters (79%) said inflation had caused them and their family a severe or moderate hardship in the past year. A fifth (21%) of those answering said it had caused them no hardship at all.
A majority of voters (59%) said they were "very concerned" about the cost of petrol and diesel and a similar proportion (58%) gave this answer about the cost of food and groceries.
More than six in 10 respondents (62%) said they thought that higher than usual prices were more because of Trump's policies.
And 38% said it was more due to factors beyond his control.

Geoff Bennett:
Let's turn now to our expert panel for analysis.

Amna Nawaz:
Also with us is Mo Elleithee. He's a Democratic strategist. He's former spokesman for the Democratic National Committee. Doug Heye is here. He's a Republican strategist and the former spokesman for the Republican National Committee. And Tiffany Smileyis back with us. Welcome to you all. We're in for a long night. Thank you for being here.
Amy, kick us off here. I know we have some early results coming in from the voter poll, which is sort of a collaboration between the Associated Press, who we are relying on for results, and broadcast networks. It tells us about who voted and why so far.
Amy Walter:
Right.
Amna Nawaz:
What are we hearing from voters so far about what's driving them to the polls?
Amy Walter:
Not surprisingly, the economy is driving everything; 39 percent of voters saying this was their top issue that they were voting on.
We have known now throughout the last two years that voters have been telling us over and over again that the economy, especially inflation, is something that continues to frustrate them. And I think that's something else that we have seen in this poll as well, that the issue of the cost of stuff, especially the cost, the high cost of gasoline, big factor for so many of these voters.
Geoff Bennett:
And, Tiffany Smiley, there's, of course, the Trump fact you hear. According to the same data, 43 percent of voters say they cast their ballots to express opposition to President Trump, compared to just 16 percent who voted to express support.
How much of a challenge is that going to be for Republicans tonight? And what does it tell you about the president's political standing?
Tiffany Smiley:
Yes, well, I think he's shown that he is willing to work hard and get out there, go to red states and really drive out his voters. He knows, when he's at the top of the ticket, his voters turn out and vote.
And so that's what he's he's been working so hard at doing. I think there's a couple factors going on. I think the Democrat Party has really lacked leadership. And so instead of voting for someone, they're just voting against Donald Trump. We have seen this played out over and over again.
So I think maybe the question is, are Trump's voters going to be as enthusiastic as they were in 2024? And are they going to come out and give the Republicans another shot at continuing to get the economy, like you mentioned, Amy, back on track? Do they really believe that the Republicans hold the answer?
Because right now the Democrats really aren't even giving them a solution to a better future. So I think that's sort of what we will see tonight played out.
Amna Nawaz:
Well, so Doug and Mo, weigh in on this and what we have heard from Amy and Tiffany so far.

Voters are now saying Democrats are better able to handle the following issues, the economy, foreign policy, health care, and government corruption. The only issue they said Republicans could handle better right now is immigration.
This is a big change for Democrats.
Mo Elleithee:
Yes, I can't remember in my career a time when Democrats led on the economy and foreign policy. Like, that's -- that portends a good night for us.
Look, at the end of the day, it's a midterm election. The president in power is typically the question on the ballot, right? That's typically what voters are responding to. And, man, are they -- does it seem like they're responding this year.
In race after race in states that should not even be on the map, Democrats are in play. So, I think -- look, I'm not one to measure drapes prematurely, except maybe in the speaker's office. That feels pretty cooked. But -- and this could be a very long night, particularly when it comes to the Senate.

They have got the opportunity tonight to get unified control of at least seven new state legislatures and break up unified Republican control of another six.
If that happens, if this wave plays out that way, that has a chance to fundamentally change the way we govern ourselves, at least for the next couple of years.
Amna Nawaz:
Doug.
Doug Heye:
Yes, look, I go back to 2010 when, I was at the RNC. Our magic number for Obama was 46 percent. We thought if he was at or below that, we'd take back the House.
There's not been a number that's shown Donald Trump that starts with a four in a long time. And it's why you have seen some candidates, certainly Ashley Hinson and Mike Rogers being two, trying to create separation.
It's a really hard thing to do, because when Amy Walter was hounding me in 2006, a tough year for Republicans, about, well, all the Democrats are doing is tying your candidate to George W. Bush, there was nothing we could do. And it's been that same dynamic for Democrats, they certainly feel the wind at their back on because of this.
And it's why the closing message and events from Trump have been to me so, at best, questionable. A closing speech, your closing message of your campaign talking about a Reflecting Pool and the real details and the piping of the Reflecting Pool?

722db43ca2ea.text: In recent months, the Trump administration and the Department of Justice have led an extraordinary effort to exert federal control over state-run elections. Nearly all of those efforts, so far, have been blocked or rejected by the courts. To discuss election security and the prospect of potential election interference, Geoff Bennett spoke with Rick Hasen and Juliette Kayyem. Amna Nawaz: This election cycle has been compared to the midterms of 2006, when Democrats won back control of Congress and, in an historic first, elected Nancy Pelosi to be the first female speaker of the House. That was 20 years ago. Today, Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi is in the final months of her political career. And like she's done every election night since 2016, Speaker Pelosi joins us now. Madam Speaker, welcome back. Thank you for continuing this tradition with us. I want to begin, of course, with your predictions. How big a majority do you think Democrats can win in the House tonight? And will you win control of the Senate? Rep. Nancy Pelosi(D-CA): Well, thank you, Amna, for the opportunity to share some thoughts with you once again on election night. One thing I will say, following up on your previous guests, be not afraid to voters. Just go out and vote. Hakeem Jeffries has worked very hard to do three things, one, to win the election, two, to protect the election, and, three, to show the people what will happen once we do. So, your vote is protected, go vote. Whether it's litigation, whether it's legislation, whether it's communication or mobilization, we're ready. We're ready for anything they might come up with. Amna Nawaz: Always good to underscore that. You're absolutely right. What will you think will happen tonight now? Rep. Nancy Pelosi: I think, tonight, we will have a big victory. It will be many seats in the House of Representatives. I put -- I want 30. But the fact is, they will be very slim victories. So I don't want anybody to think, oh, well, you have won, so let's move on to other things. No, we -- every race will be close, but there will be many of them. You mentioned 2006. And, in 2006, he who shall be nameless was at 44 percent favorable. Now it's -- 45 percent favorable. Now it's 38, a seven-points difference. And, in 18, we won 40 seats, 31 of them in Trump districts. So now he's down to 38. We expect to have a big Democratic victory in the House and hopefully also in the Senate. In my own district, I'm supporting Connie Chan. And, for me, what is interesting is, when I went to Congress, there were 12 women, Democratic women out of 435 people, 12 Democratic women. So my passion over the years has been to increase that number. And I'm so happy to still be in Congress for the election, but we will go over 100, and hopefully Connie Chan will take us there as well. So, we're prepared for victory. Amna Nawaz: We have certainly seen some big changes on that front. You're absolutely right. I do want to ask you about some specific races, though, because Democrats have been sort of reeling from some late-breaking stories in Michigan, in particular, in the Senate race. I'm sure you were tracking Haley Stevens on Sunday stepping in after she lost the Democratic primary to actually endorse the Republican candidate there, Mike Rogers. He's running against Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee. What do you think -- or how do you think, rather, that impacts the race? Will that hurt El-Sayed? Rep. Nancy Pelosi: By all reports that I have from Michigan -- and we have races there too in the House -- of course, we're concerned about the Senate and the governor's race -- it's going to be a landslide in Michigan. We will win that Senate seat in Michigan. Unfortunately, and with all the respect in the world that I have for my former colleague Haley Stevens, this distraction from what we should be talking about is, what are the Democrats going to do when they win, rather than why did Haley Stevens change her support in that race? So let's not be distracted by that. That was then. This is now, today. The Democrats will win big in Michigan, and it will not -- it will not affect whether we win the House -- excuse me -- the Senate and the House, as a matter of fact, as well. Amna Nawaz: So, to that point... Rep. Nancy Pelosi: It's a pretty exciting night. It's going to be a big victory for us. Amna Nawaz: To that point, as you mentioned, what Democrats should prioritize if they do win control of both chambers -- rather, in the House especially, I know you have supported Hakeem Jeffries to be the eventual speaker if the Democrats do win the majority there. I'm sure you have seen a number of sort of anti-establishment candidates, though, reserve their judgment and say they're not ready to support him to be speaker. They say they're frustrated with the status quo. They say Democrats and leaders aren't fighting hard enough. Are there concerns valid, in your view? Rep. Nancy Pelosi: Hakeem Jeffries will be a very strong speaker of the House, and he will be the speaker of the House. And with all due respect for all members, they represent their district. Their job title and their job description are one and the same, representative. So we respect that. But we also respect the consensus of the House Democrats, again, respecting everybody's point of view, but with enough votes, just win big, baby. And that's the answer to all this. I always had that. Everybody -- I was always fighting. But, nonetheless, we always prevailed and we got our votes and we won, even when we were down to like two- or three-vote majority. So Hakeem will be fine with that. I think that more is made of those differences. Those people are wonderful. They're welcome to Congress, but they're not going to hold up a Democratic agenda to reduce the cost of living, to make sure that people have access to health care and overturn what Trump did to take a trillion dollars out of Medicaid, half-a-trillion out of Medicare, hundreds of billions out of food

36cb11f7cd41.text: Ronna McDaniel served as chairwoman of the Republican National Committee during President Trump’s first term. Now, she’s a surrogate for Mike Rogers’ Senate campaign in Michigan. McDaniel joined Geoff Bennett to discuss the race. Geoff Bennett: And now, for a Republican perspective, we're joined tonight by Ronna McDaniel. She chaired the Republican National Committee for seven years, including throughout President Trump's first term. She's now a campaign surrogate for Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan. And she joins us tonight from Lansing. It's good to see you. Welcome to the "News Hour." Ronna McDaniel: Great to be with you. Thanks for having me. Geoff Bennett: And we should say you chaired the RNC during President Trump's first midterm back in 2018. House Republicans then lost a net total of 41 seats. In your view, how does the political environment right now compare to then, eight years ago? Ronna McDaniel: Well, I would also add that we picked up Senate seats in that first midterm, which was unprecedented to pick up Senate seats in a midterm. Listen, in the first midterm of a sitting president, you typically lose seats in the House or flip a chamber. That's been the precedent for over 100 years. And when I was RNC chair in 2022, we actually flipped the House and won that back for Republicans under Biden. So that's what happens in midterms, and I think this is something that we're seeing this midterm. I do think that the House probably will flip to Democrats this cycle. Geoff Bennett: Let me ask you this, though. As you look across the electorate, where do you see the greatest opportunities for Republicans? What are you watching most closely tonight? Ronna McDaniel: Well, I'm in Michigan, so I'm looking at Mike Rogers. This is a Democrat seat that they have held. We haven't had a Republican in the Senate here since 1994. Mike has run a very good race. He has made inroads in traditionally Democrat constituencies, the Jewish vote, the Black vote. He actually has a whole Democrats for Rogers coalition. And then we saw the endorsement of Haley Stevens, a sitting Democrat congresswoman come out and endorse Mike Rogers. So I think this is a seat that we're looking at very, very closely. Geoff Bennett: And looking nationally, you said recently that Republicans shouldn't be spending hundreds of millions of dollars defending a Texas Senate seat. How did the party find itself fighting for seats that should have been safely Republican? Ronna McDaniel: Well, I don't know if I said they shouldn't be. I said it's concerning to have to spend that much, because that means you're not spending in races where you can pick up, right? Like, if you're spending in a safe -- in a safe seat in a safe state, that takes away resources from potential gains. But, of course, we are battling in red areas right now. I do think we're going to hold the Senate. I do think Texas comes through, Kansas comes through. These are states that Donald Trump won by double digits. And so, while I think we may lose the House, I think the Senate stays in Republican hands. Geoff Bennett: Republicans are asking to give -- asking voters, rather, to give President Trump two more years of unified Republican control. What would Republicans deliver that they haven't already? Ronna McDaniel: Well, the Big Beautiful Bill did provide no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, no tax on Social Security. I think getting out of this Iran war, you will see gas prices go down, which I know is heavy on the minds of many voters across this country. Affordability is a huge issue. And as you see the policies of deregulation come forward, things that Trump has enacted, I think you will see a better economy in the next two years. And he wants to complete that with Republicans. He may not have that opportunity. I hope the Democrats don't go in and just go into lawfare and trying to attack Republicans in retribution, which we have heard our own Senator Elissa Slotkin say is on the agenda for them. I actually hope that we can work together and find ways to help the American people, because that's what they want. Geoff Bennett: President Trump will not be on the ballot again. Is the Republican Party prepared for a political future without him? Ronna McDaniel: I think he will have a lot of say in the nominee for 2028. I -- he's not somebody who fades to the background very easily. The Democrats look like they're going to have something like 20 candidates running for president. I don't think our field has shaped up yet. And I think whoever our nominees are or whoever's running, they're probably going to go and talk to President Trump first, and he will have a lot of impact in that primary because he does have huge sway with our base, specifically in primaries, and we saw that across this cycle as well. Geoff Bennett: President Trump, his approval rating is underwater. His numbers on the economy are even worse. They're in the 20 percent range. When he tells voters to act as if he's on the ballot, is he helping Republicans or hurting them, in your view? Ronna McDaniel: Yes, there are Republicans that just don't turn out, or there are Trump voters that just don't turn out unless he's on the ballot. So him saying that to his voters is key, because we have seen in past midterms -- and I know this personally as former RNC chair -- those Trump voters sit out without his name on the ballot. So those are the people he's talking to. And Republicans are going to need those voters to turn out, traditional Republicans to turn out, and we are certainly going to need independents if we're going to win in states like Michigan, Maine, some of these battleground states. In Kansas and Texas, I think him saying that does mean a lot to those Republican voters because he did win those states by double digits, and that is where he can really help. Geoff Bennett: Ronna McDaniel, former RNC chair, great to have your perspectives as part of our coverage. Thanks for being

365cc6777796.text: On Election Day, candidates, campaigns and analysts are looking for more than the total number of voters. They also want to know who showed up to the polls and what issues were on their minds. Traditional exit polls are evolving as the way people vote has changed. Deema Zein takes a closer look at some of the data behind the election. Geoff Bennett: Well, on this Election Day, candidates and campaigns and all of us watching closely are interested in more than just how many people voted. We want to know who turned out, what motivated them to vote, and which issues mattered most as they cast their ballots. Amna Nawaz: Traditional exit polls are evolving, as the way people vote has changed. Deema Zein takes a closer look at some of the data behind the election. Deema Zein: To know exactly who showed up to the polls and why they voted for a particular candidate, you have to ask the voters. This year, "News Hour" is getting some of that information from the voter poll. It's a new collaboration between the Associated Press and other news outlets to survey voters directly by phone, Internet, and in person. To explain how it works, I'm joined by David Scott, V.P. of election services at the Associated Press. David, thanks for joining us. David Scott: Glad to be here. Deema Zein: So this is a new system this year, joining forces with broadcast networks after about a decade of developing and using your own system to measure the vote. Why? David Scott: We wanted to reach voters where they are. That's the most important thing. So if you're conducting a survey as Americans are casting their ballot, you need to be in all of the places where they cast a ballot. We needed to be able to interview voters who are casting their ballots in person on Election Day. But, at the same time, most Americans vote in advance. And so we look at the voter file and look at who's cast a ballot, and then we try to interview them either online, by mail, by phone. Whatever way that they would like to interact with us once we see that they have cast a ballot, then we're able to interview them, ask them questions about who they voted for and why. Deema Zein: So people are familiar with this term exit poll. This is different. Can we talk a little bit about how exactly? David Scott: Well, part of it is an exit poll, right? We are going to have thousands of people who are out in the 50 states interviewing people as they cast their ballot on Election Day. But we also will interview people before Election Day, because people cast their ballots before Election Day. Really, what we have tried to do with our colleagues at the broadcast networks is design a methodology that reaches Americans. No matter how you cast your ballot, you have the opportunity for us to ask you questions, so we can understand the fullness of the American electorate. Deema Zein: And how many people are you talking to as part of this new process? David Scott: Yes, it's an enormous survey. So, like a normal political poll that you might see in a state about a Senate race might be based on 500 interviews. We're going to aim for somewhere between 80,000 and 100,000 interviews taking place leading up to Election Day and then on Election Day itself. So it's an enormous survey. And it's one of the things that we think is really important, that we're going to have results in every state where there's a statewide election this year. It's not just about the battlegrounds. Deema Zein: What does this help tell you guys at the AP? David Scott: We're looking for insights in the data about who has voted, what they cared about, what issues were resonating. We know which issues each candidate was talking about in a race, and so which ones were most important to voters. We look at the demographics of a state and we look at the demographics of the electorate and see how that matches up. One of the things that we saw in 2024 was some of those demographic shifts that pointed early in the night to success for President Trump. You could see in the data about who was voting that he was poised to have a good night. We were able to get a sense that this is where the election was going, and so those are the types of things that we will be looking at. Deema Zein: David Scott, vice president of election services at the Associated Press, thanks again for joining us. David Scott: Happy to be here.

e1ce6b4c85b2.text: By — Associated Press Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/ap-voter-poll-the-economy-and-the-state-of-democracy-are-voters-top-issues Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter AP Voter Poll: The economy and the state of democracy are voters' top issues Politics Updated on Nov 3, 2026 7:55 PM EST — Published on Nov 3, 2026 6:26 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check Voters overwhelmingly feel frustrated with the way things are going in the U.S. today, according to The AP Voter Poll, which points to a midterm electorate that is deeply unhappy with the country's direction and pessimistic about the future. About three-quarters of voters say they feel "angry" or "dissatisfied" with the country's current trajectory. Only about one-quarter feel "satisfied" or "enthusiastic." Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Dissatisfaction was particularly high in blue states like California and Massachusetts, but even in deep-red states, a majority of voters were at least "dissatisfied." Voters are also displeased with the condition of the economy, with roughly three-quarters saying it is "not so good" or "poor." That's in line with what U.S. adults have said in recent months in AP-NORC polling. The economy and the state of democracy are voters' top issues Voters say the economy and the state of democracy are the top issues facing the country, with high costs and government corruption weighing heavily on many Americans' minds as they cast a ballot in Tuesday's midterm elections. READ MORE: A guide to the key ballot measures voters will decide on Election Day About 4 in 10 U.S. voters nationally say the economy is the most important issue facing the country, as most express concern about gas prices and the cost of groceries. About 3 in 10 say the state of democracy is the top issue. Only about 1 in 10 say the same about immigration or health care, and few name foreign policy or crime. Roughly half of U.S. voters say government corruption and the cost of living are "crucial" to their vote for Congress, much higher than the share who say that about immigration enforcement policies, the war in Iran or AI data centers. Most voters believe Trump's policies have harmed the U.S. economy Relatively few voters have positive things to say about Trump's economic leadership. About two-thirds of U.S. midterm voters say Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions in the U.S., while only about 3 in 10 say they've improved things, The AP Voter Poll found. Similarly, about two-thirds of voters said Trump's tariff policies have hurt the national economy. READ MORE: AP Voter Poll: Voters want Congress to impose more checks on an unpopular president Views of Trump's priorities more broadly — and his capabilities as a leader — are also mostly negative. More than half of voters say Trump is not a strong leader, does not fight for people like them, does not have the right priorities and does not have the mental capability to serve effectively as president. About 6 in 10 voters said Trump places a higher priority on his own personal interests than the country's interests, while about 4 in 10 said he puts more weight on the country's interests. Voters express severe concerns about inflation About 8 in 10 voters say inflation has caused a "severe" or "moderate" financial hardship on their households, according to The AP Voter Poll. The drag caused by prices rising faster than wages over the past year has made it harder for many voters to afford basic essentials such as gasoline, groceries and their utilities. READ MORE: 13 races that will determine control of the Senate The persistent concern is a carryover from the 2024 presidential election when voters specifically tasked Trump to solve the problem, but inflation is now higher than it was when he returned to the White House. More than 8 in 10 voters say they are "very" or "somewhat" concerned about the cost of gas, groceries, utilities and healthcare. Capitalism viewed more positively than socialism The AP Voter Poll found that more than half of voters strongly or somewhat favor the free market principles of capitalism. Only about 3 in 10 feel similarly positive about socialism, in which the government plays a greater role in economic activity. Trump and other Republicans campaigned on the idea that many Democratic candidates with their plans for universal healthcare were socialist. Democrats countered that the Trump administration had taken ownership stakes in dozens of private companies. 41b6eafd4ec4.text: By — Kelvin Chan, Associated Press Kelvin Chan, Associated Press By — Emma Burrows, Associated Press Emma Burrows, Associated Press By — Menelaos Hadjicostis, Associated Press Menelaos Hadjicostis, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/heres-what-to-know-about-another-cyberattack-on-european-supermarket-fridges Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Here's what to know about another cyberattack on European supermarket fridges World Nov 3, 2026 6:01 PM EST LONDON (AP) — Mysterious cyberattacks on European supermarket fridges have sent officials around the continent scrambling to figure out the cold, hard facts. Supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros). READ MORE: Freezers at supermarkets in several European countries hit by apparent cyberattacks, ruining food One Swedish supermarket said its fridges and freezers had been hacked and set to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit). It's a repeat of an earlier incident that struck refrigeration systems in hundreds of supermarkets and independent stores across France, Belgium and the Netherlands. Here's a closer look: What happened and who was affected Supermarkets in at least half a dozen European countries, including Sweden, Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, Italy and Estonia, reported problems on Monday. It wasn't just big chains. The owner of a butcher shop in Athens told private Greek Skai TV Tuesday that someone hacked into the temperature control of a refrigeration unit, raising the temperature to 150 degrees Celsius (302 degrees Fahrenheit). George Boubas said his employees who start their shift at 4 a.m. at the shop in the Kifisia suburb first noticed the problem. It took a technician two hours to wrest back control of the unit's temperature settings, although the meat products weren't affected, he said. Boubas said the technician told him that an area supermarket and a fast-food restaurant experienced the same issue. He said they resorted to switching off the Wi-Fi connection to the refrigeration units to restrict outside access. Experts said the cyberattacks were a reminder of the risks that come as more things get connected to the internet. "This attack is a wake-up call. We have filled our homes and shops with devices that are really small computers, yet we still treat them like ordinary appliances," said Katerina Mitrokotsa, a cybersecurity professor at the University of St. Gallen, in Switzerland. "A fridge doesn't look like a security risk, and that's exactly why attackers like it." Fridges are connected to save money and cut waste The cyberattack mirrors one that happened weeks earlier that affected mainly French and Dutch retailers. French cybersecurity investigators blamed problems with outdated remote control modules made by Danish company Danfoss as well as U.S.-based Copeland. Danfoss said most affected systems were older products that no longer received software or security updates, while Copeland identified a vulnerability in discontinued controllers. "Supermarkets connect their fridges so they can monitor temperatures around the clock across hundreds of stores, get alerts before food spoils, cut energy costs and let technicians fix faults remotely," Mitrokotsa said. "This saves money and reduces food waste, but every connected fridge is also an entry point that needs to be secured like any other IT system." Experts said many businesses are rushing to embrace trendy new technology while neglecting the vast network of connections that they rely on for their daily operations, from payment and ordering systems to warehouses, refrigeration and other building controls. "Organizations are pouring budget into AI and digital transformation while the systems that keep food cold, water clean, and lights on often run on hardware that has not been funded since installation," said Nicole Carignan, senior vice president of security and AI strategy at cybersecurity company Darktrace. "Nobody broke into these refrigeration systems with a zero-day," she said, using a term for a flaw that has gone undetected by the system's creators and security reviews. "They got in through internet-facing controllers, end-of-life firmware, and default passwords. That is technical debt coming due." British cybersecurity officials on Tuesday shed little light on the latest attack, while pointing to what they called "legacy technology." "The cyberattack on French supermarkets was a result of exploitation of known vulnerabilities," U.K. cyber minister Liz Lloyd said in a speech. "It's a clear demonstration that poor cyber hygiene, like weak passwords, continues to put organizations at risk." READ MORE: Cyberattacks disrupt refrigeration systems at European supermarkets Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center, told reporters the French fridges were "connected directly to the internet with default passwords." A team from the center issued warnings and worked through Monday night contacting organizations that had "vulnerable technology exposed," he said. No evidence so far that AI was involved Advanced artificial intelligence systems from companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have come under fire recently after a string of revelations that they hacked into organizations while evading human control. Experts, however, said Tuesday that they didn't think these attacks were powered by AI. "There is no evidence AI was used, and the techniques did not require it," said Carignan. "I think the key element of that is that this wasn't an AI attack" said Paul Chichester, director of operations at the U.K. cyber center. "This is using vulnerabilities that absolutely have been out there for a long period of time. And that's where we really need to sort of focus on." Who's behind it and what'

There is a "terrifying prospect" of more UK wildfires in future due to climate change and preparation will be "crucial", the Prince of Wales has said.
Visiting Treherbert in Rhondda Cynon Taf, which was threatened by a huge mountain fire in August, Prince William praised a "gargantuan" effort to save homes, land and lives.
"We need to start taking wildfires as seriously as the continent has done," he said, raising issues such as a lack of firefighting aircraft.
He also suggested the community's response to the incident was an example for others to follow, after locals rallied around to support those fighting the flames.
The hillside, just metres away from the community centre where Prince William met fire crews, military personnel and local volunteers is burnt black.
"You looked up [and] the mountain was alight - it was like lava," explained Kath Edwards, managing director of charity Valleys Kids, which runs the building.
"I genuinely thought we were going to lose the centre - but more importantly people were going to lose their homes.
"You never think this is going to come literally to your door and that's what it was - it was just crazy."
South Wales Fire and Rescue Service (SWFRS) declared a major incident as it was forced to respond to 14 wildfires at the same time in August, including the one above Treherbert.
Support was drafted in from 22 other UK fire services while soldiers were deployed to dig fire breaks and help supply 2.1 million litres of water to douse the flames, including 200 members of the Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment.
Aled Bound, who is crew manager at Maesteg fire station and a retained - on-call - firefighter at Treorchy told Prince William it was "the hardest wildfire season" he and his colleagues had ever dealt with.
Months of record-breaking heat and dry conditions sparked a wave of wildfires across the UK through spring and summer.
He described it was "mentally and physically draining".
"I've never had to take so much water up a mountain to put on a fire and still come back the next day because that fire has relit, because it's so deep-seated," Bound said.
With climate change, he warned it "could well be a sign of what's to come".
Figures from the National Fire Chiefs Council show a new all-time high for recorded significant wildfires - 1,350 across England and Wales, up by more than 300 on 2025 and more than 1,000 on 2024.
Prince William told firefighters that 2026 was the first summer "where I've felt generally worried about the scale of the wildfires in the country".
He added: "We might go again next season... it's quite a terrifying prospect if we're not... on the ball."
He asked about availability of firefighting aircraft, noting that "the need for aerial assets has been hoisted quite high up in government" as an area "we're lacking".
The prince served a three-year tour flying Sea King helicopters with the Search and Rescue team at RAF Valley on Anglesey between 2010 and 2013, qualifying as a captain.
He recalled flying water bowsers in the Falklands "putting out range fires... and once the Sea King went, we don't have the assets any more".
"I think it's front and centre of many people's minds now, how do we recreate that."
Conversation turned to the kit available to fire crews working in unbearable heat, proactive land management practices and whether social media firms could do more to discourage people from setting fires.
Recently, the UK government announced that the RAF's Chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft, external would be equipped to fight fires in future.
A separate Welsh government wildfire summit also led to promises of action to improve preparedness, external.
"It feels like this is something we're going to have to live with as a country or as a world now every summer," Prince William said.
"It's fair to say that we've learnt a lot from this season... and there's lots that we'll be putting into place, particularly following the wildfire summits," said Adam Openshaw, deputy chief fire officer for SWFRS.
He described the response of people in Treherbert as "the best demonstration of the community coming together to support the wildfire response".
He said it really helped as fire crews worked "tirelessly" in "challenging circumstances".
Edwards explained that volunteers kept the community centre open 24 hours a day from the Saturday evening of the fire until the following Thursday "to provide whatever service we could".
Due to the unprecedented nature of the fire, the centre became a control hub for the firefighting operation, a place to rest and regroup and a focal point for people wanting to show their support.
Businesses donated food - "40 pizzas arrived within the first 20 minutes" - and there were regular visits from an ice cream van.
Prince William asked whether volunteers should be used more in future and was told the community's efforts, hand in hand with military support, enabled the fire service to focus on bringing the incident under control.
"From something really quite horrific, the valleys did what the valleys do very, very well - we pulled together to make a difference," Edwards said.
Communities in the south Wales valleys were already experiencing the effects of climate change, she warned.
"We've had floods, fires... we've got [coal] tips that move as well.
"I think the message I was keen to get across is... we are motivated as a community to ask how do we solve this?
"How can we work together as a community and voluntary sector to support agencies [like the fire service]?"

A new satellite tracking system finds that the United States has lost 350,000 acres of forest land per year—a rate of approximately one football field every two minutes—which is the equivalent of 2.3 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions through the release of stored CO2 in the forests and lost potential carbon storage.
Researchers at Clark University in Massachusetts announced the initial findings of the U.S. Forest Monitor tool Thursday, tracking “persistent” forest loss in the lower 48 states and showing 9.8 million acres of forest land was lost to development or agriculture from 1990 to 2017.
Lead author Christopher Williams said the tool establishes an important historical baseline for tracking land use changes across the country and shows the need for more consistent monitoring of forest loss nationwide.
“When we think about forest loss and conversion, our minds often go to the Amazon or other tropical locations,” Williams said in an interview with Inside Climate News. “What this study shows is that forest loss is something that’s happening in the United States as well, and in our own backyards, and that it deserves our attention.”
The tool relies on land cover time-series imaging from the U.S. Geological Survey, identifying land that was previously forest but had been used for development or agriculture for at least five years. Williams said the researchers focused on those two segments because the resulting forest loss is often permanent and won’t revert back to forest for decades, if ever.
“It’s very rare, I would say, for us to see from the land cover dataset that a pixel goes from forest to development and then back to forest, or from forest to cropland and back to forest,” Williams said. “That’s unusual, but we just wanted to be really careful.”
Williams said the researchers are working to update the findings and hope to publish data through 2024 within the next year or so.
The monitor is funded and maintained by the Forest Carbon Data Partnership, a collaboration of conservation and academic organizations including the Open Space Institute, The Nature Conservancy, American Forests, the Trust for Public Land, the Land Trust Alliance and Clark University.
Williams said roughly half of the documented forest loss was for development and half was for cropland, a surprise to some of the researchers.
“I think at least some of our colleagues had expected most of it would be for development, you know, subdivisions and urban expansion and so forth,” Williams said. “But we actually still are converting a lot of our forest land to croplands.”
The report finds forest loss has been particularly dramatic in the Southeast.
The 11 states showing the most forest loss—Georgia, Texas, North Carolina, Florida, Arkansas, Alabama, Virginia, Mississippi, Missouri, South Carolina and Tennessee—accounted for approximately 70 percent of the total losses, but in different ways.
In Alabama, the sixth state in terms of forest loss, 79 percent of the forest lost was converted to cropland, while development accounted for 21 percent.
In Texas and South Carolina, nearly 60 percent of identified forest loss was for development.
Georgia was the most heavily deforested state, according to the report, both by total loss (almost 1.2 million acres) and percentage of total forest lost (4.4 percent) during the study period.
The 9.8 million acres lost nationwide represents about 2 percent of the total U.S. forestland over 28 years.

b3b3ac799e1e.text: By — Sophie Austin, Associated Press Sophie Austin, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-and-the-high-cost-of-living-loom-over-california-governors-race-between-becerra-and-hilton Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Trump and the high cost of living loom over California governor's race between Becerra and Hilton Politics Nov 3, 2026 5:51 PM EST 2026 ELECTION COVERAGE: Watch Live | Poll Closing Times | All Live Results | Live Updates | Live Fact Check SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — President Donald Trump, California's notoriously high cost of living and political experience are on the ballot as voters decide Tuesday whether to elect Democrat Xavier Becerra or Republican Steve Hilton as the next governor of the nation's most populous state. WATCH LIVE: Election night 2026 PBS News special coverage The winner will succeed Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, who can't seek a third term but is considering a White House run. Becerra, a former state attorney general, has promised to reaffirm California's status as a liberal counterweight to the Trump administration's Republican policies. Hilton, a former political adviser in the United Kingdom and Fox News host, has pitched himself as a fresh face ready to set the state back on track after 15 years of Democratic leadership. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News Hilton faces steep odds. Democrats make up roughly 45% of registered voters in California, compared to Republicans' 25%. Mail voting has been underway for nearly a month. The Trump administration has sought to sow distrust in the state's election system by alleging up to 20,000 noncitizens could be registered to vote. The Department of Justice has sued the state in an attempt to stop officials from counting any ballots cast by those people. The U.S. Supreme Court rejected the Trump administration's demand on Monday after several lower courts also sided with California. State and local election officials say they follow federal law and the federal government's numbers are likely inflated. Election experts say voting by noncitizens is rare and has not been shown to change the outcome of elections. Candidates argue over the value of experience Becerra, who also served in Congress and as U.S. health secretary in President Joe Biden's administration, has argued that he's best positioned for the job as someone with more than 35 years of experience in politics and government. Hilton has never held elected office. Becerra said at a CNN debate in September that the state needed a leader who could keep the "California dream" alive. "You can't do it with someone who's never served, who's never balanced a budget the size of California, who's never actually been there to defend people against the tyrant like Donald Trump," he said. Meanwhile, Hilton has tried to turn his lack of political experience into an asset, arguing the more experienced Democrats who have been in charge have left Californians struggling to afford gas, housing and a college degree. READ MORE: What to look for on Election Day as questions loom over Trump "This is the most amazing state and the most amazing country on Earth, and it's because we've got this rebel spirit," he said at the debate. "That spirit is being crushed by this bloated, nanny-state bureaucratic government that Xavier has been a part of for 36 years." A chaotic primary gave way to a low-key general election matchup The two candidates emerged from a large primary field with half a dozen prominent Democrats and two notable Republicans. Becerra wasn't considered a top contender for the first months of his campaign. That changed when former Democratic Rep. Eric Swalwell, who had been viewed as a front-runner, dropped out of the race and resigned from Congress following allegations he sexually assaulted several women. He's denied the accusations. His departure caused the party establishment and voters to look for a more reliable alternative, and they found one in Becerra. Since then, Becerra has run a relatively low-key campaign, not holding nearly as many public events or press availabilities as Hilton. He's sought to take advantage of Trump's deep unpopularity in the state by tying Hilton to Trump, noting the president has endorsed the Republican. Becerra's campaign launched a website that lists quotes of Hilton expressing support for the president and his policies. The site includes illustrations of the two Republicans standing side by side. Hilton, meanwhile, has tried to break through by releasing splashy ads, sometimes with AI-generated content, to encourage voters who typically choose Democrats to try something new. He's also tried to appeal to the public by making ambitious promises, including pledging to abolish the DMV and cut gas prices to $3 a gallon, a rate the state hasn't seen in years. Richard Hartman, an independent voter living outside Sacramento who works in the construction industry, said he was leaning toward voting for Hilton to bring balance to the Democrat-dominated state. 110169c6461f.text: Voters in Minneapolis and Houston are among those leaving "I Voted" stickers at memorials for people killed by federal immigration agents. Why it matters: The tributes highlight how the Trump administration's unpopular immigration crackdown is motivating voters this election cycle. Zoom in: In Minneapolis , people are placing stickers on memorials for Alex Pretti , an ICU nurse, and Renee Good , a writer and mother, who were killed by federal agents in January. In Houston , voters have covered a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo , a construction worker and father who was fatally shot by ICE agents in July, with stickers and handwritten messages like "I voted for you" and "Por usted" — "for you" in Spanish. A voter places an "I Voted" sticker on a memorial for Lorenzo Salgado Araujo. Photo: Mark Felix/Bloomberg via Getty Images Ronaldo Salgado, Araujo's oldest son, placed his sticker on his father's memorial in the first week of early voting and hundreds followed him, the Houston Chronicle reports . "I am beyond touched that this community and that the entire city is voting with my dad in mind ... I didn't realize it would grow this big," he told the Washington Post. The big picture: These midterms are testing whether President Trump's 2024 gains with Latino voters have lasted. National polls in the lead-up to Election Day showed Latino voters swinging back toward Democrats , with immigration as a key area of disagreement with the administration. In an October NBC News/Telemundo poll , 67% of Latino voters said Trump's enforcement has gone too far, 31% said they or someone close now carries ID because of ICE concerns, and 27% know someone detained or deported. 726e024249ae.text: By — Suman Naishadham, Associated Press Suman Naishadham, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/spains-transport-minister-steps-down-6-days-after-high-speed-train-crash-that-killed-69-people Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Spain's transport minister steps down 6 days after high-speed train crash that killed 69 people World Nov 3, 2026 5:27 PM EST MADRID (AP) — Spain's Transport Minister Óscar Puente announced Tuesday that he is stepping down, six days after a high-speed train collision south of Madrid killed 69 people. WATCH: Shock, anger and mourning in Spain after 2nd major train crash this year He made the announcement at the end of an hourslong appearance before lawmakers about the crash — the second such deadly collision this year involving Spain's extensive high-speed rail network. "A transport minister in a country like Spain cannot remain in office after two accidents of this seriousness in less than a year," Puente said. The Oct. 28 crash took place when a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks. The chain of events that led to disaster started when the communication system key to the functioning of the security system on the Madrid-Seville line went down. Central controllers in Madrid took over and gave the go-ahead for a state-operated Renfe high-speed train to proceed, even though there was a stationary train ahead operated by the company Iryo. It was the second major crash on the Madrid-Seville line this year. In January, more than two hours further south along the route, a train derailed and struck another traveling in the opposite direction, killing 46 people. That crash remains under investigation. Puente said he had taken the decision to resign immediately after the deadly crash, but had not made it public. The collisions have raised fresh concerns about the safety of the country's rail network, and the most recent crash came four weeks before a national election. Spain's high-speed rail network has been considered one of the country's crowning achievements. It is the world's second-largest, after China's. Until this year, it had not experienced a deadly crash since coming into service over three decades ago. Earlier Tuesday, Puente announced safety measures the government would implement on the rail network, including improving conditions in control centers and pushing for a faster rollout of the standardized European Rail Traffic Management System for safety and signaling.
